senses.d: A syllable applied to the fourth tone of the diatonic scale in solmization.
The tone F.
A Feigned story or tale, intended to instruct or amuse; a fictitious narration intended to enforce some useful truth or precept; an apologue. See the Note under Apologue.
q: Jotham's fable of the trees is the oldest extant.

senses.d: The plot, story, or connected series of events, forming the subject of an epic or dramatic poem.
q: The moral is the first business of the poet; this being formed, he contrives such a design or fable as may be most suitable to the moral.

senses.d: Any story told to excite wonder; common talk; the theme of talk.
q: We grew The fable of the city where we dwelt.

senses.d: Fiction; untruth; falsehood.
q: It would look like a fable to report that this gentleman gives away a great fortune by secret methods.

Fable.etym: [F., fr. L. fabula, fr. fari to speak, say. See Ban, and cf. Fabulous, Fame.]

senses.d: To compose fables; hence, to write or speak fiction ; to write or utter what is not true.
q: Vain now the tales which fabling poets tell.
He fables, yet speaks truth.

senses.d: To feign; to invent; to devise, and speak of, as true or real; to tell of falsely.
q: The hell thou fablest.

senses.d: A large ornamental letter used, esp. by the early printers, at the commencement of the chapters and other divisions of a book.

The exterior form or appearance of anything; that part which presents itself to the view; especially, the front or upper part or surface; that which particularly offers itself to the view of a spectator.
q: A mist . . . watered the whole face of the ground.
Lake Leman wooes me with its crystal face.

senses.d: That part of a body, having several sides, which may be seen from one point, or which is presented toward a certain direction; one of the bounding planes of a solid; as, a cube has six faces.
The principal dressed surface of a plate, disk, or pulley; the principal flat surface of a part or object.
The upper surface, or the character upon the surface, of a type, plate, etc.
Outside appearance; surface show; look; external aspect, whether natural, assumed, or acquired.
q: To set a face upon their own malignant design.
This would produce a new face of things in Europe.
We wear a face of joy, because We have been glad of yore.

senses.d: That part of the head, esp. of man, in which the eyes, cheeks, nose, and mouth are situated; visage; countenance.
q: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.

senses.d: Cast of features; expression of countenance; look; air; appearance.
q: We set the best faceon it we could.

senses.d: Ten degrees in extent of a sign of the zodiac.
Maintenance of the countenance free from abashment or confusion; confidence; boldness; shamelessness; effrontery.
q: This is the man that has the face to charge others with false citations.

senses.d: Presence; sight; front; as in the phrases, before the face of, in the immediate presence of; in the face of, before, in, or against the front of; as, to fly in the face of danger; to the face of, directly to; from the face of, from the presence of.
Mode of regard, whether favorable or unfavorable; favor or anger; mostly in Scriptural phrases.
q: The Lord make his face to shine upon thee.
My face will I turn also from them.

senses.d: The end or wall of the tunnel, drift, or excavation, at which work is progressing or was last done.

Face.etym: [F., from L. facies form, shape, face, perh. from facere to make (see Fact); or perh. orig. meaning appearance, and from a root meaning to shine, and akin to E. fancy. Cf. Facetious.]

senses.d: To meet in front; to oppose with firmness; to resist, or to meet for the purpose of stopping or opposing; to confront; to encounter; as, to face an enemy in the field of battle.
q: I'll face This tempest, and deserve the name of king.

senses.d: To Confront impudently; to bully.
q: I will neither be facednor braved.

senses.d: To stand opposite to; to stand with the face or front toward; to front upon; as, the apartments of the general faced the park.
q: He gained also with his forces that part of Britain which faces Ireland.

senses.d: To cover in front, for ornament, protection, etc.; to put a facing upon; as, a building faced with marble.
To line near the edge, esp. with a different material; as, to face the front of a coat, or the bottom of a dress.
To cover with better, or better appearing, material than the mass consists of, for purpose of deception, as the surface of a box of tea, a barrel of sugar, etc.

To make the surface of (anything) flat or smooth; to dress the face of (a stone, a casting, etc.); esp., in turning, to shape or smooth the flat surface of, as distinguished from the cylindrical surface.
To cause to turn or present a face or front, as in a particular direction.
To carry a false appearance; to play the hypocrite.
To turn the face; as, to face to the right or left.
q: Face about, man; a soldier, and afraid!

senses.d: To present a face or front.
A hobby ; freak; whim.
q: It is your favorite fad to draw plans.

senses.d: Weak; insipid; tasteless; commonplace.
q: His masculine taste gave him a sense of something fade and ludicrous.

Fade.etym: [F., prob. fr. L. vapidus vapid, or possibly fr,fatuus foolish, insipid.]

senses.d: To become fade; to grow weak; to lose strength; to decay; to perish gradually; to wither, as a plant.
q: The earth mourneth and fadeth away.

senses.d: To lose freshness, color, or brightness; to become faint in hue or tint; hence, to be wanting in color.
To sink away; to disappear gradually; to grow dim; to vanish.
q: The stars shall fade away.
He makes a swanlike end, Fading in music.

Fade.etym: [OE. faden, vaden, prob. fr. fade, a.; cf. Prov. D. vadden to fade, wither, vaddigh languid, torpid. Cf. Fade, a., Vade.]

senses.d: To cause to wither; to deprive of freshness or vigor; to wear away.
q: No winter could his laurels fade.

senses.d: Losing freshness, color, brightness, or vigor.
Loss of color, freshness, or vigor.
An Irish dance; also, the burden of a song.

To be wanting; to fall short; to be or become deficient in any measure or degree up to total absence; to cease to be furnished in the usual or expected manner, or to be altogether cut off from supply; to be lacking; as, streams fail; crops fail.
q: As the waters fail from the sea.
Till Lionel's issue fails, his should not reign.

senses.d: To be affected with want; to come short; to lack; to be deficient or unprovided; — used with of.
q: If ever they fail of beauty, this failure is not be attributed to their size.

senses.d: To fall away; to become diminished; to decline; to decay; to sink.
q: When earnestly they seek Such proof, conclude they then begin to fail.

senses.d: To deteriorate in respect to vigor, activity, resources, etc.; to become weaker; as, a sick man fails.
To perish; to die; — used of a person.
q: Had the king in his last sickness failed.

senses.d: To be found wanting with respect to an action or a duty to be performed, a result to be secured, etc.; to miss; not to fulfill expectation.
q: Take heed now that ye fail not to do this.
Either my eyesight fails, or thou look'st pale.

senses.d: To come short of a result or object aimed at or desired ; to be baffled or frusrated.
q: Our envious foe hath failed.

senses.d: To err in judgment; to be mistaken.
q: Which ofttimes may succeed, so as perhaps Shall grieve him, if I fail not.

senses.d: To become unable to meet one's engagements; especially, to be unable to pay one's debts or discharge one's business obligation; to become bankrupt or insolvent.

Fail.etym: [F. failir, fr. L. fallere, falsum, to deceive, akin to E. fall. See Fail, and cf. Fallacy, False, Fault.]

senses.d: To be wanting to ; to be insufficient for; to disappoint; to desert.
q: There shall not fail thee a man on the throne.

senses.d: To miss of attaining; to lose.
q: Though that seat of earthly bliss be failed.

senses.d: Miscarriage; failure; deficiency; fault; — mostly superseded by failure or failing, except in the phrase without fail.
Death; decease.

Fail.etym: [OF. faille, from failir. See Fail, v. i.]

senses.d: A failing short; a becoming deficient; failure; deficiency; imperfection; weakness; lapse; fault; infirmity; as, a mental failing.
q: And ever in her mind she cast about For that unnoticed failing in herself.

senses.d: The act of becoming insolvent of bankrupt.
Well-pleased; glad; apt; wont; fond; inclined.
q: Men and birds are fain of climbing high.
To a busy man, temptation is fainto climb up together with his business.

senses.d: Satisfied; contented; also, constrained.
q: The learned Castalio was fain to make trechers at Basle to keep himself from starving.

Fain.etym: [OE. fain, fagen, AS. fægen; akin to OS. fagan, Icel. faginn glad; AS. fægnian to rejoice, OS. faganōn, Icel. fagna, Goth. faginōn, cf. Goth. fahēds joy; and fr. the same root as E. fair. Srr Fair, a., and cf. Fawn to court favor.]

senses.d: With joy; gladly; — with wold.
q: He would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat.
Fain Would I woo her, yet I dare not.

senses.d: To be glad ; to wish or desire.
q: Whoso fair thing does fain to see.

senses.d: Lacking strength; weak; languid; inclined to swoon; as, faint with fatigue, hunger, or thirst.
Wanting in courage, spirit, or energy; timorous; cowardly; dejected; depressed; as, “Faint heart ne'er won fair lady.”
Lacking distinctness; hardly perceptible; striking the senses feebly; not bright, or loud, or sharp, or forcible; weak; as, a faint color, or sound.
Performed, done, or acted, in a weak or feeble manner; not exhibiting vigor, strength, or energy; slight; as, faint efforts; faint resistance.
q: The faint prosecution of the war.

Faint.etym: [OE. feint, faint, false, faint, F. feint, p. p. of feindre to feign, suppose, hesitate. See Feign, and cf. Feint.]

senses.d: The act of fainting, or the state of one who has fainted; a swoon. See Fainting, n.
q: The saint, Who propped the Virgin in her faint.

senses.d: To become weak or wanting in vigor; to grow feeble; to lose strength and color, and the control of the bodily or mental functions; to swoon; — sometimes with away. See Fainting, n.
q: Hearing the honor intended her, she fainted away.
If I send them away fasting . . . they will faint by the way.

senses.d: To sink into dejection; to lose courage or spirit; to become depressed or despondent.
q: If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small.

senses.d: To decay; to disappear; to vanish.
q: Gilded clouds, while we gaze upon them, faint before the eye.

senses.d: To cause to faint or become dispirited; to depress; to weaken.
q: It faints me to think what follows.

senses.d: The state of being faint; loss of strength, or of consciousness, and self-control.
Want of vigor or energy.
Feebleness, as of color or light; lack of distinctness; as, faintness of description.
Faint-heartedness; timorousness; dejection.
q: I will send a faintness into their hearts.

senses.d: Free from spots, specks, dirt, or imperfection; unblemished; clean; pure.
q: A fair white linen cloth.

senses.d: Pleasing to the eye; handsome; beautiful.
q: Who can not see many a fair French city, for one fair French made.

senses.d: Without a dark hue; light; clear; as, a fair skin.
q: The northern people large and fair-complexioned.

senses.d: Not overcast; cloudless; clear; pleasant; propitious; favorable; — said of the sky, weather, or wind, etc.; as, a fair sky; a fair day.
q: You wish fair winds may waft him over.

senses.d: Free from obstacles or hindrances; unobstructed; unincumbered; open; direct; — said of a road, passage, etc.; as, a fair mark; in fair sight; a fair view.
q: The caliphs obtained a mighty empire, which was in a fair way to have enlarged.

senses.d: Without sudden change of direction or curvature; smooth; flowing; — said of the figure of a vessel, and of surfaces, water lines, and other lines.

Characterized by frankness, honesty, impartiality, or candor; open; upright; free from suspicion or bias; equitable; just; — said of persons, character, or conduct; as, a fair man; fair dealing; a fair statement.
Pleasing; favorable; inspiring hope and confidence; — said of words, promises, etc.
q: When fair words and good counsel will not prevail on us, we must be frighted into our duty.

senses.d: Distinct; legible; as, fair handwriting.
Free from any marked characteristic; average; middling; so-so; as, a fair specimen.
q: The news is very fair and good, my lord.

Fair.syn: Candid; open; frank; ingenuous; clear; honest; equitable; impartial; reasonable. See Candid.
Fair.etym: [OE. fair, fayer, fager, AS. fæger; akin to OS. & OHG. fagar, Icel. fagr, Sw. fager, Dan. faver, Goth. fagrs fit, also to E. fay, G. fügen, to fit. fegen to sweep, cleanse, and prob. also to E. fang, peace, pact, Cf. Fang, Fain, Fay to fit.]

senses.d: Clearly; openly; frankly; civilly; honestly; favorably; auspiciously; agreeably.
Fairness, beauty.
A fair woman; a sweetheart.
q: I have found out a gift for my fair.

senses.d: Good fortune; good luck.
q: Now fair befall thee !

senses.d: To make fair or beautiful.
q: Fairing the foul.

senses.d: To make smooth and flowing, as a vessel's lines.
A gathering of buyers and sellers, assembled at a particular place with their merchandise at a stated or regular season, or by special appointment, for trade.
A festival, and sale of fancy articles. erc., usually for some charitable object; as, a Grand Army fair.
A competitive exhibition of wares, farm products, etc., not primarily for purposes of sale; as, the Mechanics' fair; an agricultural fair.

Fair.etym: [OE. feire, OF. feire, F. foire, fr. L. fariae, pl., days of rest, holidays, festivals, akin to festus festal. See Feast.]

senses.d: Belief; the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another, resting solely and implicitly on his authority and veracity; reliance on testimony.

The assent of the mind to the statement or proposition of another, on the ground of the manifest truth of what he utters; firm and earnest belief, on probable evidence of any kind, especially in regard to important moral truth.
q: Faith, that is, fidelity, — the fealty of the finite will and understanding to the reason.

senses.d: The belief in the historic truthfulness of the Scripture narrative, and the supernatural origin of its teachings, sometimes called historical and speculative faith.
q: Without faith it is impossible to please him .
The faith of the gospel is that emotion of the mind which is called “trust” or “confidence” exercised toward the moral character of God, and particularly of the Savior.
Faith is an affectionate, practical confidence in the testimony of God.

senses.d: That which is believed on any subject, whether in science, politics, or religion; especially (Theol.), a system of religious belief of any kind; as, the Jewish or Mohammedan faith; and especially, the system of truth taught by Christ; as, the Christian faith; also, the creed or belief of a Christian society or church.
q: Which to believe of her, Must be a faith that reason without miracle Could never plant in me.
Now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed.

senses.d: Fidelity to one's promises, or allegiance to duty, or to a person honored and beloved; loyalty.
q: Children in whom is no faith.
Whose failing, while her faith to me remains, I should conceal.

senses.d: Word or honor pledged; promise given; fidelity; as, he violated his faith.
q: For you alone I broke me faith with injured Palamon.

senses.d: Credibility or truth.
q: The faith of the foregoing narrative.

Faith.etym: [OE. feith, fayth, fay, OF. feid, feit, fei, F. foi, fr. L. fides; akin to fidere to trust, Gr. πείθειν to persuade. The ending th is perhaps due to the influence of such words as truth, health, wealth. See Bid, Bide, and cf. Confide, Defy, Fealty.]

senses.d: By my faith; in truth; verily.
Full of faith, or having faith; disposed to believe, especially in the declarations and promises of God.
q: You are not faithful, sir.

senses.d: Firm in adherence to promises, oaths, contracts, treaties, or other engagements.
q: The faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him.

senses.d: True and constant in affection or allegiance to a person to whom one is bound by a vow, by ties of love, gratitude, or honor, as to a husband, a prince, a friend; firm in the observance of duty; loyal; of true fidelity; as, a faithful husband or servant.
q: So spake the seraph Abdiel, faithful found, Among the faithless, faithful only he.

senses.d: Worthy of confidence and belief; conformable to truth ot fact; exact; accurate; as, a faithful narrative or representation.
q: It is a faithful saying.

Faithful.syn: Trusty; honest; upright; sincere; veracious; trustworthy.

senses.d: Not believing; not giving credit.
q: Be not faithless, but believing.

senses.d: Not believing on God or religion; specifically, not believing in the Christian religion.
Not observant of promises or covenants.
Not true to allegiance, duty, or vows; perfidious; trecherous; disloyal; not of true fidelity; inconstant, as a husband or a wife.
q: A most unnatural and faithless service.

senses.d: Serving to disappoint or deceive; delusive; unsatisfying.
To Descend, either suddenly or gradually; particularly, to descend by the force of gravity; to drop; to sink; as, the apple falls; the tide falls; the mercury falls in the barometer.
q: I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven.

senses.d: To cease to be erect; to take suddenly a recumbent posture; to become prostrate; to drop; as, a child totters and falls; a tree falls; a worshiper falls on his knees.
q: I fell at his feet to worship him.

senses.d: To find a final outlet; to discharge its waters; to empty; — with into; as, the river Rhone falls into the Mediterranean.
To become prostrate and dead; to die; especially, to die by violence, as in battle.
q: A thousand shall fall at thy side.
He rushed into the field, and, foremost fighting, fell.

senses.d: To cease to be active or strong; to die away; to lose strength; to subside; to become less intense; as, the wind falls.
To issue forth into life; to be brought forth; — said of the young of certain animals.

To decline in power, glory, wealth, or importance; to become insignificant; to lose rank or position; to decline in weight, value, price etc.; to become less; as, the price falls; stocks fell two points.
q: I am a poor fallen man, unworthy now To be thy lord and master.
The greatness of these Irish lords suddenly fell and vanished.

senses.d: To be overthrown or captured; to be destroyed.
q: Heaven and earth will witness, If Rome must fall, that we are innocent.

senses.d: To descend in character or reputation; to become degraded; to sink into vice, error, or sin; to depart from the faith; to apostatize; to sin.
q: Let us labor therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief.

senses.d: To become insnared or embarrassed; to be entrapped; to be worse off than before; as, to fall into error; to fall into difficulties.
To assume a look of shame or disappointment; to become or appear dejected; — said of the countenance.
q: Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.
I have observed of late thy looks are fallen.

senses.d: To sink; to languish; to become feeble or faint; as, our spirits rise and fall with our fortunes.

Fall.etym: [AS. feallan; akin to D. vallen, OS. & OHG. fallan, G. fallen, Icel. Falla, Sw. falla, Dan. falde, Lith. pulti, L. fallere to deceive, Gr. σφάλλειν to cause to fall, Skr. sphal, sphul, to tremble. Cf. Fail, Fell, v. t., to cause to fall.]

senses.d: To let fall; to drop.
q: For every tear he falls, a Trojan bleeds.

senses.d: To sink; to depress; as, to fall the voice.
To diminish; to lessen or lower.
q: Upon lessening interest to four per cent, you fall the price of your native commodities.

senses.d: To bring forth; as, to fall lambs.
To fell; to cut down; as, to fall a tree.
The act of falling; a dropping or descending be the force of gravity; descent; as, a fall from a horse, or from the yard of ship.
The act of dropping or tumbling from an erect posture; as, he was walking on ice, and had a fall.
Death; destruction; overthrow; ruin.
q: They thy fall conspire.
Pride goeth before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.

senses.d: Downfall; degradation; loss of greatness or office; termination of greatness, power, or dominion; ruin; overthrow; as, the fall of the Roman empire.
q: Beholds thee glorious only in thy fall.

senses.d: The surrender of a besieged fortress or town ; as, the fall of Sebastopol.
Diminution or decrease in price or value; depreciation; as, the fall of prices; the fall of rents.
A sinking of tone; cadence; as, the fall of the voice at the close of a sentence.
Declivity; the descent of land or a hill; a slope.
Descent of water; a cascade; a cataract; a rush of water down a precipice or steep; — usually in the plural, sometimes in the singular; as, the falls of Niagara.
The discharge of a river or current of water into the ocean, or into a lake or pond; as, the fall of the Po into the Gulf of Venice.
Extent of descent; the distance which anything falls; as, the water of a stream has a fall of five feet.
The season when leaves fall from trees; autumn.
q: What crowds of patients the town doctor kills, Or how, last fall, he raised the weekly bills.

senses.d: Dropped; prostrate; degraded; ruined; decreased; dead.
q: Some ruined temple or fallen monument.

senses.d: from Fall, v. i.
Pale red or pale yellow; as, a fallow deer or greyhound.
Left untilled or unsowed after plowing; uncultivated; as, fallow ground.

Fallow.etym: [AS. fealu, fealo, pale yellow or red; akin to D. vaal fallow, faded, OHG. falo, G. falb, fahl, Icel. fölr, and prob. to Lith. palvas, OSlav. plavŭ white, L. pallidus pale, pallere to be pale, Gr. πολιόσ gray, Skr. palita. Cf. Pale, Favel, a., Favor.]

senses.d: Plowed land.
q: Who . . . pricketh his blind horse over the fallows.

senses.d: Land that has lain a year or more untilled or unseeded; land plowed without being sowed for the season.
q: The plowing of fallows is a benefit to land.

senses.d: The plowing or tilling of land, without sowing it for a season; as, summer fallow, properly conducted, has ever been found a sure method of destroying weeds.
q: Be a complete summer fallow, land is rendered tender and mellow. The fallow gives it a better tilth than can be given by a fallow crop.

Fallow.etym: [So called from the fallow, or somewhat yellow, color of naked ground; or perh. akin to E. felly, n., cf. MHG. valgen to plow up, OHG. felga felly, harrow.]

senses.d: To plow, harrow, and break up, as land, without seeding, for the purpose of destroying weeds and insects, and rendering it mellow; as, it is profitable to fallow cold, strong, clayey land.
A European species of deer (Cervus dama), much smaller than the red deer. In summer both sexes are spotted with white. It is common in England, where it is often domesticated in the parks.

Fallowdeer.etym: [So called from its fallow or pale yellow color.]

senses.d: Uttering falsehood; unveracious; given to deceit; dishnest; as, a false witness.
Not faithful or loyal, as to obligations, allegiance, vows, etc.; untrue; treacherous; perfidious; as, a false friend, lover, or subject; false to promises.
q: I to myself was false, ere thou to me.

senses.d: Not according with truth or reality; not true; fitted or likely to deceive or disappoint; as, a false statement.
Not genuine or real; assumed or designed to deceive; counterfeit; hypocritical; as, false tears; false modesty; false colors; false jewelry.
q: False face must hide what the false heart doth know.

senses.d: Not well founded; not firm or trustworthy; erroneous; as, a false claim; a false conclusion; a false construction in grammar.
q: Whose false foundation waves have swept away.

senses.d: Not essential or permanent, as parts of a structure which are temporary or supplemental.
Not in tune.

False.etym: [L. falsus, p. p. of fallere to deceive; cf. OF. faus, fals, F. faux, and AS. fals fraud. See Fail, Fall.]

senses.d: Not truly; not honestly; falsely.
To report falsely; to falsify.
To betray; to falsify.
q: hath his truthe falsed in this wise.

senses.d: To mislead by want of truth; to deceive.
q: In his falsed fancy.

senses.d: To feign; to pretend to make.

False.etym: [L. falsare to falsify, fr. falsus: cf. F. fausser. See False, a.]

senses.d: Want of truth or accuracy; an untrue assertion or representation; error; misrepresentation; falsity.
q: Though it be a lie in the clock, it is but a falsehood in the hand of the dial when pointing at a wrong hour, if rightly following the direction of the wheel which moveth it.

senses.d: A deliberate intentional assertion of what is known to be untrue; a departure from moral integrity; a lie.
Treachery; deceit; perfidy; unfaithfulness.
q: Betrayed by falsehood of his guard.

senses.d: A counterfeit; a false appearance; an imposture.
q: For his molten image is falsehood.
No falsehood can endure Touch of celestial temper.

Falsehood.syn: Falsity; lie; untruth; fiction; fabrication. See Falsity.

senses.d: In a false manner; erroneously; not truly; perfidiously or treacherously.
q: Oppositions of science, falsely so called.
Will ye steal, murder . . . and swear falsely ?

senses.d: To make false; to represent falsely.
q: The Irish bards use to forge and falsify everything as they list, to please or displease any man.

senses.d: To counterfeit; to forge; as, to falsify coin.
To prove to be false, or untrustworthy; to confute; to disprove; to nullify; to make to appear false.
q: By how much better than my word I am, By so much shall I falsify men's hope.
Jews and Pagans united all their endeavors, under Julian the apostate, to baffie and falsify the prediction.

senses.d: To violate; to break by falsehood; as, to falsify one's faith or word.
To baffle or escape; as, to falsify a blow.
To avoid or defeat; to prove false, as a judgment.
To show, in accounting, (an inem of charge inserted in an account) to be wrong.
To make false by multilation or addition; to tamper with; as, to falsify a record or document.

Falsify.etym: [L. falsus false + -ly: cf. F. falsifier. See False, a.]

senses.d: To tell lies; to violate the truth.
q: It is absolutely and universally unlawful to lie and falsify.
South.

senses.d: Public report or rumor.
q: The fame thereof was heard in Pharaoh's house.

senses.d: Report or opinion generally diffused; renown; public estimation; celebrity, either favorable or unfavorable; as, the fame of Washington.
q: I find thou art no less than fame hath bruited.

Fame.etym: [OF. fame, L. fama, fr. fari to speak, akin to Gr. ���� a saying, report, ����� to speak. See Ban, and cf. Fable, Fate, Euphony, Blame.]

senses.d: To report widely or honorably.
q: The field where thou art famed To have wrought such wonders.

senses.d: To make famous or renowned.
q: Those Hesperian gardens famed of old.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a family; domestic.
Closely acquainted or intimate, as a friend or companion; well versed in, as any subject of study; as, familiar with the Scriptures.
Characterized by, or exhibiting, the manner of an intimate friend; not formal; unconstrained; easy; accessible.
q: Be thou familiar, but by no means vulgar.

senses.d: Well known; well understood; common; frequent; as, a familiar illustration.
q: That war, or peace, or both at once, may be As things acquainted and familiar to us.
There is nothing more familiar than this.

senses.d: Improperly acquainted; wrongly intimate.

Familiar.etym: [OE. familer, familier, F. familier, fr. L. familiaris, fr. familia family. See Family.]

senses.d: An intimate; a companion.
q: All my familiars watched for my halting.

senses.d: An attendant demon or evil spirit.
A confidential officer employed in the service of the tribunal, especially in apprehending and imprisoning the accused.
The collective body of persons who live in one house, and under one head or manager; a household, including parents, children, and servants, and, as the case may be, lodgers or boarders.
The group comprising a husband and wife and their dependent children, constituting a fundamental unit in the organization of society.
q: The welfare of the family underlies the welfare of society.

senses.d: Those who descend from one common progenitor; a tribe, clan, or race; kindred; house; as, the human family; the family of Abraham; the father of a family.
q: Go ! and pretend your family is young.

senses.d: Course of descent; genealogy; line of ancestors; lineage.
Honorable descent; noble or respectable stock; as, a man of family.
A group of kindred or closely related individuals; as, a family of languages; a family of States; the chlorine family.

A group of organisms, either animal or vegetable, related by certain points of resemblance in structure or development, more comprehensive than a genus, because it is usually based on fewer or less pronounced points of likeness. In zoölogy a family is less comprehesive than an order; in botany it is often considered the same thing as an order.

Family.etym: [L. familia, fr. famulus servant; akin to Oscan famel servant, cf. faamat he dwells, Skr. dhāman house, fr. dhāto set, make, do: cf. F. famille. Cf. Do, v. t., Doom, Fact, Feat.]

senses.d: General scarcity of food; dearth; a want of provisions; destitution.
q: There was a famine in the land.

Famine.etym: [F. famine, fr. L. fames hunger; cf. Gr. ����� want, need, Skr. hāni loss, lack, hā to leave.]

senses.d: To starve, kill, or destroy with hunger.
To exhaust the strength or endurance of, by hunger; to distress with hanger.
q: And when all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread.
The pains of famished Tantalus he'll feel.

senses.d: To kill, or to cause to suffer extremity, by deprivation or denial of anything necessary.
q: And famish him of breath, if not of bread.

senses.d: To force or constrain by famine.
q: He had famished Paris into a surrender.

Famish.etym: [OE. famen; cf. OF. afamer, L. fames. See Famine, and cf. Affamish.]

senses.d: To die of hunger; to starve.
To suffer extreme hunger or thirst, so as to be exhausted in strength, or to come near to perish.
q: You are all resolved rather to die than to famish?

senses.d: To suffer extremity from deprivation of anything essential or necessary.
q: The Lord will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish.

senses.d: Celebrated in fame or public report; renowned; mach talked of; distinguished in story; — used in either a good or a bad sense, chiefly the former; often followed by for; as, famous for erudition, for eloquence, for military skill; a famous pirate.
q: Famous for a scolding tongue.

Famous.syn: Noted; remarkable; signal; conspicuous; celebrated; renowned; illustrious; eminent; transcendent; excellent.
Famous.etym: [L. famosus, fr. fama fame: cf. F. fameux. See Fame.]

senses.d: An instrument used for producing artificial currents of air, by the wafting or revolving motion of a broad surface
q: Clean provender, which hath been winnowed with the shovel and with the fan.

senses.d: That which produces effects analogous to those of a fan, as in exciting a flame, etc.; that which inflames, heightens, or strengthens; as, it served as a fan to the flame of his passion.
A quintain; — from its form.

Fan.etym: [AS. fann, fr. L. vannus fan, van for winnowing grain; cf. F. van. Cf. Van a winnowing machine, Winnow.]

senses.d: To move as with a fan.
q: The air . . . fanned with unnumbered plumes.

senses.d: To cool and refresh, by moving the air with a fan; to blow the air on the face of with a fan.
To ventilate; to blow on; to affect by air put in motion.
q: Calm as the breath which fans our eastern groves.

senses.d: To winnow; to separate chaff from, and drive it away by a current of air; as, to fan wheat.
To excite or stir up to activity, as a fan excites a flame; to stimulate; as, this conduct fanned the excitement of the populace.

Fan.etym: [Cf. OF. vanner, L. vannere. See Fan, n., Van a winnowing machine.]

senses.d: One who fans.
A fan wheel; a fan blower. See under Fan.
A young pig, or a litter of pigs.
Distant in any direction; not near; remote; mutually separated by a wide space or extent.
q: They said, . . . We be come from a far country.
The nations far and near contend in choice.

senses.d: Remote from purpose; contrary to design or wishes; as, far be it from me to justify cruelty.
Remote in affection or obedience; at a distance, morally or spiritually; t enmity with; alienated.
q: They that are far from thee ahsll perish.

senses.d: Widely different in nature or quality; opposite in character.
q: He was far from ill looking, though he thought himself still farther.

senses.d: The more distant of two; as, the far side (called also off side) of a horse, that is, the right side, or the one opposite to the rider when he mounts.

Far.etym: [OE. fer, feor, AS. feor; akin to OS. fer, D. ver, OHG. ferro, adv., G. fern, a., Icel. fjarri, Dan. fjirn, Sw. fjerran, adv., Goth. faīrra, adv., Gr. ����� beyond, Skr. paras, adv., far, and prob. to L. per through, and E. prefix for-, as in forgive, and also to fare. Cf. Farther, Farthest.]

senses.d: To a great extent or distance of space; widely; as, we are separated far from each other.
To a great distance in time from any point; remotely; as, he pushed his researches far into antiquity.
In great part; as, the day is far spent.
In a great proportion; by many degrees; very much; deeply; greatly.
q: Who can find a virtuous woman ? for her price is far above rubies.

senses.d: To go; to pass; to journey; to travel.
q: So on he fares, and to the border comes Of Eden.

senses.d: To be in any state, or pass through any experience, good or bad; to be attended with any circummstances or train of events, fortunate or unfortunate; as, he fared well, or ill.
q: So fares the stag among the enraged hounds.
I bid you most heartily well to fare.
So fared the knight between two foes.

senses.d: To be treated or entertained at table, or with bodily or social comforts; to live.
q: There was a certain rich man which . . . fared sumptuously every day.

senses.d: To happen well, or ill; — used impersonally; as, we shall see how it will fare with him.
q: So fares it when with truth falsehood contends.

senses.d: To behave; to conduct one's self.
q: She ferde as she would die.

Fare.etym: [AS. faran to travel, fare; akin to OS., Goth., & OHG. faran to travel, go, D. varen, G. fahren, OFries., Icel., & Sw. fara, Dan. fare, Gr. ����� a way through, ������� a ferry, strait, �������� to convey, ���������� to go, march, ����� beyond, on the other side, ����� to pass through, L. peritus ex

senses.d: A journey; a passage.
q: That nought might stay his fare.

senses.d: The price of passage or going; the sum paid or due for conveying a person by land or water; as, the fare for crossing a river; the fare in a coach or by railway.
Ado; bustle; business.
q: The warder chid and made fare.

senses.d: Condition or state of things; fortune; hap; cheer.
q: What fare? what news abroad ?

senses.d: Food; provisions for the table; entertainment; as, coarse fare; delicious fare.
The person or persons conveyed in a vehicle; as, a full fare of passengers.
The catch of fish on a fishing vessel.

Fare.etym: [AS. faru journey, fr. faran. See Fare, v.]

senses.d: Go well; good-by; adieu; — originally applied to a person departing, but by custom now applied both to those who depart and those who remain. It is often separated by the pronoun; as, fare you well; and is sometimes used as an expression of separation only; as, farewell the year; farewell, ye sweet groves; that is, I bid you farewell.
q: So farewell hope, and with hope, farewell fear.
Fare thee well! and if forever, Still forever fare thee well.

senses.d: A wish of happiness or welfare at parting; the parting compliment; a good-by; adieu.
Act of departure; leave-taking; a last look at, or reference to something.
q: And takes her farewell of the glorious sun.
Before I take my farewell of the subject.

senses.d: Parting; valedictory; final; as, a farewell discourse; his farewell bow.
q: Leans in his spear to take his farewell view.

senses.d: The rent of land, — originally paid by reservation of part of its products.
The term or tenure of a lease of land for cultivation; a leasehold.
q: It is great willfulness in landlords to make any longer farms to their tenants.

senses.d: The land held under lease and by payment of rent for the purpose of cultivation.
Any tract of land devoted to agricultural purposes, under the management of a tenant or the owner.
A district of country leased (or farmed) out for the collection of the revenues of government.
q: The province was devided into twelve farms.

senses.d: A lease of the imposts on particular goods; as, the sugar farm, the silk farm.
q: Whereas G. H. held the farm of sugars upon a rent of 10,000 marks per annum.

Farm.etym: [OE. ferme rent, lease, F. ferme, LL. firma, fr. L. firmus firm, fast, firmare to make firm or fast. See Firm, a. & n.]

senses.d: To lease or let for an equivalent, as land for a rent; to yield the use of to proceeds.
q: We are enforced to farm our royal realm.

senses.d: To give up to another, as an estate, a business, the revenue, etc., on condition of receiving in return a percentage of what it yields; as, to farm the taxes.
q: To farm their subjects and their duties toward these.

senses.d: To take at a certain rent or rate.
To devote (land) to agriculture; to cultivate, as land; to till, as a farm.
To engage in the business of tilling the soil; to labor as a farmer.
More remote; more distant than something else.
Tending to a greater distance; beyond a certain point; additional; further.
q: Before our farther way the fates allow.
Let me add a farther Truth.
Some farther change awaits us.

Farther.etym: [For farrer, OE. ferrer, compar. of far; confused with further. Cf. Farthest.]

senses.d: At or to a greater distance; more remotely; beyond; as, let us rest with what we have, without looking farther.
Moreover; by way of progress in treating a subject; as, farther, let us consider the probable event.
To help onward. See Further.
The fourth of a penny; a small copper coin of Great Britain, being a cent in United States currency.
A very small quantity or value.
q: In her cup was no farthing seen of grease.

senses.d: A division of land.
q: Thirty acres make a farthing land; nine farthings a Cornish acre; and four Cornish acres a knight's fee.

Farthing.etym: [OE. furthing, AS. feórðung, fr. feórða fourth, feór, feówer, four. See Four.]

senses.d: The make or form of anything; the style, shape, appearance, or mode of structure; pattern, model; as, the fashion of the ark, of a coat, of a house, of an altar, etc.; workmanship; execution.
q: The fashion of his countenance was altered.
I do not like the fashion of your garments.

senses.d: The prevailing mode or style, especially of dress; custom or conventional usage in respect of dress, behavior, etiquette, etc.; particularly, the mode or style usual among persons of good breeding; as, to dress, dance, sing, ride, etc., in the fashion.
q: The innocent diversions in fashion.
As now existing, fashion is a form of social regulation analogous to constitutional government as a form of political regulation.

senses.d: Polite, fashionable, or genteel life; social position; good breeding; as, men of fashion.
Mode of action; method of conduct; manner; custom; sort; way.

Fashion.etym: [OE. fasoun, facioun, shape, manner, F. facon, orig., a making, fr. L. factio a making, fr. facere to make. See Fact, Feat, and cf. Faction.]

senses.d: To form; to give shape or figure to; to mold.
q: Here the loud hammer fashions female toys.
Ingenious art . . . Steps forth to fashion and refine the age.

senses.d: To fit; to adapt; to accommodate; — with to.
q: Laws ought to be fashioned to the manners and conditions of the people.

senses.d: To make according to the rule prescribed by custom.
q: Fashioned plate sells for more than its weight.

senses.d: To forge or counterfeit.
Having a certain style or fashion; as old-fashioned; new-fashioned.
To abstain from food; to omit to take nourishment in whole or in part; to go hungry.
q: Fasting he went to sleep, and fasting waked.

senses.d: To practice abstinence as a religious exercise or duty; to abstain from food voluntarily for a time, for the mortification of the body or appetites, or as a token of grief, or humiliation and penitence.
q: Thou didst fast and weep for the child.

Fast.etym: [AS. fæstan; akin to D. vasten, OHG. fastēn, G. fasten, Icel. & Sw. fasta, Dan. faste, Goth. fastan to keep, observe, fast, and prob. to E. fast firm.]

senses.d: Abstinence from food; omission to take nourishment.
q: Surfeit is the father of much fast.

senses.d: Voluntary abstinence from food, for a space of time, as a spiritual discipline, or as a token of religious humiliation.
A time of fasting, whether a day, week, or longer time; a period of abstinence from food or certain kinds of food; as, an annual fast.

Fast.etym: [OE. faste, fast; cf. AS. fæsten, OHG. fasta, G. faste. See Fast, v. i.]

senses.d: Firmly fixed; closely adhering; made firm; not loose, unstable, or easily moved; immovable; as, to make fast the door.
q: There is an order that keeps things fast.

senses.d: Firm against attack; fortified by nature or art; impregnable; strong.
q: Outlaws . . . lurking in woods and fast places.

senses.d: Firm in adherence; steadfast; not easily separated or alienated; faithful; as, a fast friend.
Permanent; not liable to fade by exposure to air or by washing; durable; lasting; as, fast colors.
Tenacious; retentive.
q: Roses, damask and red, are fast flowers of their smells.

senses.d: Not easily disturbed or broken; deep; sound.
q: All this while in a most fast sleep.

senses.d: Moving rapidly; quick in mition; rapid; swift; as, a fast horse.
Given to pleasure seeking; disregardful of restraint; reckless; wild; dissipated; dissolute; as, a fast man; a fast liver.

Fast.etym: [OE., firm, strong, not loose, AS. f�st; akin to OS. fast, D. vast, OHG. fasti, festi, G. fest, Icel. fastr, Sw. & Dan. fast, and perh. to E. fetter. The sense swift comes from the idea of keeping close to what is pursued; a Scandinavian use. Cf. Fast, adv., Fast, v., Avast.]

senses.d: In a fast, fixed, or firmly established manner; fixedly; firmly; immovably.
q: We will bind thee fast.

senses.d: In a fast or rapid manner; quickly; swiftly; extravagantly; wildly; as, to run fast; to live fast.
q: He, after Eve seduced, unminded slunk Into the wood fast by.
Fast by the throne obsequious Fame resides.

Fast.etym: [OE. faste firmly, strongly, quickly, AS. fæste. See Fast, a.]

senses.d: That which fastens or holds; especially, (Naut.) a mooring rope, hawser, or chain; — called, according to its position, a bow, head, quarter, breast, or stern fast; also, a post on a pier around which hawsers are passed in mooring.
In such a condition, as to resilience, etc., as to make possible unusual rapidity of play or action; as, a fast racket, or tennis court; a fast track; a fast billiard table, etc.
To fix firmly; to make fast; to secure, as by a knot, lock, bolt, etc.; as, to fasten a chain to the feet; to fasten a door or window.

To cause to hold together or to something else; to attach or unite firmly; to cause to cleave to something , or to cleave together, by any means; as, to fasten boards together with nails or cords; to fasten anything in our thoughts.
q: The words Whig and Tory have been pressed to the service of many successions of parties, with very different ideas fastened to them.

senses.d: To cause to take close effect; to make to tell; to lay on; as, to fasten a blow.
q: If I can fasten but one cup upon him.

Fasten.syn: To fix; cement; stick; link; affix; annex.
Fasten.etym: [AS. fæstnian; akin to OHG. festinōn. See Fast, a.]

senses.d: To fix one's self; to take firm hold; to clinch; to cling.
q: A horse leech will hardly fasten on a fish.

senses.d: Anything that binds and makes fast, as a lock, catch, bolt, bar, buckle, etc.
A large tub, cistern, or vessel; a vat.
q: The fats shall overflow with wine and oil.

senses.d: A measure of quantity, differing for different commodities.
Abounding with fat
Exhibiting the qualities of a fat animal; coarse; heavy; gross; dull; stupid.
q: Making our western wits fat and mean.
Make the heart of this people fat.

senses.d: Fertile; productive; as, a fat soil; a fat pasture.
Rich; producing a large income; desirable; as, a fat benefice; a fat office; a fat job.
q: Now parson of Troston, a fat living in Suffolk.

senses.d: Abounding in riches; affluent; fortunate.
q: Persons grown fat and wealthy by long impostures.

senses.d: Of a character which enables the compositor to make large wages; — said of matter containing blank, cuts, or many leads, etc.; as, a fat take; a fat page.

Fat.etym: [AS. fǣtt; akin to D. vet, G. fett, feist, Icel. feitr, Sw. fet, Dan. fed, and perh. to Gr. πι̑δαξ spring, fountain, πιδύειν to gush forth, πίων fat, Skr. pi to swell.]

senses.d: An oily liquid or greasy substance making up the main bulk of the adipose tissue of animals, and widely distributed in the seeds of plants. See Adipose tissue, under Adipose.
The best or richest productions; the best part; as, to live on the fat of the land.
Work. containing much blank, or its equivalent, and, therefore, profitable to the compositor.
To make fat; to fatten; to make plump and fleshy with abundant food; as, to fat fowls or sheep.
q: We fat all creatures else to fat us.

Fat.etym: [OE. fatten, AS. fǣttian. See Fat, a., and cf. Fatten.]

senses.d: To grow fat, plump, and fleshy.
q: An old ox fats as well, and is as good, as a young one.

senses.d: One who has begotten a child, whether son or daughter; a generator; a male parent.
q: A wise son maketh a glad father.

senses.d: A male ancestor more remote than a parent; a progenitor; especially, a first ancestor; a founder of a race or family; — in the plural, fathers, ancestors.
q: David slept with his fathers.
Abraham, who is the father of us all.

senses.d: One who performs the offices of a parent by maintenance, affetionate care, counsel, or protection.
q: I was a father to the poor.
He hath made me a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house.

senses.d: A respectful mode of address to an old man.
q: And Joash the king of Israel came down unto him , . . . and said, O my father, my father!

senses.d: A senator of ancient Rome.
A dignitary of the church, a superior of a convent, a confessor (called also father confessor), or a priest; also, the eldest member of a profession, or of a legislative assembly, etc.
q: Bless you, good father friar !

senses.d: One of the chief ecclesiastical authorities of the first centuries after Christ; — often spoken of collectively as the Fathers; as, the Latin, Greek, or apostolic Fathers.
One who, or that which, gives origin; an originator; a producer, author, or contriver; the first to practice any art, profession, or occupation; a distinguished example or teacher.
q: The father of all such as handle the harp and organ.
Might be the father, Harry, to that thought.
The father of good news.

senses.d: The Supreme Being and Creator; God; in theology, the first person in the Trinity.
q: Our Father, which art in heaven.
Now had the almighty Father from above . . . Bent down his eye.

Father.etym: [OE. fader, AS. fæder; akin to OS. fadar, D. vader, OHG. fatar, G. vater, Icel. faðir Sw. & Dan. fader, OIr. athir, L. pater, Gr. πατήρ, Skr. pitr, perh. fr. Skr. pā protect. √75, 247. Cf. Papa, Paternal, Patriot, Potential, Pablum.]

senses.d: To make one's self the father of; to beget.
q: Cowards father cowards, and base things sire base.

senses.d: To take as one's own child; to adopt; hence, to assume as one's own work; to acknowledge one's self author of or responsible for (a statement, policy, etc.).
q: Men of wit Often fathered what he writ.

senses.d: To provide with a father.
q: Think you I am no stronger than my sex, Being so fathered and so husbanded ?

senses.d: Destitute of a living father; as, a fatherless child.
Without a known author.
A measure of length, containing six feet; the space to which a man can extend his arms; — used chiefly in measuring cables, cordage, and the depth of navigable water by soundings.
The measure or extant of one's capacity; depth, as of intellect; profundity; reach; penetration.
q: Another of his fathom they have none To lead their business.

Fathom.etym: [OE. fadme, faðme, AS. fæðm fathom, the embracing arms; akin to OS. faðmos the outstretched arms, D. vadem, vaam, fathom, OHG. fadom, fadum, G. faden fathom, thread, Icel. faðmr fathom, Sw. famn, Dan. favn; cf. Gr. ���������� to spread out, ������� outspread, flat, L. patere to lie open, extend. Cf.

senses.d: To encompass with the arms extended or encircling; to measure by throwing the arms about; to span.
To measure by a sounding line; especially, to sound the depth of; to penetrate, measure, and comprehend; to get to the bottom of.
q: The page of life that was spread out before me seemed dull and commonplace, only because I had not fathomed its deeper import.

senses.d: A calf, lamb, kid, or other young animal fattened for slaughter; a fat animal; — said of such animals as are used for food.
q: He sacrificed oxen and fatlings.

senses.d: The quality or state of being fat, plump, or full-fed; corpulency; fullness of flesh.
q: Their eyes stand out with fatness.

senses.d: Hence; Richness; fertility; fruitfulness.
q: Rich in the fatness of her plenteous soil.

senses.d: That which makes fat or fertile.
q: The clouds drop fatness.

senses.d: Defect; want; lack; default.
q: One, it pleases me, for fault of a better, to call my friend.

senses.d: Anything that fails, that is wanting, or that impairs excellence; a failing; a defect; a blemish.
q: As patches set upon a little breach Discredit more in hiding of the fault.

senses.d: A moral failing; a defect or dereliction from duty; a deviation from propriety; an offense less serious than a crime.
A dislocation of the strata of the vein.
A lost scent; act of losing the scent.
q: Ceasing their clamorous cry till they have singled, With much ado, the cold fault cleary out.

senses.d: Failure to serve the ball into the proper court.

Fault.syn: — Error; blemish; defect; imperfection; weakness; blunder; failing; vice.
Fault.etym: [OE. faut, faute, F. faute (cf. It., Sp., & Pg. falta), fr. a verb meaning to want, fail, freq., fr. L. fallere to deceive. See Fail, and cf. Default.]

senses.d: To charge with a fault; to accuse; to find fault with; to blame.
q: For that I will not fault thee.

senses.d: To interrupt the continuity of (rock strata) by displacement along a plane of fracture; — chiefly used in the p. p.; as, the coal beds are badly faulted.
To err; to blunder, to commit a fault; to do wrong.
q: If after Samuel's death the people had asked of God a king, they had not faulted.

senses.d: A defective point in an electric circuit due to a crossing of the parts of the conductor, or to contact with another conductor or the earth, or to a break in the circuit.
A dislocation caused by a slipping of rock masses along a plane of facture; also, the dislocated structure resulting from such slipping.
Without fault; not defective or imperfect; free from blemish; free from incorrectness, vice, or offense; perfect; as, a faultless poem.
q: Whoever thinks a faultless piece to see, Thinks what ne'er was, nor is, nor e'er shall be.

senses.d: Containing faults, blemishes, or defects; imperfect; not fit for the use intended.
q: Created once So goodly and erect, though faulty since.

senses.d: Guilty of a fault, or of faults; hence, blamable; worthy of censure.
q: The king doth speak . . . as one which is faulty.

senses.d: A fairy; an elf.

Fay.etym: [F. fée. See Fate, and cf. Fairy.]

senses.d: Faith; as, by my fay.
To fit; to join; to unite closely, as two pieces of wood, so as to make the surface fit together.

Fay.etym: [OE. feien, v.t. & i., AS. fēgan to join, unite; akin to OS. fōgian, D. voegen, OHG. fuogen, G. fügen, Sw. foga. See Fair, and cf. Fadge.]

senses.d: To lie close together; to fit; to fadge; — often with in, into, with, or together.
A variant of Fere, a mate, a companion.
A painful emotion or passion excited by the expectation of evil, or the apprehension of impending danger; apprehension; anxiety; solicitude; alarm; dread.
q: Fear is an uneasiness of the mind, upon the thought of future evil likely to befall us.
Where no hope is left, is left no fear.

senses.d: Apprehension of incurring, or solicitude to avoid, God's wrath; the trembling and awful reverence felt toward the Supreme Being.
q: I will put my fear in their hearts.
I will teach you the fear of the Lord.
Render therefore to all their dues; tribute to whom tribute is due . . . fear to whom fear.

senses.d: That which causes, or which is the object of, apprehension or alarm; source or occasion of terror; danger; dreadfulness.
q: There were they in great fear, where no fear was.
The fear of your adventure would counsel you to a more equal enterprise.

Fear.etym: [OE. fer, feer, fere, AS. fǣr a coming suddenly upon, fear, danger; akin to D. vaar, OHG. fāra danger, G. gefahr, Icel. fār harm, mischief, plague, and to E. fare, peril. See Fare.]

senses.d: To feel a painful apprehension of; to be afraid of; to consider or expect with emotion of alarm or solicitude.
q: I will fear no evil, for thou art with me.

senses.d: To have a reverential awe of; to be solicitous to avoid the displeasure of.
q: Leave them to God above; him serve and fear.

senses.d: To be anxious or solicitous for.
q: The sins of the father are to be laid upon the children, therefore . . . I fear you.

senses.d: To suspect; to doubt.
q: Ay what else, fear you not her courage?

senses.d: To affright; to terrify; to drive away or prevent approach of by fear.
q: Fear their people from doing evil.
Tush, tush! fear boys with bugs.

Fear.etym: [OE. feren, faeren, to frighten, to be afraid, AS. fǣran to terrify. See Fear, n.]

senses.d: To be in apprehension of evil; to be afraid; to feel anxiety on account of some expected evil.
q: I exceedingly fear and quake.

senses.d: Full of fear, apprehension, or alarm; afraid; frightened.
q: Anxious amidst all their success, and fearful amidst all their power.

senses.d: Inclined to fear; easily frightened; without courage; timid.
q: What man is there that is fearful and faint-hearted?

senses.d: Indicating, or caused by, fear.
q: Cold fearful drops stand on my trembling flesh.

senses.d: Inspiring fear or awe; exciting apprehension or terror; terrible; frightful; dreadful.
q: This glorious and fearful name, The Lord thy God.
Death is a fearful thing.
In dreams they fearful precipices tread.

Fearful.syn: Apprehensive; afraid; timid; timorous; horrible; distressing; shocking; frightful; dreadful; awful.

senses.d: In a fearful manner.
The state of being fearful.
A festival; a holiday; a solemn, or more commonly, a joyous, anniversary.
q: The seventh day shall be a feast to the Lord.
Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover.

senses.d: A festive or joyous meal; a grand, ceremonious, or sumptuous entertainment, of which many guests partake; a banquet characterized by tempting variety and abundance of food.
q: Enough is as good as a feast.
Belshazzar the King made a great feast to a thousand of his lords.

senses.d: That which is partaken of, or shared in, with delight; something highly agreeable; entertainment.
q: The feast of reason, and the flow of soul.

Feast.syn: Entertainment; regale; banquet; treat; carousal; festivity; festival.
Feast.etym: [OE. feste festival, holiday, feast, OF. feste festival, F. fête, fr. L. festum, pl. festa, fr. festus joyful, festal; of uncertain origin. Cf. Fair, n., Festal, Fête.]

senses.d: To eat sumptuously; to dine or sup on rich provisions, particularly in large companies, and on public festivals.
q: And his sons went and feasted in their houses.

senses.d: To be highly gratified or delighted.
q: With my love's picture then my eye doth feast.

Feast.etym: [OE. festen, cf. OF. fester to rest from work, F. fêter to celebrate a holiday. See Feast, n.]

senses.d: To entertain with sumptuous provisions; to treat at the table bountifully; as, he was feasted by the king.
To delight; to gratify; as, to feast the soul.
q: Feast your ears with the music a while.

senses.d: One of the peculiar dermal appendages, of several kinds, belonging to birds, as contour feathers, quills, and down.
Kind; nature; species; — from the proverbial phrase, “Birds of a feather,” that is, of the same species.
q: I am not of that feather to shake off My friend when he must need me.

senses.d: The fringe of long hair on the legs of the setter and some other dogs.
A tuft of peculiar, long, frizzly hair on a horse.
One of the fins or wings on the shaft of an arrow.
A longitudinal strip projecting as a fin from an object, to strengthen it, or to enter a channel in another object and thereby prevent displacement sidwise but permit motion lengthwise; a spline.
A thin wedge driven between the two semicylindrical parts of a divided plug in a hole bored in a stone, to rend the stone.
The angular adjustment of an oar or paddle-wheel float, with reference to a horizontal axis, as it leaves or enters the water.

Feather.etym: [OE. fether, AS. feðer; akin to D. veder, OHG. fedara, G. feder, Icel. fjöðr, Sw. fjäder, Dan. fjæder, Gr. πτερόν wing, feather, πέτεσθαι to fly, Skr. pattra wing, feather, pat to fly, and prob. to L. penna feather, wing. √76, 248. Cf. Pen a feather.]

senses.d: To furnish with a feather or feathers, as an arrow or a cap.
q: An eagle had the ill hap to be struck with an arrow feathered from her own wing.

senses.d: To adorn, as with feathers; to fringe.
q: A few birches and oaks still feathered the narrow ravines.

senses.d: To render light as a feather; to give wings to.
q: The Polonian story perhaps may feather some tedious hours.

senses.d: To enrich; to exalt; to benefit.
q: They stuck not to say that the king cared not to plume his nobility and people to feather himself.

senses.d: To tread, as a cock.
To grow or form feathers; to become feathered; — often with out; as, the birds are feathering out.
To curdle when poured into another liquid, and float about in little flakes or “feathers;” as, the cream feathers.
To turn to a horizontal plane; — said of oars.
q: The feathering oar returns the gleam.
Stopping his sculls in the air to feather accurately.

senses.d: To have the appearance of a feather or of feathers; to be or to appear in feathery form.
q: A clump of ancient cedars feathering in evergreen beauty down to the ground.
The ripple feathering from her bows.

senses.d: Clothed, covered, or fitted with (or as with) feathers or wings; as, a feathered animal; a feathered arrow.
q: Rise from the ground like feathered Mercury.
Nonsense feathered with soft and delicate phrases and pointed with pathetic accent.

senses.d: Furnished with anything featherlike; ornamented; fringed; as, land feathered with trees.
Having a fringe of feathers, as the legs of certian birds; or of hairs, as the legs of a setter dog.
Having feathers; — said of an arrow, when the feathers are of a tincture different from that of the shaft.
property; possession; tenure.
q: Once did she hold the gorgeous East in fee.

senses.d: Reward or compensation for services rendered or to be rendered; especially, payment for professional services, of optional amount, or fixed by custom or laws; charge; pay; perquisite; as, the fees of lawyers and physicians; the fees of office; clerk's fees; sheriff's fees; marriage fees, etc.
q: To plead for love deserves more fee than hate.

senses.d: A right to the use of a superior's land, as a stipend for services to be performed; also, the land so held; a fief.
An estate of inheritance supposed to be held either mediately or immediately from the sovereign, and absolutely vested in the owner.
An estate of inheritance belonging to the owner, and transmissible to his heirs, absolutely and simply, without condition attached to the tenure.

Fee.etym: [OE. fe, feh, feoh, cattle, property, money, fief, AS. feoh cattle, property, money; the senses of “property, money,” arising from cattle being used in early times as a medium of exchange or payment, property chiefly consisting of cattle; akin to OS. fehu cattle, property, D. vee cattle, OHG. fihu,

senses.d: To reward for services performed, or to be performed; to recompense; to hire or keep in hire; hence, to bribe.
q: The patient . . . fees the doctor.
There's not a one of them but in his house I keep a servant feed.

senses.d: Deficient in physical strength; weak; infirm; debilitated.
q: Carried all the feeble of them upon asses.

senses.d: Wanting force, vigor, or efficiency in action or expression; not full, loud, bright, strong, rapid, etc.; faint; as, a feeble color; feeble motion.

Feeble.etym: [OE. feble, OF. feble, flebe, floibe, floible, foible, F. faible, L. flebilis to be wept over, lamentable, wretched, fr. flere to weep. Cf. Foible.]

senses.d: To make feble; to enfeeble.
q: Shall that victorious hand be feebled here?

senses.d: The quality or condition of being feeble; debility; infirmity.
q: That shakes for age and feebleness.

senses.d: To give food to; to supply with nourishment; to satisfy the physical huger of.
q: If thine enemy hunger, feed him.
Unreasonable creatures feed their young.

senses.d: To satisfy; gratify or minister to, as any sense, talent, taste, or desire.
q: I will feed fat the ancient grudge I bear him.
Feeding him with the hope of liberty.

senses.d: To fill the wants of; to supply with that which is used or wasted; as, springs feed ponds; the hopper feeds the mill; to feed a furnace with coal.
To nourish, in a general sense; to foster, strengthen, develop, and guard.
q: Thou shalt feed my people Israel.
Mightiest powers by deepest calms are fed.

senses.d: To graze; to cause to be cropped by feeding, as herbage by cattle; as, if grain is too forward in autumn, feed it with sheep.
q: Once in three years feed your mowing lands.

senses.d: To give for food, especially to animals; to furnish for consumption; as, to feed out turnips to the cows; to feed water to a steam boiler.
To supply (the material to be operated upon) to a machine; as, to feed paper to a printing press.

Feed.etym: [AS. fēdan, fr. fōda food; akin to OS. fōdian, OFries. fēda, fōda, D. voeden, OHG. fuottan, Icel. fæða, Sw. föda, Dan. föde. √75. See Food.]

senses.d: To take food; to eat.
q: Her kid . . . which I afterwards killed because it would not feed.

senses.d: To subject by eating; to satisfy the appetite; to feed one's self (upon something); to prey; — with on or upon.
q: Leaving thy trunk for crows to feed upon.

senses.d: To be nourished, strengthened, or satisfied, as if by food.
To place cattle to feed; to pasture; to graze.
q: If a man . . . shall put in his beast, and shall feed in another man's field.

senses.d: That which is eaten; esp., food for beasts; fodder; pasture; hay; grain, ground or whole; as, the best feed for sheep.
A grazing or pasture ground.
An allowance of provender given to a horse, cow, etc.; a meal; as, a feed of corn or oats.
A meal, or the act of eating.
q: For such pleasure till that hour At feed or fountain never had I found.

senses.d: The water supplied to steam boilers.

The motion, or act, of carrying forward the stuff to be operated upon, as cloth to the needle in a sewing machine; or of producing progressive operation upon any material or object in a machine, as, in a turning lathe, by moving the cutting tool along or in the work.
the act of eating, or of supplying with food; the process of fattening.
That which is eaten; food.
That which furnishes or affords food, especially for animals; pasture land.

To perceive by the touch; to take cognizance of by means of the nerves of sensation distributed all over the body, especially by those of the skin; to have sensation excited by contact of (a thing) with the body or limbs.
q: Who feel Those rods of scorpions and those whips of steel.

senses.d: To touch; to handle; to examine by touching; as, feel this piece of silk;
q: Come near, . . . that I may feel thee, my son.
He hath this to feel my affection to your honor.

senses.d: To perceive by the mind; to have a sense of; to experience; to be affected by; to be sensible of, or sensitive to; as, to feel pleasure; to feel pain.
q: Teach me to feel another's woe.
Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing.
He best can paint them who shall feel them most.
Mankind have felt their strength and made it felt.

senses.d: To take internal cognizance of; to be conscious of; to have an inward persuasion of.
q: For then, and not till then, he felt himself.

senses.d: To perceive; to observe.

Feel.etym: [AS. fēlan; akin to OS. gifōlian to perceive, D. voelen to feel, OHG. fuolen, G. fühlen, Icel. fālma to grope, and prob. to AS. folm palm of the hand, L. palma. Cf. Fumble, Palm.]

senses.d: To have perception by the touch, or by contact of anything with the nerves of sensation, especially those upon the surface of the body.
To have the sensibilities moved or affected.
q: feels with the dignity of a Roman matron
And mine as man, who feel for all mankind.

senses.d: To be conscious of an inward impression, state of mind, persuasion, physical condition, etc.; to perceive one's self to be; — followed by an adjective describing the state, etc.; as, to feel assured, grieved, persuaded.
q: I then did feel full sick.

senses.d: To know with feeling; to be conscious; hence, to know certainly or without misgiving.
q: Garlands . . . which I feel I am not worthy yet to wear.

senses.d: To appear to the touch; to give a perception; to produce an impression by the nerves of sensation; — followed by an adjective describing the kind of sensation.
q: Blind men say black feels rough, and white feels smooth.

senses.d: Feeling; perception.
q: To intercept and have a more kindly feel of its genial warmth.

senses.d: A sensation communicated by touching; impression made upon one who touches or handles; as, this leather has a greasy feel.
q: The difference between these two tumors will be distinguished by the feel.

senses.d: Possessing great sensibility; easily affected or moved; as, a feeling heart.
Expressive of great sensibility; attended by, or evincing, sensibility; as, he made a feeling representation of his wrongs.

The sense by which the mind, through certain nerves of the body, perceives external objects, or certain states of the body itself; that one of the five senses which resides in the general nerves of sensation distributed over the body, especially in its surface; the sense of touch; nervous sensibility to external objects.
q: Why was the sight To such a tender ball as the eye confined, . . . And not, as feeling, through all parts diffused?

senses.d: An act or state of perception by the sense above described; an act of apprehending any object whatever; an act or state of apprehending the state of the soul itself; consciousness.
q: The apprehension of the good Gives but the greater feeling to the worse.

senses.d: The capacity of the soul for emotional states; a high degree of susceptibility to emotions or states of the sensibility not dependent on the body; as, a man of feeling; a man destitute of feeling.

Any state or condition of emotion; the exercise of the capacity for emotion; any mental state whatever; as, a right or a wrong feeling in the heart; our angry or kindly feelings; a feeling of pride or of humility.
q: A fellow feeling makes one wondrous kind.
Tenderness for the feelings of others.

senses.d: That quality of a work of art which embodies the mental emotion of the artist, and is calculated to affect similarly the spectator.

Feeling.syn: Sensation; emotion; passion; sentiment; agitation; opinion. See Emotion, Passion, Sentiment.

senses.d: Fact; performance.
To give a mental existence to, as to something not real or actual; to imagine; to invent; hence, to pretend; to form and relate as if true.
q: There are no such things done as thou sayest, but thou feignest them out of thine own heart.
The poet Did feign that Orpheus drew trees, stones, and floods.

senses.d: To represent by a false appearance of; to pretend; to counterfeit; as, to feign a sickness.
To dissemble; to conceal.

Feign.etym: [OE. feinen, F. feindre (p. pr. feignant), fr. L. fingere; akin to L. figura figure,and E. dough. See Dough, and cf. Figure, Faint, Effigy, Fiction.]

senses.d: Not real or genuine; pretended; counterfeit; insincere; false.
q: Give ear unto my prayer, that goeth not out of feigned lips.
Her treacherous sister Judah hath not turned unto me with her whole heart, but feignedly.

senses.d: Cruel; barbarous; inhuman; fierce; savage; ravenous.
q: While we devise fell tortures for thy faults.

senses.d: Eager; earnest; intent.
q: I am so fell to my business.

Fell.etym: [OE. fel, OF. fel cruel, fierce, perfidious; cf. AS. fel (only in comp.) OF. fel, as a noun also accus. felon, is fr. LL. felo, of unknown origin; cf. Arm fall evil, Ir. feal, Arm. falloni treachery, Ir. & Gael. feall to betray; or cf. OHG. fillan to flay, torment, akin to E. fell skin. Cf. Felon.]

senses.d: Gall; anger; melancholy.
q: Untroubled of vile fear or bitter fell.

Fell.etym: [Cf. L. fel gall, bile, or E. fell, a.]

senses.d: A skin or hide of a beast with the wool or hair on; a pelt; — used chiefly in composition, as woolfell.
q: We are still handling our ewes, and their fells, you know, are greasy.

Fell.etym: [AS. fell; akin to D. vel, OHG. fel, G. fell, Icel. fell (in comp.), Goth fill in þrutsfill leprosy, L. pellis skin, Gr. πέλλα. Cf. Film, Peel, Pell, n.]

senses.d: A barren or rocky hill.
A wild field; a moor.

Fell.etym: [Icel. fell, fjally; akin to Sw. fjäll a ridge or chain of mountains, Dan. fjeld mountain, rock and prob. to G. fels rock, or perh. to feld field, E. field.]

senses.d: To cause to fall; to prostrate; to bring down or to the ground; to cut down.
q: Stand, or I'll fell thee down.

Fell.etym: [AS. fellan, a causative verb fr. feallan to fall; akin to D. vellen, G. fällen, Icel. fella, Sw. fälla, Dan. fælde. See Fall, v. i.]

senses.d: The finer portions of ore which go through the meshes, when the ore is sorted by sifting.
To sew or hem; — said of seams.

Fell.etym: [Cf. Gael. fill to fold, plait, Sw. fåll a hem.]

senses.d: A form of seam joining two pieces of cloth, the edges being folded together and the stitches taken through both thicknesses.
The end of a web, formed by the last thread of the weft.
One who, or that which, fells, knocks or cuts down; a machine for felling trees.
An appliance to a sewing machine for felling a seam.
A companion; a comrade; an associate; a partner; a sharer.
q: The fellows of his crime.
We are fellows still, Serving alike in sorrow.
That enormous engine was flanked by two fellows almost of equal magnitude.

senses.d: A man without good breeding or worth; an ignoble or mean man.
q: Worth makes the man, and want of it, the fellow.

senses.d: An equal in power, rank, character, etc.
q: It is impossible that ever Rome Should breed thy fellow.

senses.d: One of a pair, or of two things used together or suited to each other; a mate; the male.
q: When they be but heifers of one year, . . . they are let go to the fellow and breed.
This was my glove; here is the fellow of it.

senses.d: A person; an individual.
q: She seemed to be a good sort of fellow.

senses.d: In the English universities, a scholar who is appointed to a foundation called a fellowship, which gives a title to certain perquisites and privileges.
In an American college or university, a member of the corporation which manages its business interests; also, a graduate appointed to a fellowship, who receives the income of the foundation.
A member of a literary or scientific society; as, a Fellow of the Royal Society.
q: Were the great duke himself here, and would lift up My head to fellow pomp amongst his nobles.

Fellow.etym: [OE. felawe, felaghe, Icel. fēlagi, fr. fēlag companionship, prop., a laying together of property; fē property + lag a laying, pl. lög law, akin to liggja to lie. See Fee, and Law, Lie to be low.]

senses.d: To suit with; to pair with; to match.
The state or relation of being or associate.
Companionship of persons on equal and friendly terms; frequent and familiar intercourse.
q: In a great town, friends are scattered, so that there is not that fellowship which is in less neighborhods.
Men are made for society and mutual fellowship.

senses.d: A state of being together; companionship; partnership; association; hence, confederation; joint interest.
q: The great contention of the sea and skies Parted our fellowship.
Fellowship in pain divides not smart
Fellowship in woe doth woe assuage
The goodliest fellowship of famous knights, Whereof this world holds record.

senses.d: Those associated with one, as in a family, or a society; a company.
q: The sorrow of Noah with his fellowship.
With that a joyous fellowship issued Of minstrels.

senses.d: A foundation for the maintenance, on certain conditions, of a scholar called a fellow, who usually resides at the university.
The rule for dividing profit and loss among partners; — called also partnership, company, and distributive proportion.
To acknowledge as of good standing, or in communion according to standards of faith and practice; to admit to Christian fellowship.
A cloth or stuff made of matted fibers of wool, or wool and fur, fulled or wrought into a compact substance by rolling and pressure, with lees or size, without spinning or weaving.
q: It were a delicate stratagem to shoe A troop of horse with felt.

senses.d: A hat made of felt.
A skin or hide; a fell; a pelt.
q: To know whether sheep are sound or not, see that the felt be loose.

Felt.etym: [AS. felt; akin to D. vilt, G. filz, and possibly to Gr. � hair or wool wrought into felt, L. pilus hair, pileus a felt cap or hat.]

senses.d: To make into felt, or a feltike substance; to cause to adhere and mat together.
To cover with, or as with, felt; as, to felt the cylinder of a steam engine.
An individual of the sex which conceives and brings forth young, or (in a wider sense) which has an ovary and produces ova.
q: The male and female of each living thing.

senses.d: A plant which produces only that kind of reproductive organs which are capable of developing into fruit after impregnation or fertilization; a pistillate plant.

Female.etym: [OE. femel, femal, F. femelle, fr. L. femella, dim. of femina woman. See Feminine.]

senses.d: Belonging to the sex which conceives and gives birth to young, or (in a wider sense) which produces ova; not male.
q: As patient as the female dove When that her golden couplets are disclosed.

senses.d: Belonging to an individual of the female sex; characteristic of woman; feminine; as, female tenderness.
q: To the generous decision of a female mind, we owe the discovery of America.

senses.d: Having pistils and no stamens; pistillate; or, in cryptogamous plants, capable of receiving fertilization.
Low land overflowed, or covered wholly or partially with water, but producing sedge, coarse grasses, or other aquatic plants; boggy land; moor; marsh.
q: 'Mid reedy fens wide spread.

Fen.etym: [AS. fen, fenn, marsh, mud, dirt; akin to D. veen, OFries. fenne, fene, OHG. fenna, G. fenn, Icel. fen, Goth. fani mud.]

senses.d: That which fends off attack or danger; a defense; a protection; a cover; security; shield.
q: Let us be backed with God and with the seas, Which he hath given for fence impregnable.
A fence betwixt us and the victor's wrath.

senses.d: An inclosure about a field or other space, or about any object; especially, an inclosing structure of wood, iron, or other material, intended to prevent intrusion from without or straying from within.
q: Leaps o'er the fence with ease into the fold.

senses.d: A projection on the bolt, which passes through the tumbler gates in locking and unlocking.
Self-defense by the use of the sword; the art and practice of fencing and sword play; hence, skill in debate and repartee. See Fencing.
q: Enjoy your dear wit, and gay rhetoric, That hath so well been taught her dazzing fence.
Of dauntless courage and consummate skill in fence.

senses.d: A receiver of stolen goods, or a place where they are received.
To fend off danger from; to give security to; to protect; to guard.
q: To fence my ear against thy sorceries.

senses.d: To inclose with a fence or other protection; to secure by an inclosure.
q: O thou wall! . . . dive in the earth, And fence not Athens.
A sheepcote fenced about with olive trees.

senses.d: To make a defense; to guard one's self of anything, as against an attack; to give protection or security, as by a fence.
q: Vice is the more stubborn as well as the more dangerous evil, and therefore, in the first place, to be fenced against.

senses.d: To practice the art of attack and defense with the sword or with the foil, esp. with the smallsword, using the point only.
q: He will fence with his own shadow.

senses.d: Hence, to fight or dispute in the manner of fencers, that is, by thrusting, guarding, parrying, etc.
q: They fence and push, and, pushing, loudly roar; Their dewlaps and their sides are bat�ed in gore.
As when a billow, blown against, Falls back, the voice with which I fenced A little ceased, but recommenced.

senses.d: An animal of the Weasel family (Mustela or Putorius furo), about fourteen inches in length, of a pale yellow or white color, with red eyes. It is a native of Africa, but has been domesticated in Europe. Ferrets are used to drive rabbits and rats out of their holes.

Ferret.etym: [F. furet, cf. LL. furo; prob. fr. L. fur thief (cf. Furtive); cf. Arm. fur wise, sly.]

senses.d: To drive or hunt out of a lurking place, as a ferret does the cony; to search out by patient and sagacious efforts; — often used with out; as, to ferret out a secret.
q: Master Fer! I'll fer him, and firk him, and ferret him.

senses.d: A kind of narrow tape, usually made of woolen; sometimes of cotton or silk; — called also ferreting.

Ferret.etym: [Ital. foretto, dim. of fiore flower; or F. fleuret. Cf. Floret.]

senses.d: The iron used for trying the melted glass to see if is fit to work, and for shaping the rings at the mouths of bottles.

Ferret.etym: [F. feret, dim. or fer iron, L. ferrum.]

senses.d: To carry or transport over a river, strait, or other narrow water, in a boat.

Ferry.etym: [OE. ferien to convey, AS. ferian, from faran to go; akin to Icel. ferja to ferry, Goth. farjan to sail. See Fare.]

senses.d: To pass over water in a boat or by a ferry.
q: They ferry over this Lethean sound Both to and fro.

senses.d: A place where persons or things are carried across a river, arm of the sea, etc., in a ferryboat.
q: It can pass the ferry backward into light.
To row me o'er the ferry.

senses.d: A vessel in which passengers and goods are conveyed over narrow waters; a ferryboat; a wherry.
A franchise or right to maintain a vessel for carrying passengers and freight across a river, bay, etc., charging tolls.

Ferry.etym: [OE. feri; akin to Icel. ferja, Sw. färja, Dan. færge, G. fähre. See Ferry, v. t.]

senses.d: Hot; glowing; boiling; burning; as, a fervent summer.
q: The elements shall melt with fervent heat.

senses.d: Warm in feeling; ardent in temperament; earnest; full of fervor; zealous; glowing.
