q: Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit.
So spake the fervent angel.
A fervent desire to promote the happiness of mankind.
Laboring fervently for you in prayers.

Fervent.etym: [F. fervent, L. fervens, -entis. p. pr. of fervere o the boiling hot, to boil, glow.]

senses.d: To bear toward the person speaking, or the person or thing from whose point of view the action is contemplated; to go and bring; to get.
q: Time will run back and fetch the age of gold.

He called to her, and said, Fetch me, I pray thee, a little water in a vessel, that I may drink. And as she was going to fetch it he called to her, and said, Bring me, I pray thee, a morsel of bread in thine hand.

senses.d: To obtain as price or equivalent; to sell for.
q: Our native horses were held in small esteem, and fetched low prices.

senses.d: To recall from a swoon; to revive; — sometimes with to; as, to fetch a man to.
q: Fetching men again when they swoon.

senses.d: To reduce; to throw.
q: The sudden trip in wrestling that fetches a man to the ground.

senses.d: To bring to accomplishment; to achieve; to make; to perform, with certain objects; as, to fetch a compass; to fetch a leap; to fetch a sigh.
q: I'll fetch a turn about the garden.
He fetches his blow quick and sure.

senses.d: To bring or get within reach by going; to reach; to arrive at; to attain; to reach by sailing.
q: Meantine flew our ships, and straight we fetched The siren's isle.

senses.d: To cause to come; to bring to a particular state.
q: They could n't fetch the butter in the churn.

Fetch.etym: [OE. fecchen, AS. feccan, perh. the same word as fetian; or cf. facian to wish to get, OFries. faka to prepare. √ 77. Cf. Fet, v. t.]

senses.d: To bring one's self; to make headway; to veer; as, to fetch about; to fetch to windward.
A stratagem by which a thing is indirectly brought to pass, or by which one thing seems intended and another is done; a trick; an artifice.
q: Every little fetch of wit and criticism.

senses.d: The apparation of a living person; a wraith.
q: The very fetch and ghost of Mrs. Gamp.

senses.d: A chain or shackle for the feet; a chain by which an animal is confined by the foot, either made fast or disabled from free and rapid motion; a bond; a shackle.
q: bound him with fetters of brass.

senses.d: Anything that confines or restrains; a restraint.
q: Passion's too fierce to be in fetters bound.

Fetter.etym: [AS. fetor, feter; akin to OS. feterōs, pl., OD. veter, OHG. fezzera, Icel. fjöturr, L. pedica, Gr. πέδη, and to E. foot. √ 77. See Foot.]

senses.d: To put fetters upon; to shackle or confine the feet of with a chain; to bind.
q: My heels are fettered, but my fist is free.

senses.d: To restrain from motion; to impose restraints on; to confine; to enchain; as, fettered by obligations.
q: My conscience! thou art fettered More than my shanks and wrists.

Fetter.etym: [imp. & p. p. Fettered (�); p. pr. & vb. n. Fettering.]

senses.d: A diseased state of the system, marked by increased heat, acceleration of the pulse, and a general derangement of the functions, including usually, thirst and loss of appetite. Many diseases, of which fever is the most prominent symptom, are denominated fevers; as, typhoid fever; yellow fever.
Excessive excitement of the passions in consequence of strong emotion; a condition of great excitement; as, this quarrel has set my blood in a fever.
q: An envious fever Of pale and bloodless emulation.
After life's fitful fever he sleeps well.

Fever.etym: [OE. fever, fefer, AS. fefer, fefor, L. febris: cf. F. fièvre. Cf. Febrile.]

senses.d: To put into a fever; to affect with fever; as, a fevered lip.
q: The white hand of a lady fever thee.

senses.d: Not many; small, limited, or confined in number; — indicating a small portion of units or individuals constituting a whole; often, by ellipsis of a noun, a few people.
q: Few know and fewer care.

Few.etym: [OE. fewe, feawe, AS. feá, pl. feáwe; akin to OS. fāh, OHG. fō fao, Icel. fār, Sw. få, pl., Dan. faa, pl., Goth. faus, L. paucus, cf. Gr. παυ̑ροσ. Cf. Paucity.]

senses.d: The state of being few; smallness of number; paucity.
Brevity; conciseness.
Faithfulness; adherence to right; careful and exact observance of duty, or discharge of obligations.
Adherence to a person or party to which one is bound; loyalty.
q: Whose courageous fidelity was proof to all danger.
The best security for the fidelity of men is to make interest coincide with duty.

senses.d: Adherence to the marriage contract.
Adherence to truth; veracity; honesty.
q: The principal thing required in a witness is fidelity.

Fidelity.syn: Faithfulness; honesty; integrity; faith; loyalty; fealty.
Fidelity.etym: [L. fidelitas: cf. F. fidélité. See Fealty.]

senses.d: Cleared land; land suitable for tillage or pasture; cultivated ground; the open country.
A piece of land of considerable size; esp., a piece inclosed for tillage or pasture.
q: Fields which promise corn and wine.

senses.d: A place where a battle is fought; also, the battle itself.
q: In this glorious and well-foughten field.
What though the field be lost?

senses.d: An open space; an extent; an expanse.
q: Without covering, save yon field of stars.
Ask of yonder argent fields above.

senses.d: The whole surface of an escutcheon; also, so much of it is shown unconcealed by the different bearings upon it. See Illust. of Fess, where the field is represented as gules (red), while the fess is argent (silver).
An unresticted or favorable opportunity for action, operation, or achievement; province; room.
q: Afforded a clear field for moral experiments.

senses.d: A collective term for all the competitors in any outdoor contest or trial, or for all except the favorites in the betting.
That part of the grounds reserved for the players which is outside of the diamond; — called also outfield.

Field.etym: [OE. feld, fild, AS. feld; akin to D. veld, G. feld, Sw. fält, Dan. felt, Icel. fold field of grass, AS. folde earth, land, ground, OS. folda.]

senses.d: To take the field.
To stand out in the field, ready to catch, stop, or throw the ball.
To catch, stop, throw, etc. (the ball), as a fielder.
Furious; violent; unrestrained; impetuous; as, a fierce wind.
q: His fierce thunder drove us to the deep.

senses.d: Vehement in anger or cruelty; ready or eager to kill or injure; of a nature to inspire terror; ferocious.
q: The fierce foe hung upon our broken rear.
Thou huntest me as a fierce lion.

senses.d: Excessively earnest, eager, or ardent.

Fierce.syn: Ferocious; savage; cruel; vehement; impetuous; barbarous; fell. See Ferocious.
Fierce.etym: [OE. fers, fiers, OF. fier, nom. fiers, fierce, savage, cruel, F. fier proud, from L. ferus wild, savage, cruel; perh. akin to E. bear the animal. Cf. Feral, Ferocity.]

senses.d: Consisting of, containing, or resembling, fire; as, the fiery gulf of Etna; a fiery appearance.
q: And fiery billows roll below.

senses.d: Vehement; ardent; very active; impetuous.
q: Hath thy fiery heart so parched thine entrails?
The fiery spirit of his forefathers.

senses.d: Passionate; easily provoked; irritable.
q: You know the fiery quality of the duke.

senses.d: Unrestrained; fierce; mettlesome; spirited.
q: One curbed the fiery steed.

senses.d: heated by fire, or as if by fire; burning hot; parched; feverish.
q: The sword which is made fiery.

senses.d: Five and ten; one more than fourteen.

Fifteen.etym: [OE. fiftene, AS. fīftȳne, fīftēne. See Five, and Ten, and cf. Fifty.]

senses.d: The sum of five and ten; fifteen units or objects.
A symbol representing fifteen units, as 15, or xv.
Next in order after the fourteenth; — the ordinal of fifteen.
Consisting of one of fifteen equal parts or divisions of a thing.

Fifteenth.etym: [OE. fiftenthe; cf. fiftethe, AS. fīfteōða. See Fifteen.]

senses.d: One of fifteen equal parts or divisions; the quotient of a unit divided by fifteen.
A species of tax upon personal property formerly laid on towns, boroughs, etc., in England, being one fifteenth part of what the personal property in each town, etc., had been valued at.
A stop in an organ tuned two octaves above the diaposon.
Next in order after the fourth; — the ordinal of five.
Consisting of one of five equal divisions of a thing.

Fifth.etym: [OE. fifte, fifthe, AS. fīfta. See Five.]

senses.d: The quotient of a unit divided by five; one of five equal parts; a fifth part.
The interval of three tones and a semitone, embracing five diatonic degrees of the scale; the dominant of any key.
Next in order after the forty-ninth; — the ordinal of fifty.
Consisting of one of fifty equal parts or divisions.
One of fifty equal parts; the quotient of a unit divided by fifty.
Five times ten; as, fifty men.

Fifty.etym: [AS. fīftig; akin to OHG. finfzug, fimfzuc, G. fünfzig, funfzig, Goth. fimftigjus. See Five, and Ten, and cf. Fifteen.]

senses.d: The sum of five tens; fifty units or objects.
A symbol representing fifty units, as 50, or l.
A small fruit tree (Ficus Carica) with large leaves, known from the remotest antiquity. It was probably native from Syria westward to the Canary Islands.
The fruit of a fig tree, which is of round or oblong shape, and of various colors.
A small piece of tobacco.
The value of a fig, practically nothing; a fico; — used in scorn or contempt.

Fig.etym: [F. figue the fruit of the tree, Pr. figa, fr. L. ficus fig tree, fig. Cf. Fico.]

senses.d: To insult with a fico, or contemptuous motion. See Fico.
q: When Pistol lies, do this, and fig me like The bragging Spaniard.

senses.d: To put into the head of, as something useless o� contemptible.
Figure; dress; array.
q: Were they all in full fig, the females with feathers on their heads, the males with chapeaux bras?

senses.d: To strive or contend for victory, with armies or in single combat; to attempt to defeat, subdue, or destroy an enemy, either by blows or weapons; to contend in arms; — followed by with or against.
q: You do fight against your country's foes.
To fight with thee no man of arms will deign.

senses.d: To act in opposition to anything; to struggle against; to contend; to strive; to make resistance.

Fight.etym: [OE. fihten, fehten, AS. feohtan; akin to D. vechten, OHG. fehtan, G. fechten, Sw. fäkta, Dan. fegte, and perh. to E. fist; cf. L. pugnare to fight, pugnus fist.]

senses.d: To carry on, or wage, as a conflict, or battle; to win or gain by struggle, as one's way; to sustain by fighting, as a cause.
q: He had to fight his way through the world.
I have fought a good fight.

senses.d: To contend with in battle; to war against; as, they fought the enemy in two pitched battles; the sloop fought the frigate for three hours.
To cause to fight; to manage or maneuver in a fight; as, to fight cocks; to fight one's ship.
A battle; an engagement; a contest in arms; a combat; a violent conflict or struggle for victory, between individuals or between armies, ships, or navies, etc.
q: Who now defies thee thrice to single fight.

senses.d: A struggle or contest of any kind.
Strength or disposition for fighting; pugnacity; as, he has a great deal of fight in him.
A screen for the combatants in ships.
q: Up with your fights, and your nettings prepare.

Fight.syn: Combat; engagement; contest; struggle; encounter; fray; affray; action; conflict. See Battle.
Fight.etym: [OE. fight, feht, AS. feoht. See Fight, v. i.]

senses.d: Qualified for war; fit for battle.
q: An host of fighting men.

senses.d: Occupied in war; being the scene of a battle; as, a fighting field.
The form of anything; shape; outline; appearance.
q: Flowers have all exquisite figures.

senses.d: The representation of any form, as by drawing, painting, modeling, carving, embroidering, etc.; especially, a representation of the human body; as, a figure in bronze; a figure cut in marble.
q: A coin that bears the figure of an angel.

senses.d: A pattern in cloth, paper, or other manufactured article; a design wrought out in a fabric; as, the muslin was of a pretty figure.

A diagram or drawing; made to represent a magnitude or the relation of two or more magnitudes; a surface or space inclosed on all sides; — called superficial when inclosed by lines, and solid when inclosed by surfaces; any arrangement made up of points, lines, angles, surfaces, etc.
The appearance or impression made by the conduct or career of a person; as, a sorry figure.
q: I made some figure there.
Gentlemen of the best figure in the county.

senses.d: Distinguished appearance; magnificence; conspicuous representation; splendor; show.
q: That he may live in figure and indulgence.

senses.d: A character or symbol representing a number; a numeral; a digit; as, 1, 2,3, etc.
Value, as expressed in numbers; price; as, the goods are estimated or sold at a low figure.
q: With nineteen thousand a year at the very lowest figure.

senses.d: A person, thing, or action, conceived of as analogous to another person, thing, or action, of which it thus becomes a type or representative.
q: Who is the figure of Him that was to come.

senses.d: A mode of expressing abstract or immaterial ideas by words which suggest pictures or images from the physical world; pictorial language; a trope; hence, any deviation from the plainest form of statement.
q: To represent the imagination under the figure of a wing.

senses.d: The form of a syllogism with respect to the relative position of the middle term.
Any one of the several regular steps or movements made by a dancer.

Figure.etym: [F., figure, L. figura; akin to fingere to form, shape, feign. See Feign.]

senses.d: To represent by a figure, as to form or mold; to make an image of, either palpable or ideal; also, to fashion into a determinate form; to shape.
q: If love, alas! be pain I bear,
No thought can figure, and no tongue declare.Prior.

senses.d: To embellish with design; to adorn with figures.
q: The vaulty top of heaven Figured quite o'er with burning meteors.

senses.d: To indicate by numerals; also, to compute.
q: As through a crystal glass the figured hours are seen.

senses.d: To represent by a metaphor; to signify or symbolize.
q: Whose white vestments figure innocence.

senses.d: To prefigure; to foreshow.
q: In this the heaven figures some event.

senses.d: To write over or under the bass, as figures or other characters, in order to indicate the accompanying chords.

Figure.etym: [F. figurer, L. figurare, fr. figura. See Figure, n.]

senses.d: To make a figure; to be distinguished or conspicious; as, the envoy figured at court.
q: Sociable, hospitable, eloquent, admired, figuring away brilliantly.

senses.d: To calculate; to contrive; to scheme; as, he is figuring to secure the nomination.
An orderly succession; a line; a row
An orderly collection of papers, arranged in sequence or classified for preservation and reference; as, files of letters or of newspapers; this mail brings English files to the 15th instant.
The line, wire, or other contrivance, by which papers are put and kept in order.
q: It is upon a file with the duke's other letters.

senses.d: A roll or list.
Course of thought; thread of narration.
q: Let me resume the file of my narration.

File.etym: [F. file row (cf. Pr., Sp., Pg., & It. fila), LL. fila, fr. L. filum a thread. Cf. Enfilade, Filament, Fillet.]

senses.d: To set in order; to arrange, or lay away, esp. as papers in a methodical manner for preservation and reverence; to place on file; to insert in its proper place in an arranged body of papers.
q: I would have my several courses and my dishes well filed.

senses.d: To bring before a court or legislative body by presenting proper papers in a regular way; as, to file a petition or bill.
To put upon the files or among the records of a court; to note on (a paper) the fact date of its reception in court.
q: To file a paper, on the part of a party, is to place it in the official custody of the clerk. To file, on the part of the clerk, is to indorse upon the paper the date of its reception, and retain it in his office, subject to inspection by whomsoever it may concern.

senses.d: To march in a file or line, as soldiers, not abreast, but one after another; — generally with off.
q: My endeavors Have ever come too short of my desires, Yet filed with my abilities.

senses.d: A steel instrument, having cutting ridges or teeth, made by indentation with a chisel, used for abrading or smoothing other substances, as metals, wood, etc.
Anything employed to smooth, polish, or rasp, literally or figuratively.
q: Mock the nice touches of the critic's file.

senses.d: A shrewd or artful person.
q: Will is an old file in spite of his smooth face.

File.etym: [AS. feól; akin to D. viji, OHG. fīla, fīhala, G. feile, Sw. fil, Dan. fiil, cf. Icel. þēl, Russ. pila, and Skr. piç to cut out, adorn; perh. akin to E. paint.]

senses.d: To rub, smooth, or cut away, with a file; to sharpen with a file; as, to file a saw or a tooth.
To smooth or polish as with a file.
q: File your tongue to a little more courtesy.

senses.d: To make foul; to defile.
q: All his hairy breast with blood was filed.
For Banquo's issue have I filed my mind.

File.etym: [OE. fulen, filen, foulen, AS. f�lan, fr. f�l foul. See Foul, and cf. Defile, v. t.]

senses.d: One of the thills or shafts of a carriage.
To make full; to supply with as much as can be held or contained; to put or pour into, till no more can be received; to occupy the whole capacity of.
q: The rain also filleth the pools.
Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. Anf they filled them up to the brim.

senses.d: To furnish an abudant supply to; to furnish with as mush as is desired or desirable; to occupy the whole of; to swarm in or overrun.
q: And God blessed them, saying. Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas.
The Syrians filled the country.

senses.d: To fill or supply fully with food; to feed; to satisfy.
q: Whence should we have so much bread in the wilderness, as to fillso great a multitude?
Things that are sweet and fat are more filling.

senses.d: To possess and perform the duties of; to officiate in, as an incumbent; to occupy; to hold; as, a king fills a throne; the president fills the office of chief magistrate; the speaker of the House fills the chair.
To supply with an incumbent; as, to fill an office or a vacancy.
To press and dilate, as a sail; as, the wind filled the sails.
To make an embankment in, or raise the level of (a low place), with earth or gravel.

Fill.etym: [OE. fillen, fullen, AS. fyllan, fr. full full; akin to D. vullen, G. füllen, Icel. fylla, Sw. fylla, Dan. fylde, Goth. fulljan. See Full, a.]

senses.d: To become full; to have the whole capacity occupied; to have an abundant supply; to be satiated; as, corn fills well in a warm season; the sail fills with the wind.
To fill a cup or glass for drinking.
q: Give me some wine; fill full.

senses.d: A full supply, as much as supplies want; as much as gives complete satisfaction.
q: I'll bear thee hence, where I may weep my fill.

senses.d: That which fills; filling; specif., an embankment, as in railroad construction, to fill a hollow or ravine; also, the place which is to be filled.
A little band, especially one intended to encircle the hair of the head.
q: A belt her waist, a fillet binds her hair.

senses.d: A piece of lean meat without bone; sometimes, a long strip rolled together and tied.
A thin strip or ribbon; esp.: (a) A strip of metal from which coins are punched. (b) A strip of card clothing. (c) A thin projecting band or strip.
A concave filling in of a reëntrant angle where two surfaces meet, forming a rounded corner.
A narrow flat member; especially, a flat molding separating other moldings; a reglet; also, the space between two flutings in a shaft. See Illust. of Base, and Column.
An ordinary equaling in breadth one fourth of the chief, to the lowest portion of which it corresponds in position.
The thread of a screw.
A border of broad or narrow lines of color or gilt.
The raised molding about the muzzle of a gun.
Any scantling smaller than a batten.
A fascia; a band of fibers; applied esp. to certain bands of white matter in the brain.
The loins of a horse, beginning at the place where the hinder part of the saddle rests.

Fillet.etym: [OE. filet, felet, fr. OF. filet thread, fillet of meat, dim. of fil a thread, fr. L. filum. See Fille a row.]

senses.d: To bind, furnish, or adorn with a fillet.

That which is used to fill a cavity or any empty space, or to supply a deficiency; as, filling for a cavity in a tooth, a depression in a roadbed, the space between exterior and interior walls of masonry, the pores of open-grained wood, the space between the outer and inner planks of a vessel, etc.
The woof in woven fabrics.
Prepared wort added to ale to cleanse it.
Foul matter; anything that soils or defiles; dirt; nastiness.
Anything that sullies or defiles the moral character; corruption; pollution.
q: To purify the soul from the dross and filth of sensual delights.

Filth.etym: [OE. filthe, fulðe, AS. f�lð, fr. fūl foul; akin to OHG. fūlida. See Foul, and cf. File.]

senses.d: The state of being filthy.
q: Let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit.

senses.d: That which is filthy, or makes filthy; foulness; nastiness; corruption; pollution; impurity.
q: Carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place.

senses.d: Defiled with filth, whether material or moral; nasty; dirty; polluted; foul; impure; obscene.
q: He which is filthy let him be filthy still.

Filthy.syn: Nasty; foul; dirty; squalid; unclean; sluttish; gross; vulgar; licentious. See Nasty.

senses.d: To carve or cut up, as a chub.
End; conclusion; object.
An organ of a fish, consisting of a membrane supported by rays, or little bony or cartilaginous ossicles, and serving to balance and propel it in the water.
A membranous, finlike, swimming organ, as in pteropod and heteropod mollusks.
A finlike organ or attachment; a part of an object or product which protrudes like a fin
A mark or ridge left on a casting at the junction of the parts of a mold.
The thin sheet of metal squeezed out between the collars of the rolls in the process of rolling.
A feather; a spline.
A finlike appendage, as to submarine boats.

Fin.etym: [OE. finne, fin, AS. finn; akin to D. vin, G. & Dan. finne, Sw. fena, L. pinna, penna, a wing, feather. Cf. pen a feather.]

senses.d: A fixed stabilizing surface, usually vertical, similar in purpose to a bilge keel on a ship.
Pertaining to the end or conclusion; last; terminating; ultimate; as, the final day of a school term.
q: Yet despair not of his final pardon.

senses.d: Conclusive; decisive; as, a final judgment; the battle of Waterloo brought the contest to a final issue.
Respecting an end or object to be gained; respecting the purpose or ultimate end in view.

Final.etym: [F., fr. L. finalis, fr. finis boundary, limit, end. See Finish.]

senses.d: At the end or conclusion; ultimately; lastly; as, the contest was long, but the Romans finally conquered.
q: Whom patience finally must crown.

senses.d: Completely; beyond recovery.
q: Not any house of noble English in Ireland was utterly destroyed or finally rooted out.

senses.d: To meet with, or light upon, accidentally; to gain the first sight or knowledge of, as of something new, or unknown; hence, to fall in with, as a person.
q: Searching the window for a flint, I found This paper, thus sealed up.
In woods and forests thou art found.

senses.d: To learn by experience or trial; to perceive; to experience; to discover by the intellect or the feelings; to detect; to feel.
q: The torrid zone is now found habitable.

senses.d: To come upon by seeking; as, to find something lost.
q: Seek, and ye shall find.
Every mountain now hath found a tongue.

senses.d: To provide for; to supply; to furnish; as, to find food for workemen; he finds his nephew in money.
q: Wages £14 and all found.
Nothing a day and find yourself.

senses.d: To arrive at, as a conclusion; to determine as true; to establish; as, to find a verdict; to find a true bill (of indictment) against an accused person.
q: To find his title with some shows of truth.

Find.etym: [AS. findan; akin to D. vinden, OS. & OHG. findan, G. finden, Dan. finde, icel. & Sw. finna, Goth. finþan; and perh. to L. petere to seek, Gr. πίπτειν to fall, Skr. pat to fall, fly, E. petition.]

senses.d: To determine an issue of fact, and to declare such a determination to a court; as, the jury find for the plaintiff.
Anything found; a discovery of anything valuable; especially, a deposit, discovered by archæologists, of objects of prehistoric or unknown origin.
That which is found, come upon, or provided; esp. (pl.), that which a journeyman artisan finds or provides for himself; as tools, trimmings, etc.
q: When a man hath been laboring . . . in the deep mines of knowledge, hath furnished out his findings in all their equipage.

senses.d: Support; maintenance; that which is provided for one; expence; provision.
The result of a judicial examination or inquiry, especially into some matter of fact; a verdict; as, the finding of a jury.
q: After his friends finding and his rent.

senses.d: Finished; brought to perfection; refined; hence, free from impurity; excellent; superior; elegant; worthy of admiration; accomplished; beautiful.
q: The gain thereof than fine gold.
A cup of wine that's brisk and fine.
Not only the finest gentleman of his time, but one of the finest scholars.
To soothe the sick bed of so fine a being .

senses.d: Aiming at show or effect; loaded with ornament; overdressed or overdecorated; showy.
q: He gratified them with occasional . . . fine writing.

senses.d: Nice; delicate; subtle; exquisite; artful; skillful; dexterous.
q: The spider's touch, how exquisitely fine!
The nicest and most delicate touches of satire consist in fine raillery.
He has as fine a hand at picking a pocket as a woman.

senses.d: Not coarse, gross, or heavy
q: The eye standeth in the finer medium and the object in the grosser.

senses.d: Not coarse; comminuted; in small particles; as, fine sand or flour.
Not thick or heavy; slender; filmy; as, a fine thread.
Thin; attenuate; keen; as, a fine edge.
Made of fine materials; light; delicate; as, fine linen or silk.
Having (such) a proportion of pure metal in its composition; as, coins nine tenths fine.
(Used ironically.)
q: Ye have made a fine hand, fellows.

Fine.etym: [F. fin, LL. finus fine, pure, fr. L. finire to finish; cf. finitus, p. p., finished, completed (hence the sense accomplished, perfect.) See Finish, and cf. Finite.]

senses.d: To make fine; to refine; to purify, to clarify; as, to fine gold.
q: It hath been fined and refined by . . . learned men.

senses.d: To make finer, or less coarse, as in bulk, texture, etc.; as. to fine the soil.
To change by fine gradations; as (Naut.), to fine down a ship's lines, to diminish her lines gradually.
q: I often sate at home On evenings, watching how they fined themselves With gradual conscience to a perfect night.

senses.d: End; conclusion; termination; extinction.
q: Is this the fine of his fines?

senses.d: A sum of money paid as the settlement of a claim, or by way of terminating a matter in dispute; especially, a payment of money imposed upon a party as a punishment for an offense; a mulct.
A final agreement concerning lands or rents between persons, as the lord and his vassal.
A sum of money or price paid for obtaining a benefit, favor, or privilege, as for admission to a copyhold, or for obtaining or renewing a lease.

Fine.etym: [OE. fin, L. finis end, also in LL., a final agreement or concord between the lord and his vassal; a sum of money paid at the end, so as to make an end of a transaction, suit, or prosecution; mulct; penalty; cf. OF. fin end, settlement, F. fin end. See Finish, and cf. Finance.]

senses.d: To impose a pecuniary penalty upon for an offense or breach of law; to set a fine on by judgment of a court; to punish by fine; to mulct; as, the trespassers were fined ten dollars.
To pay a fine. See Fine, n., 3 (b).
q: Men fined for the king's good will; or that he would remit his anger; women fined for leave to marry.

senses.d: To finish; to cease; or to cause to cease.

Fine.etym: [OF. finer, F. finir. See Finish, v. t.]

senses.d: Finely; well; elegantly; fully; delicately; mincingly.
In a manner so that the driven ball strikes the object ball so far to one side as to be deflected but little, the object ball being driven to one side.
To become fine (in any one of various senses); as, the ale will fine; the weather fined.
q: I watched her . . . gradually fining down in the westward until I lost of her hull.

senses.d: One who fines or purifies.
One of the five terminating members of the hand; a digit; esp., one of the four extremities of the hand, other than the thumb.

Anything that does the work of a finger; as, the pointer of a clock, watch, or other registering machine; especially (Mech.) a small projecting rod, wire, or piece, which is brought into contact with an object to effect, direct, or restrain a motion.

The breadth of a finger, or the fourth part of the hand; a measure of nearly an inch; also, the length of finger, a measure in domestic use in the United States, of about four and a half inches or one eighth of a yard.
q: A piece of steel three fingers thick.

senses.d: Skill in the use of the fingers, as in playing upon a musical instrument.
q: She has a good finger.

Finger.etym: [AS. finger; akin to D. vinger, OS. & OHG. fingar, G. finger, Icel. fingr, Sw. & Dan. finger, Goth. figgrs; of unknown origin; perh. akin to E. fang.]

senses.d: To touch with the fingers; to handle; to meddle with.
q: Let the papers lie; You would be fingering them to anger me.

senses.d: To touch lightly; to toy with.
To perform on an instrument of music.
To take thievishly; to pilfer; to purloin.
To execute, as any delicate work.
To use the fingers in playing on an instrument.
The act of imposing a fin�.
The process of fining or refining; clarification; also (Metal.), the conversion of cast iron into suitable for puddling, in a hearth or charcoal fire.
That which is used to refine; especially, a preparation of isinglass, gelatin, etc., for clarifying beer.
To arrive at the end of; to bring to an end; to put an end to; to make an end of; to terminate.
q: And heroically hath finished A life heroic.

senses.d: To bestow the last required labor upon; to complete; to bestow the utmost possible labor upon; to perfect; to accomplish; to polish.

Finish.syn: To end; terminate; close; conclude; complete; accomplish; perfect.
Finish.etym: [F. finir (with a stem finiss- in several forms, whence E. -ish: see -ish.),fr. L. finire to limit, finish, end, fr. finis boundary, limit, end; perh. for fidnis, and akin findere to cleave, E. fissure.]

senses.d: To come to an end; to terminate.
q: His days may finish ere that hapless time.

senses.d: To end; to die.
That which finishes, puts an end to� or perfects.
The joiner work and other finer work required for the completion of a building, especially of the interior. See Inside finish, and Outside finish.
The labor required to give final completion to any work; hence, minute detail, careful elaboration, or the like.
The result of completed labor, as on the surface of an object; manner or style of finishing; as, a rough, dead, or glossy finish given to cloth, stone, metal, etc.
Completion; — opposed to start, or beginning.
Polished to the highest degree of excellence; complete; perfect; as, a finished poem; a finished education.

One who finishes, puts an end to, completes, or perfects; esp. used in the trades, as in hatting, weaving, etc., for the workman who gives a finishing touch to the work, or any part of it, and brings it to perfection.
q: O prophet of glad tidings, finisher Of utmost hope!

senses.d: Something that gives the finishing touch to, or settles, anything.

A genus (Abies) of coniferous trees, often of large size and elegant shape, some of them valued for their timber and others for their resin. The species are distinguished as the balsam fir, the silver fir, the red fir, etc. The Scotch fir is a Pinus.

Fir.etym: [Dan. fyr, fyrr; akin to Sw. furu, Icel. fura, AS. furh in furhwudu fir wood, G. föhre, OHG. forha pine, vereheih a sort of oak, L. quercus oak.]

senses.d: The evolution of light and heat in the combustion of bodies; combustion; state of ignition.
Fuel in a state of combustion, as on a hearth, or in a stove or a furnace.
The burning of a house or town; a conflagration.
Anything which destroys or affects like fire.
Ardor of passion, whether love or hate; excessive warmth; consuming violence of temper.
q: he had fire in his temper.

senses.d: Liveliness of imagination or fancy; intellectual and moral enthusiasm; capacity for ardor and zeal.
q: And bless their critic with a poet's fire.

senses.d: Splendor; brilliancy; luster; hence, a star.
q: Stars, hide your fires.
As in a zodiac representing the heavenly fires.

senses.d: Torture by burning; severe trial or affliction.
The discharge of firearms; firing; as, the troops were exposed to a heavy fire.

Fire.etym: [OE. fir, fyr, fur AS. fȳr; akin to D. vuur, OS. & OHG. fiur, G. feuer, Icel. fȳri, fūrr, Gr. πυ̑ρ, and perh. to L. purus pure, E. pure Cf. Empyrean, Pyre.]

senses.d: To set on fire; to kindle; as, to fire a house or chimney; to fire a pile.
To subject to intense heat; to bake; to burn in a kiln; as, to fire pottery.
To inflame; to irritate, as the passions; as, to fire the soul with anger, pride, or revenge.
q: Love had fired my mind.

senses.d: To animate; to give life or spirit to; as, to fire the genius of a young man.
To feed or serve the fire of; as, to fire a boiler.
To light up as if by fire; to illuminate.
q: fires the proud tops of the eastern pines.

senses.d: To cause to explode; as, to fire a torpedo; to disharge; as, to fire a musket or cannon; to fire cannon balls, rockets, etc.
To drive by fire.
q: Till my bad angel fire my good one out.

senses.d: To cauterize.
To take fire; to be kindled; to kindle.
To be irritated or inflamed with passion.
To discharge artillery or firearms; as, they fired on the town.
A piece of burning wood.
One who inflames factions, or causes contention and mischief; an incendiary.
A varying measure of capacity, usually being the fourth part of a barrel; specifically, a measure equal to nine imperial gallons.
A small wooden vessel or cask of indeterminate size, — used for butter, lard, etc.

Firkin.etym: [From AS. feówer four (or an allied word, perh. Dutch or Danish) + -kin. See Four.]

senses.d: Fixed; hence, closely compressed; compact; substantial; hard; solid; — applied to the matter of bodies; as, firm flesh; firm muscles, firm wood.
Not easily excited or disturbed; unchanging in purpose; fixed; steady; constant; stable; unshaken; not easily changed in feelings or will; strong; as, a firm believer; a firm friend; a firm adherent.
q: Under spread ensigns, moving nigh, in slow But firm battalion.
By one man's firm obediency fully tried.

senses.d: Solid; — opposed to fluid; as, firm land.
Indicating firmness; as, a firm tread; a firm countenance.

Firm.syn: Compact; dense; hard; solid; stanch; robust; strong; sturdly; fixed; steady; resolute; constant.
Firm.etym: [OE. ferme, F. ferme, fr.L. firmus; cf. Skr. dharman support, law, order, dh� to hold fast, carry. Cf. Farm, Throne.]

senses.d: The name, title, or style, under which a company transacts business; a partnership of two or more persons; a commercial house; as, the firm of Hope & Co.

Firm.etym: [It. firma the (firm, sure, or confirming) signature or subscription, or Pg. firma signature, firm, cf. Sp. firma signature; all fr. L. firmus, adj., firm. See Firm, a.]

senses.d: To fix; to settle; to confirm; to establish.
q: And Jove has firmed it with an awful nod.

senses.d: To fix or direct with firmness.
q: He on his card and compass firms his eye.

Firm.etym: [OE. fermen to make firm, F. fermer, fr. L. firmare to make firm. See Firm, a.]

senses.d: Fixed foundation; established basis.
q: Custom is the . . . firmament of the law.

senses.d: The region of the air; the sky or heavens.
q: And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.
And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament.

senses.d: The orb of the fixed stars; the most rmote of the celestial spheres.

Firmament.etym: [L. firmamentum, fr. firmare to make firm: cf. F. firmament. See Firm, v. & a.]

senses.d: Preceding all others of a series or kind; the ordinal of one; earliest; as, the first day of a month; the first year of a reign.
Foremost; in front of, or in advance of, all others.
Most eminent or exalted; most excellent; chief; highest; as, Demosthenes was the first orator of Greece.

First.syn: Primary; primordial; primitive; primeval; pristine; highest; chief; principal; foremost.
First.etym: [OE. first, furst, AS. fyrst; akin to Icel. fyrstr, Sw. & Dan. förste, OHG. furist, G. fürst prince; a superlatiye form of E. for, fore. See For, Fore, and cf. Formeer, Foremost.]

senses.d: Before any other person or thing in time, space, rank, etc.; — much used in composition with adjectives and participles.
q: Adam was first formed, then Eve.
And all are fools and lovers first or last.

senses.d: The upper part of a duet, trio, etc., either vocal or instrumental; — so called because it generally expresses the air, and has a preëminence in the combined effect.
First brought forth; first in the order of nativity; eldest; hence, most excellent; most distinguished or exalted.
The first produce or offspring; — said of animals, especially domestic animals; as, the firstlings of his flock.
The thing first thought or done.
q: The very firstlings of my heart shall be The firstlings of my hand.

senses.d: Firstborn.
q: All the firstling males.

senses.d: A counter, used in various games.

Fish.etym: [F. fiche peg, mark, fr. fisher to fix.]

senses.d: A name loosely applied in popular usage to many animals of diverse characteristics, living in the water.
An oviparous, vertebrate animal usually having fins and a covering scales or plates. It breathes by means of gills, and lives almost entirely in the water. See Pisces.
The twelfth sign of the zodiac; Pisces.
The flesh of fish, used as food.
A purchase used to fish the anchor.

Fish.etym: [OE. fisch, fisc, fis, AS. fisc; akin to D. visch, OS. & OHG. fisk, G. fisch, Icel. fiskr, Sw. & Dan. fisk, Goth. fisks, L. piscis, Ir. iasg. Cf. Piscatorial. In some cases, such as fish joint, fish plate, this word has prob. been confused with fish, fr. F. fichea peg.]

senses.d: To attempt to catch fish; to be employed in taking fish, by any means, as by angling or drawing a net.
To seek to obtain by artifice, or indirectly to seek to draw forth; as, to fish for compliments.
q: Any other fishing question.

senses.d: To catch; to draw out or up; as, to fish up an anchor.
To search by raking or sweeping.
To try with a fishing rod; to catch fish in; as, to fish a stream.

To strengthen (a beam, mast, etc.), or unite end to end (two timbers, railroad rails, etc.) by bolting a plank, timber, or plate to the beam, mast, or timbers, lengthwise on one or both sides. See Fish joint, under Fish, n.

Fish.etym: [OE. fischen, fisken, fissen, AS. fiscian; akin to G. fischen, OHG. fisc�n, Goth. fisk�n. See Fish the animal.]

senses.d: One who fishes.
A carnivorous animal of the Weasel family (Mustela Canadensis); the pekan; the “black cat.”
A hook for catching fish.
A hook with a pendant, to the end of which the fish-tackle is hooked.
The act, practice, or art of one who fishes.
A fishery.
Pertaining to fishing; used in fishery; engaged in fishing; as, fishing boat; fishing tackle; fishing village.
The hand with the fingers doubled into the palm; the closed hand, especially as clinched tightly for the purpose of striking a blow.
q: Who grasp the earth and heaven with my fist.

senses.d: The talons of a bird of prey.
q: More light than culver in the falcon's fist.

senses.d: the index mark , used to direct special attention to the passage which follows.

Fist.etym: [OE. fist, fust, AS. fȳst; akin to D. vuist, OHG. fūst, G. faust, and prob. to L. pugnus, Gr. πυγμή fist, πύξ with the fist. Cf. Pugnacious, Pigmy.]

senses.d: To strike with the fist.
To gripe with the fist.
In Old English, a song; a strain; a canto or portion of a ballad; a passus.
q: To play some pleasant fit.

senses.d: Adapted to an end, object, or design; suitable by nature or by art; suited by character, qualities, circumstances, education, etc.; qualified; competent; worthy.
q: That which ordinary men are fit for, I am qualified in.
Fit audience find, though few.

senses.d: Prepared; ready.
q: So fit to shoot, she singled forth among her foes who first her quarry's strength should feel.

senses.d: Conformed to a standart of duty, properiety, or taste; convenient; meet; becoming; proper.
q: Is it fit to say a king, Thou art wicked?

Fit.syn: Suitable; proper; appropriate; meet; becoming; expedient; congruous; correspondent; apposite; apt; adapted; prepared; qualified; competent; adequate.
Fit.etym: [OE. fit, fyt; cf. E. feat neat, elegant, well made, or icel. fitja to web, knit, OD. vitten to suit, square, Goth. fētjan to adorn. √77.]

senses.d: To make fit or suitable; to adapt to the purpose intended; to qualify; to put into a condition of readiness or preparation.
q: The time is fitted for the duty.
The very situation for which he was peculiarly fitted by nature.

senses.d: To bring to a required form and size; to shape aright; to adapt to a model; to adjust; — said especially of the work of a carpenter, machinist, tailor, etc.
q: The carpenter . . . marketh it out with a line; he fitteth it with planes.

senses.d: To supply with something that is suitable or fit, or that is shaped and adjusted to the use required.
q: No milliner can so fit his customers with gloves.

senses.d: To be suitable to; to answer the requirements of; to be correctly shaped and adjusted to; as, if the coat fits you, put it on.
q: That's a bountiful answer that fits all questions.
That time best fits the work.

senses.d: To be proper or becoming.
q: Nor fits it to prolong the feast.

senses.d: To be adjusted to a particular shape or size; to suit; to be adapted; as, his coat fits very well.
The quality of being fit; adjustment; adaptedness; as of dress to the person of the wearer.
The coincidence of parts that come in contact.
A stroke or blow.
q: Curse on that cross, quoth then the Sarazin, That keeps thy body from the bitter fit.

senses.d: A sudden and violent attack of a disorder; a stroke of disease, as of epilepsy or apoplexy, which produces convulsions or unconsciousness; a convulsion; a paroxysm; hence, a period of exacerbation of a disease; in general, an attack of disease; as, a fit of sickness.
q: And when the fit was on him, I did mark How he did shake.

senses.d: A mood of any kind which masters or possesses one for a time; a temporary, absorbing affection; a paroxysm; as, a fit of melancholy, of passion, or of laughter.
q: All fits of pleasure we balanced by an equal degree of pain.
The English, however, were on this subject prone to fits of jealously.

senses.d: A passing humor; a caprice; a sudden and unusual effort, activity, or motion, followed by relaxation or inaction; an impulsive and irregular action.
q: The fits of the season.

senses.d: A darting point; a sudden emission.
q: A tongue of light, a fit of flame.

Fit.etym: [AS. fit strife, fight; of uncertain origin. √ 77.]

senses.d: A vetch.

A word found in the Authorized Version of the Bible, representing different Hebrew originals. In Isaiah xxviii. 25, 27, it means the black aromatic seeds of Nigella sativa, still used as a flavoring in the East. In Ezekiel iv. 9, the Revised Version now reads spelt.
The European polecat; also, its fur.
In a fit manner; suitably; properly; conveniently; as, a maxim fitly applied.
Four and one added; one more than four.

Five.etym: [OE. fif, five, AS. fīf, fīfe; akin to D. vijf, OS. fīf, OHG. finf, funf, G. fünf, Icel. fimm, Sw. & Sw. Dan. fem, Goth. fimf, Lith. penki, W. pump, OIr. cóic, L. quinque, Gr. �, Æol. �, Skr. pa�can. √303. Cf. Fifth, Cinque, Pentagon, Punch the drink, Quinary.]

senses.d: The number next greater than four, and less than six; five units or objects.
q: Five of them were wise, and five were foolish.

senses.d: A symbol representing this number, as 5, or V.
Fixed; solidified.

Fix.etym: [OE., fr. L. fixus, p. p. of figere to fix; cf. F. fixe.]

senses.d: To make firm, stable, or fast; to set or place permanently; to fasten immovably; to establish; to implant; to secure; to make definite.
q: An ass's nole I fixed on his head.
O, fix thy chair of grace, that all my powers May also fix their reverence.
His heart is fixed, trusting in the Lord.
And fix far deeper in his head their stings.

senses.d: To hold steadily; to direct unwaveringly; to fasten, as the eye on an object, the attention on a speaker.
q: Sat fixed in thought the mighty Stagirite.
One eye on death, and one full fix'd on heaven.

senses.d: To transfix; to pierce.
To render (an impression) permanent by treating with such applications as will make it insensible to the action of light.

To put in order; to arrange; to dispose of; to adjust; to set to rights; to set or place in the manner desired or most suitable; hence, to repair; as, to fix the clothes; to fix the furniture of a room.
To line the hearth of (a puddling furnace) with fettling.

Fix.syn: To arrange; prepare; adjust; place; establish; settle; determine.

senses.d: To become fixed; to settle or remain permanently; to cease from wandering; to rest.
q: Your kindness banishes your fear, Resolved to fix forever here.

senses.d: To become firm, so as to resist volatilization; to cease to flow or be fluid; to congeal; to become hard and malleable, as a metallic substance.
A position of difficulty or embarassment; predicament; dilemma.
q: Is he not living, then? No. is he dead, then? No, nor dead either. Poor Aroar can not live, and can not die, — so that he is in an almighty fix.

senses.d: fettling.
Securely placed or fastened; settled; established; firm; imovable; unalterable.
Stable; non-volatile.
To hang loose without stiffness; to bend down, as flexible bodies; to be loose, yielding, limp.
q: As loose it flagged around the mast.

senses.d: To droop; to grow spiritless; to lose vigor; to languish; as, the spirits flag; the strength flags.
q: The pleasures of the town begin to flag.

Flag.syn: To droop; decline; fail; languish; pine.
Flag.etym: [Cf. Icel. flaka to droop, hang loosely. Cf. Flacker, Flag an ensign.]

senses.d: To let droop; to suffer to fall, or let fall, into feebleness; as, to flag the wings.
To enervate; to exhaust the vigor or elasticity of.
q: Nothing so flags the spirits.

senses.d: That which flags or hangs down loosely.

A cloth usually bearing a device or devices and used to indicate nationality, party, etc., or to give or ask information; — commonly attached to a staff to be waved by the wind; a standard; a banner; an ensign; the colors; as, the national flag; a military or a naval flag.
A group of feathers on the lower part of the legs of certain hawks, owls, etc.

Flag.etym: [Cf. LG. & G. flagge, Sw. flagg, Dan. flag, D. vlag. See Flag to hang loose.]

senses.d: To signal to with a flag; as, to flag a train.
To convey, as a message, by means of flag signals; as, to flag an order to troops or vessels at a distance.
An aquatic plant, with long, ensiform leaves, belonging to either of the genera Iris and Acorus.

Flag.etym: [From Flag to hang loose, to bend down.]

senses.d: To furnish or deck out with flags.
A flat stone used for paving.
Any hard, evenly stratified sandstone, which splits into layers suitable for flagstones.

Flag.etym: [Icel. flaga, cf. Icel. flag spot where a turf has been cut out, and E. flake layer, scale. Cf. Floe.]

senses.d: To lay with flags of flat stones.
q: The sides and floor are all flagged with . . . marble.

senses.d: One of the wing feathers next the body of a bird; — called also flag feather.
To decoy (game) by waving a flag, handkerchief, or the like to arouse the animal's curiosity.
q: The antelope are getting continually shyer and more difficult to flag.

senses.d: A vessel with a narrow mouth, used for holding and conveying liquors. It is generally larger than a bottle, and of leather or stoneware rather than of glass.
q: A trencher of mutton chops, and a flagon of ale.

Flagon.etym: [F. flacon, for flascon, fr. OF. flasche, from LL. flasco. See Flask.]

senses.d: A paling; a hurdle.
A platform of hurdles, or small sticks made fast or interwoven, supported by stanchions, for drying codfish and other things.
q: You shall also, after they be ripe, neither suffer them to have straw nor fern under them, but lay them either upon some smooth table, boards, or flakes of wands, and they will last the longer.

senses.d: A small stage hung over a vessel's side, for workmen to stand on in calking, etc.

Flake.etym: [Cf. Icel. flaki, fleki, Dan. flage, D. vlaak.]

senses.d: A loose filmy mass or a thin chiplike layer of anything; a film; flock; lamina; layer; scale; as, a flake of snow, tallow, or fish.
q: Great flakes of ice encompassing our boat.

senses.d: A little particle of lighted or incandescent matter, darted from a fire; a flash.
q: With flakes of ruddy fire.

senses.d: A sort of carnation with only two colors in the flower, the petals having large stripes.

Flake.etym: [Cf. Icel. flakna to flake off, split, flagna to flake off, Sw. flaga flaw, flake, flake plate, Dan. flage snowflake. Cf. Flag a flat stone.]

senses.d: To form into flakes.
To separate in flakes; to peel or scale off.
A flat layer, or fake, of a coiled cable.
q: Flake after flake ran out of the tubs, until we were compelled to hand the end of our line to the second mate.

senses.d: A freak or whim; also, a falsehood; a lie; an illusory pretext; deception; delusion.
q: A perpetual abuse and flam upon posterity.

Flam.etym: [Cf. AS. fleám, flǣm, flight. √ 84 . Cf. Flimflam.]

senses.d: To deceive with a falsehood.
q: God is not to be flammed off with lies.

senses.d: A stream of burning vapor or gas, emitting light and heat; darting or streaming fire; a blaze; a fire.
Burning zeal or passion; elevated and noble enthusiasm; glowing imagination; passionate excitement or anger.
q: Where flames refin'd in breasts seraphic glow.
Smit with the love of sister arts we came, And met congenial, mingling flame with flame.

senses.d: Ardor of affection; the passion of love.
A person beloved; a sweetheart.

Flame.etym: [OE. flame, flaume, flaumbe, OF. flame, flambe, F. flamme, fr. L. flamma, fr. flamma, fr. flagrare to burn. See Flagrant, and cf. Flamneau, Flamingo.]

senses.d: To burn with a flame or blaze; to burn as gas emitted from bodies in combustion; to blaze.
q: The main blaze of it is past, but a small thing would make it flame again.

senses.d: To burst forth like flame; to break out in violence of passion; to be kindled with zeal or ardor.
q: He flamed with indignation.

Flame.etym: [OE. flamen, flaumben, F. flamber, OF. also, flamer. See Flame, n.]

senses.d: To kindle; to inflame; to excite.
q: And flamed with zeal of vengeance inwardly.

senses.d: Emitting flames; afire; blazing; consuming; illuminating.
Of the color of flame; high-colored; brilliant; dazzling.
Ardent; passionate; burning with zeal; irrepressibly earnest; as, a flaming proclomation or harangue.
The fleshy or muscular part of the side of an animal, between the ribs and the hip. See Illust. of Beef.
The side of an army, or of any division of an army, as of a brigade, regiment, or battalion; the extreme right or left; as, to attack an enemy in flank is to attack him on the side.
q: When to right and left the front
Divided, and to either flank retired.

senses.d: That part of a bastion which reaches from the curtain to the face, and defends the curtain, the flank and face of the opposite bastion; any part of a work defending another by a fire along the outside of its parapet.
The side of any building.
That part of the acting surface of a gear wheel tooth that lies within the pitch line.

Flank.etym: [F. flanc, prob. fr. L. flaccus flabby, with n inserted. Cf. Flaccid, Flanch, Flange.]

senses.d: To stand at the flank or side of; to border upon.
q: Stately colonnades are flanked with trees.

senses.d: To overlook or command the flank of; to secure or guard the flank of; to pass around or turn the flank of; to attack, or threaten to attack; the flank of.

Flank.etym: [Cf. F. flanquer. See Flank, n., and cf. Flanker, v. t.]

senses.d: To border; to touch.
To be posted on the side.
To burst or break forth with a sudden and transient flood of flame and light; as, the lighting flashes vividly; the powder flashed.
To break forth, as a sudden flood of light; to burst instantly and brightly on the sight; to show a momentary brilliancy; to come or pass like a flash.
q: Names which have flashed and thundered as the watch words of unnumbered struggles.
The object is made to flash upon the eye of the mind.
A thought flashed through me, which I clothed in act.

senses.d: To burst forth like a sudden flame; to break out violently; to rush hastily.
q: Every hour He flashes into one gross crime or other.

Flash.etym: [Cf. OE. flaskien, vlaskien to pour, sprinkle, dial. Sw. flasa to blaze, E. flush, flare.]

senses.d: To send out in flashes; to cause to burst forth with sudden flame or light.
q: The chariot of paternal Deity, Flashing thick flames.

senses.d: To convey as by a flash; to light up, as by a sudden flame or light; as, to flash a message along the wires; to flash conviction on the mind.
To cover with a thin layer, as objects of glass with glass of a different color. See Flashing, n., 3 (b).
To trick up in a showy manner.
q: Limning and flashing it with various dyes.

senses.d: To strike and throw up large bodies of water from the surface; to splash.
q: He rudely flashed the waves about.

senses.d: A sudden burst of light; a flood of light instantaneously appearing and disappearing; a momentary blaze; as, a flash of lightning.
A sudden and brilliant burst, as of wit or genius; a momentary brightness or show.
q: The flash and outbreak of a fiery mind.
No striking sentiment, no flash of fancy.

senses.d: The time during which a flash is visible; an instant; a very brief period.
q: The Persians and Macedonians had it for a flash.

senses.d: A preparation of capsicum, burnt sugar, etc., for coloring and giving a fictitious strength to liquors.
Showy, but counterfeit; cheap, pretentious, and vulgar; as, flash jewelry; flash finery.

Wearing showy, counterfeit ornaments; vulgarly pretentious; as, flash people; flash men or women; — applied especially to thieves, gamblers, and prostitutes that dress in a showy way and wear much cheap jewelry.
Slang or cant of thieves and prostitutes.
A pool.
A reservoir and sluiceway beside a navigable stream, just above a shoal, so that the stream may pour in water as boats pass, and thus bear them over the shoal.

Flash.etym: [OE. flasche, flaske; cf. OF. flache, F. flaque.]

senses.d: Having an even and horizontal surface, or nearly so, without prominences or depressions; level without inclination; plane.
q: Though sun and moon Were in the flat sea sunk.

senses.d: Lying at full length, or spread out, upon the ground; level with the ground or earth; prostrate; as, to lie flat on the ground; hence, fallen; laid low; ruined; destroyed.
q: What ruins kingdoms, and lays cities flat!
I feel . . . my hopes all flat.

senses.d: Wanting relief; destitute of variety; without points of prominence and striking interest.
q: A large part of the work is, to me, very flat.

senses.d: Tasteless; stale; vapid; insipid; dead; as, fruit or drink flat to the taste.
Unanimated; dull; uninteresting; without point or spirit; monotonous; as, a flat speech or composition.
q: How weary, stale, flat, and unprofitable Seem to me all the uses of this world.

senses.d: Lacking liveliness of commercial exchange and dealings; depressed; dull; as, the market is flat.
Clear; unmistakable; peremptory; absolute; positive; downright.
q: Flat burglary as ever was committed.
A great tobacco taker too, — that's flat.

senses.d: Below the true pitch; hence, as applied to intervals, minor, or lower by a half step; as, a flat seventh; A flat.
Sonant; vocal; — applied to any one of the sonant or vocal consonants, as distinguished from a nonsonant (or sharp) consonant.

Flat.etym: [Akin to Icel. flatr, Sw. flat, Dan. flad, OHG. flaz, and AS. flet floor, G. flötz stratum, layer.]

senses.d: In a flat manner; directly; flatly.
q: Sin is flat opposite to the Almighty.

senses.d: Without allowance for accrued interest.
A level surface, without elevation, relief, or prominences; an extended plain; specifically, in the United States, a level tract along the along the banks of a river; as, the Mohawk Flats.
q: Envy is as the sunbeams that beat hotter upon a bank, or steep rising ground, than upon a flat.

senses.d: A level tract lying at little depth below the surface of water, or alternately covered and left bare by the tide; a shoal; a shallow; a strand.
q: Half my power, this night Passing these flats, are taken by the tide.

senses.d: Something broad and flat in form
The flat part, or side, of anything; as, the broad side of a blade, as distinguished from its edge.
A floor, loft, or story in a building; especially, a floor of a house, which forms a complete residence in itself.
A horizontal vein or ore deposit auxiliary to a main vein; also, any horizontal portion of a vein not elsewhere horizontal.
A dull fellow; a simpleton; a numskull.
q: Or if you can not make a speech, Because you are a flat.

senses.d: A character before a note, indicating a tone which is a half step or semitone lower.
A homaloid space or extension.
To make flat; to flatten; to level.
To render dull, insipid, or spiritless; to depress.
q: Passions are allayed, appetites are flatted.

senses.d: To depress in tone, as a musical note; especially, to lower in pitch by half a tone.
To become flat, or flattened; to sink or fall to an even surface.
To fall form the pitch.
Having a head at a very obtuse angle to the shaft; — said of a club.

Not having an inflectional ending or sign, as a noun used as an adjective, or an adjective as an adverb, without the addition of a formative suffix, or an infinitive without the sign to. Many flat adverbs, as in run fast, buy cheap, are from AS. adverbs in -ë, the loss of this ending having made them like the adjectives. Some having forms in ly, such as exceeding, wonderful, true, are now archaic.
Flattening at the ends; — said of certain fruits.
One who, or that which, makes flat or flattens.
A flat-faced fulling hammer.
To treat with praise or blandishments; to gratify or attempt to gratify the self-love or vanity of, esp. by artful and interested commendation or attentions; to blandish; to cajole; to wheedle.
q: When I tell him he hates flatterers, He says he does, being then most flattered.
A man that flattereth his neighbor, spreadeth a net for his feet.
Others he flattered by asking their advice.

senses.d: To raise hopes in; to encourage or favorable, but sometimes unfounded or deceitful, representations.
To portray too favorably; to give a too favorable idea of; as, his portrait flatters him.

Flatter.etym: [OE. flateren, cf. OD. flatteren; akin to G. flattern to flutter, Icel. fla�ra to fawn, flatter: cf. F. flatter. Cf. Flitter, Flutter, Flattery.]

senses.d: To use flattery or insincere praise.
q: If it may stand him more in stead to lie, Say and unsay, feign, flatter, or adjure.

senses.d: That flatters (in the various senses of the verb); as, a flattering speech.
q: Lay not that flattering unction to your soul.
A flattering painter, who made it his care, To draw men as they ought be, not as they are.

senses.d: The act or practice of flattering; the act of pleasing by artful commendation or compliments; adulation; false, insincere, or excessive praise.
q: Just praise is only a debt, but flattery is a present.
Flattery corrupts both the receiver and the giver.

Flattery.etym: [OE. flaterie, OF. flaterie, F. flaterie, fr. flater to flatter, F. flatter; of uncertain origin. See Flatter, v. t.]

senses.d: A plant of the genus Linum, esp. the L. usitatissimum, which has a single, slender stalk, about a foot and a half high, with blue flowers. The fiber of the bark is used for making thread and cloth, called linen, cambric, lawn, lace, etc. Linseed oil is expressed from the seed.
The skin or fibrous part of the flax plant, when broken and cleaned by hatcheling or combing.

Flax.etym: [AS. fleax; akin to D. vlas, OHG. flahs, G. flachs, and prob. to flechten to braid, plait,m twist, L. plectere to weave, plicare to fold, Gr. � to weave, plait. See Ply.]

senses.d: To skin; to strip off the skin or surface of; as, to flay an ox; to flay the green earth.
q: With her nails She 'll flay thy wolfish visage.

Flay.etym: [OE. flean, flan, AS. fleán; akin to D. vlaen, Icel. flā, Sw. flå, Dan. flaae, cf. Lith. pleszti to tear, plyszti, v.i., to burst, tear; perh. akin to E. flag a flat stone, flaw.]

senses.d: To flay.
q: He will be fleaed first And horse collars made of's skin.

senses.d: An insect belonging to the genus Pulex, of the order Aphaniptera. Fleas are destitute of wings, but have the power of leaping energetically. The bite is poisonous to most persons. The human flea (Pulex irritans), abundant in Europe, is rare in America, where the dog flea (P. canis) takes its place. See Aphaniptera, and Dog flea. See Illustration in Appendix.

Flea.etym: [OE. fle, flee, AS. fleá, fleáh; akin to D. vtoo, OHG. flōh, G. floh, Icel. flō, Russ. blocha; prob. from the root of E. flee. √84. See Flee.]

senses.d: To run away, as from danger or evil; to avoid in an alarmed or cowardly manner; to hasten off; — usually with from. This is sometimes omitted, making the verb transitive.
q: cowardly fled, not having struck one stroke.
Flee fornication.
So fled his enemies my warlike father.

Flee.etym: [OE. fleon, fleen, AS. fleón (imperf. fleáh); akin to D. vlieden, OHG. & OS. fliohan, G. fliehen, Icel. flȳja (imperf. flȳði), Dan. flye, Sw. fly (imperf. flydde), Goth. þliuhan. √84. Cf. Flight.]

senses.d: The entire coat of wool that covers a sheep or other similar animal; also, the quantity shorn from a sheep, or animal, at one time.
q: Who shore me Like a tame wether, all my precious fleece.

senses.d: Any soft woolly covering resembling a fleece.
The fine web of cotton or wool removed by the doffing knife from the cylinder of a carding machine.

Fleece.etym: [OE. flees, AS. fleós; akin to D. flies, vlies .]

senses.d: To deprive of a fleece, or natural covering of wool.
To strip of money or other property unjustly, especially by trickery or fraud; to bring to straits by oppressions and exactions.
q: Whilst pope and prince shared the wool betwixt them, the people were finely fleeced.

senses.d: To spread over as with wool.
The aggregate of the muscles, fat, and other tissues which cover the framework of bones in man and other animals; especially, the muscles.
Animal food, in distinction from vegetable; meat; especially, the body of beasts and birds used as food, as distinguished from fish.
q: With roasted flesh, or milk, and wastel bread.

senses.d: The human body, as distinguished from the soul; the corporeal person.
q: As if this flesh, which walls about our life, Were brass impregnable.

senses.d: The human eace; mankind; humanity.
q: All flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth.

senses.d: Human nature
q: There is no flesh in man's obdurate heart.

senses.d: In a bad sense, tendency to transient or physical pleasure; desire for sensual gratification; carnality.
The character under the influence of animal propensities or selfish passions; the soul unmoved by spiritual influences.
Kindred; stock; race.
q: He is our brother and our flesh.

senses.d: The soft, pulpy substance of fruit; also, that part of a root, fruit, and the like, which is fit to be eaten.

Flesh.etym: [OE. flesch, flesc, AS. fl�sc; akin to OFries. flāsk, D. vleesch, OS. fl�sk, OHG. fleisc, G. fleisch, Icel. & Dan. flesk lard, bacon, pork, Sw. fläsk.]

senses.d: To feed with flesh, as an incitement to further exertion; to initiate; — from the practice of training hawks and dogs by feeding them with the first game they take, or other flesh. Hence, to use upon flesh (as a murderous weapon) so as to draw blood, especially for the first time.
q: Full bravely hast thou fleshed Thy maiden sword.
The wild dog Shall flesh his tooth on every innocent.

senses.d: To glut; to satiate; hence, to harden, to accustom.
q: Old soldiers Fleshed in the spoils of Germany and France.

senses.d: To remove flesh, membrance, etc., from, as from hides.
Of or pertaining to the flesh; corporeal.
Animal; not vegetable.
Human; not celestial; not spiritual or divine.
q: Much ostentation vain of fleshly arm And fragile arms.

senses.d: Carnal; wordly; lascivious.
q: Abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul.

senses.d: In a fleshly manner; carnally; lasciviously.
Full of, or composed of, flesh; plump; corpulent; fat; gross.
q: The sole of his foot is fleshy.

senses.d: Human.
Composed of firm pulp; succulent; as, the houseleek, cactus, and agave are fleshy plants.
The act of flying; a passing through the air by the help of wings; volitation; mode or style of flying.
q: Like the night owl's lazy flight.

senses.d: The act of fleeing; the act of running away, to escape danger or expected evil; hasty departure.
q: Pray ye that your flight be not in the winter.
Fain by flight to save themselves.

senses.d: Lofty elevation and excursion; a mounting; a soaring; as, a flight of imagination, ambition, folly.
q: Could he have kept his spirit to that flight, He had been happy.
His highest flights were indeed far below those of Taylor.

senses.d: A number of beings or things passing through the air together; especially, a flock of birds flying in company; the birds that fly or migrate together; the birds produced in one season; as, a flight of arrows.
q: Swift flights of angels ministrant.
Like a flight of fowl Scattered winds and tempestuous gusts.

senses.d: A series of steps or stairs from one landing to another.
A kind of arrow for the longbow; also, the sport of shooting with it. See Shaft.
q: Challenged Cupid at the flight.
Not a flight drawn home E'er made that haste that they have.

senses.d: The husk or glume of oats.

Flight.etym: [AS. fliht, flyht, a flying, fr. fleógan to fly; cf. flyht a fleeing, fr. fleón to flee, G. flucht a fleeing, Sw. flykt, G. flug a flying, Sw. flygt, D. vlugt a fleeing or flying, Dan. flugt. √84. See Flee, Fly.]

senses.d: A massive, somewhat impure variety of quartz, in color usually of a gray to brown or nearly black, breaking with a conchoidal fracture and sharp edge. It is very hard, and strikes fire with steel.
A piece of flint for striking fire; — formerly much used, esp. in the hammers of gun locks.
Anything extremely hard, unimpressible, and unyielding, like flint.

Flint.etym: [AS. flint, akin to Sw. flinta, Dan. flint; cf. OHG. flins flint, G. flinte gun (cf. E. flintlock), perh. akin to Gr. � brick. Cf. Plinth.]

senses.d: Consisting of, composed of, abounding in, or resembling, flint; as, a flinty rock; flinty ground; a flinty heart.
Anything which floats or rests on the surface of a fluid, as to sustain weight, or to indicate the height of the surface, or mark the place of, something.
q: This reform bill . . . had been used as a float by the conservative ministry.

senses.d: A float board. See Float board (below).
A contrivance for affording a copious stream of water to the heated surface of an object of large bulk, as an anvil or die.
The act of flowing; flux; flow.
A quantity of earth, eighteen feet square and one foot deep.
The trowel or tool with which the floated coat of plastering is leveled and smoothed.
A polishing block used in marble working; a runner.
A single-cut file for smoothing; a tool used by shoemakers for rasping off pegs inside a shoe.
A coal cart.
The sea; a wave. See Flote, n.

Float.etym: [OE. flote ship, boat, fleet, AS. flota ship, fr. fleótan to float; akin to D. vloot fleet, G. floss raft, Icel. floti float, raft, fleet, Sw. flotta. √ 84. See Fleet, v. i., and cf. Flotilla, Flotsam, Plover.]

senses.d: To rest on the surface of any fluid; to swim; to be buoyed up.
q: The ark no more now floats, but seems on ground.
Three blustering nights, borne by the southern blast, I floated.

senses.d: To move quietly or gently on the water, as a raft; to drift along; to move or glide without effort or impulse on the surface of a fluid, or through the air.
q: They stretch their broad plumes and float upon the wind.
There seems a floating whisper on the hills.

Float.etym: [OE. flotien, flotten, AS. flotian to float, swim, fr. fleótan. See Float, n.]

senses.d: To cause to float; to cause to rest or move on the surface of a fluid; as, the tide floated the ship into the harbor.
q: Had floated that bell on the Inchcape rock.

senses.d: To flood; to overflow; to cover with water.
q: Proud Pactolus floats the fruitful lands.

senses.d: To pass over and level the surface of with a float while the plastering is kept wet.
To support and sustain the credit of, as a commercial scheme or a joint-stock company, so as to enable it to go into, or continue in, operation.
A company or collection of living creatures; — especially applied to sheep and birds, rarely to persons or (except in the plural) to cattle and other large animals; as, a flock of ravenous fowl.
q: The heathen . . . came to Nicanor by flocks.

senses.d: A Christian church or congregation; considered in their relation to the pastor, or minister in charge.
q: As half amazed, half frighted all his flock.

Flock.etym: [AS. flocc flock, company; akin to Icel. flokkr crowd, Sw. flock, Dan. flok; prob. orig. used of flows, and akin to E. fly. See Fly.]

senses.d: To gather in companies or crowds.
q: Friends daily flock.

senses.d: To flock to; to crowd.
q: Good fellows, trooping, flocked me so.

senses.d: A lock of wool or hair.
q: I prythee, Tom, beat Cut's saddle, put a few flocks in the point .

senses.d: Woolen or cotton refuse (sing. or pl.), old rags, etc., reduced to a degree of fineness by machinery, and used for stuffing unpholstered furniture.

Very fine, sifted, woolen refuse, especially that from shearing the nap of cloths, used as a coating for wall paper to give it a velvety or clothlike appearance; also, the dust of vegetable fiber used for a similar purpose.

Flock.etym: [OE. flokke; cf. D. vlok, G. flocke, OHG. floccho, Icel. flōki, perh. akin to E. flicker, flacker, or cf. L. floccus, F. floc.]

senses.d: To coat with flock, as wall paper; to roughen the surface of (as glass) so as to give an appearance of being covered with fine flock.

A great flow of water; a body of moving water; the flowing stream, as of a river; especially, a body of water, rising, swelling, and overflowing land not usually thus covered; a deluge; a freshet; an inundation.
q: A covenant never to destroy The earth again by flood.

senses.d: The flowing in of the tide; the semidiurnal swell or rise of water in the ocean; — opposed to ebb; as, young flood; high flood.
q: There is a tide in the affairs of men, Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.

senses.d: A great flow or stream of any fluid substance; as, a flood of light; a flood of lava; hence, a great quantity widely diffused; an overflowing; a superabundance; as, a flood of bank notes; a flood of paper currency.
Menstrual disharge; menses.

Flood.etym: [OE. flod a flowing, stream, flood, AS. flōd; akin to D. vloed, OS. flōd, OHG. fluot, G. flut, Icel. flōð, Sw. & Dan. flod, Goth. flōdus; from the root of E. flow. √80. See Flow, v. i.]

senses.d: To overflow; to inundate; to deluge; as, the swollen river flooded the valley.

To cause or permit to be inundated; to fill or cover with water or other fluid; as, to flood arable land for irrigation; to fill to excess or to its full capacity; as, to flood a country with a depreciated currency.
The bottom or lower part of any room; the part upon which we stand and upon which the movables in the room are supported.
The structure formed of beams, girders, etc., with proper covering, which divides a building horizontally into stories. Floor in sense 1 is, then, the upper surface of floor in sense 2.
The surface, or the platform, of a structure on which we walk or travel; as, the floor of a bridge.
A story of a building. See Story.
The part of the house assigned to the members.
That part of the bottom of a vessel on each side of the keelson which is most nearly horizontal.
The rock underlying a stratified or nearly horizontal deposit.

Floor.etym: [AS. fl�r; akin to D. vloer, G. flur field, floor, entrance hall, Icel. fl�r floor of a cow stall, cf. Ir. & Gael. lar floor, ground, earth, W. llawr, perh. akin to L. planus level. Cf. Plain smooth.]

senses.d: To cover with a floor; to furnish with a floor; as, to floor a house with pine boards.
To strike down or lay level with the floor; to knock down; hence, to silence by a conclusive answer or retort; as, to floor an opponent.
q: Floored or crushed by him.

senses.d: To finish or make an end of; as, to floor a college examination.
q: I've floored my little-go work.

senses.d: The finely ground meal of wheat, or of any other grain; especially, the finer part of meal separated by bolting; hence, the fine and soft powder of any substance; as, flour of emery; flour of mustard.

Flour.etym: [F. fleur de farine the flower (i.e., the best) of meal, cf. Sp. flor de la harina superfine flour, Icel. flür flower, flour. See Flower.]

senses.d: To grind and bolt; to convert into flour; as, to flour wheat.
To sprinkle with flour.
To grow luxuriantly; to increase and enlarge, as a healthy growing plant; a thrive.
q: A tree thrives and flourishes in a kindly . . . soil.

senses.d: To be prosperous; to increase in wealth, honor, comfort, happiness, or whatever is desirable; to thrive; to be prominent and influental; specifically, of authors, painters, etc., to be in a state of activity or production.
q: When all the workers of iniquity do flourish.
Bad men as frequently prosper and flourish, and that by the means of their wickedness.
We say Of those that held their heads above the crowd, They flourished then or then.

senses.d: To use florid language; to indulge in rhetorical figures and lofty expressions; to be flowery.
q: They dilate . . . and flourish long on little incidents.

senses.d: To make bold and sweeping, fanciful, or wanton movements, by way of ornament, parade, bravado, etc.; to play with fantastic and irregular motion.
q: Impetuous spread The stream, and smoking flourished o'er his head.

senses.d: To make ornamental strokes with the pen; to write graceful, decorative figures.
To execute an irregular or fanciful strain of music, by way of ornament or prelude.
q: Why do the emperor's trumpets flourish thus?

senses.d: To boast; to vaunt; to brag.

Flourish.etym: [OE. florisshen, flurisshen, OF. flurir, F. fleurir, fr. L. florere to bloom, fr. flos, floris, flower. See Flower, and -ish.]

senses.d: To adorn with flowers orbeautiful figures, either natural or artificial; to ornament with anything showy; to embellish.
To embellish with the flowers of diction; to adorn with rhetorical figures; to grace with ostentatious eloquence; to set off with a parade of words.
q: Sith that the justice of your title to him Doth flourish the deceit.

senses.d: To move in bold or irregular figures; to swing about in circles or vibrations by way of show or triumph; to brandish.
q: And flourishes his blade in spite of me.

senses.d: To develop; to make thrive; to expand.
q: Bottoms of thread . . . which with a good needle, perhaps may be flourished into large works.

senses.d: A flourishing condition; prosperity; vigor.
q: The Roman monarchy, in her highest flourish, never had the like.

senses.d: Decoration; ornament; beauty.
q: The flourish of his sober youth Was the pride of naked truth.

senses.d: Something made or performed in a fanciful, wanton, or vaunting manner, by way of ostentation, to excite admiration, etc.; ostentatious embellishment; ambitious copiousness or amplification; parade of words and figures; show; as, a flourish of rhetoric or of wit.
q: He lards with flourishes his long harangue.

senses.d: A fanciful stroke of the pen or graver; a merely decorative figure.
q: The neat characters and flourishes of a Bible curiously printed.

senses.d: A fantastic or decorative musical passage; a strain of triumph or bravado, not forming part of a regular musical composition; a cal; a fanfare.
q: A flourish, trumpets! strike alarum, drums!

senses.d: The waving of a weapon or other thing; a brandishing; as, the flourish of a sword.
To move with a continual change of place among the particles or parts, as a fluid; to change place or circulate, as a liquid; as, rivers flow from springs and lakes; tears flow from the eyes.
To become liquid; to melt.
q: The mountains flowed down at thy presence.

senses.d: To proceed; to issue forth; as, wealth flows from industry and economy.
q: Those thousand decencies that daily flow From all her words and actions.

senses.d: To glide along smoothly, without harshness or asperties; as, a flowing period; flowing numbers; to sound smoothly to the ear; to be uttered easily.
q: Virgil is sweet and flowingin his hexameters.

senses.d: To have or be in abundance; to abound; to full, so as to run or flow over; to be copious.
q: In that day . . . the hills shall flow with milk.
The exhilaration of a night that needed not the influence of the flowing bowl.

senses.d: To hang loose and waving; as, a flowing mantle; flowing locks.
q: The imperial purple flowing in his train.

senses.d: To rise, as the tide; — opposed to ebb; as, the tide flows twice in twenty-four hours.
q: The river hath thrice flowed, no ebb between.

senses.d: To discharge blood in excess from the uterus.

Flow.etym: [AS. flōwan; akin to D. vloeijen, OHG. flawen to wash, Icel. flōa to deluge, Gr. πλώειν to float, sail, and prob. ultimately to E. float, fleet. √80. Cf. Flood.]

senses.d: To cover with water or other liquid; to overflow; to inundate; to flood.
To cover with varnish.
A stream of water or other fluid; a current; as, a flow of water; a flow of blood.
A continuous movement of something abundant; as, a flow of words.
Any gentle, gradual movement or procedure of thought, diction, music, or the like, resembling the quiet, steady movement of a river; a stream.
q: The feast of reason and the flow of soul.

senses.d: The tidal setting in of the water from the ocean to the shore. See Ebb and flow, under Ebb.
A low-lying piece of watery land; — called also flow moss and flow bog.
In the popular sense, the bloom or blossom of a plant; the showy portion, usually of a different color, shape, and texture from the foliage.

That part of a plant destined to produce seed, and hence including one or both of the sexual organs; an organ or combination of the organs of reproduction, whether inclosed by a circle of foliar parts or not. A complete flower consists of two essential parts, the stamens and the pistil, and two floral envelopes, the corolla and callyx. In mosses the flowers consist of a few special leaves surrounding or subtending organs called archegonia. See Blossom, and Corolla.
The fairest, freshest, and choicest part of anything; as, the flower of an army, or of a family; the state or time of freshness and bloom; as, the flower of life, that is, youth.
