q: The choice and flower of all things profitable the Psalms do more briefly contain.
The flower of the chivalry of all Spain.
A simple maiden in her flower Is worth a hundred coats of arms.

senses.d: Grain pulverized; meal; flour.
q: The flowers of grains, mixed with water, will make a sort of glue.

senses.d: A substance in the form of a powder, especially when condensed from sublimation; as, the flowers of sulphur.
A figure of speech; an ornament of style.
Ornamental type used chiefly for borders around pages, cards, etc.
Menstrual discharges.

Flower.etym: [OE. flour, OF. flour, flur, flor, F. fleur, fr. L. flos, floris. Cf. Blossom, Effloresce, Floret, Florid, Florin, Flour, Flourish.]

senses.d: To blossom; to bloom; to expand the petals, as a plant; to produce flowers; as, this plant flowers in June.
To come into the finest or fairest condition.
q: Their lusty and flowering age.
When flowered my youthful spring.

senses.d: To froth; to ferment gently, as new beer.
q: That beer did flower a little.

senses.d: To come off as flowers by sublimation.
q: Observations which have flowered off.

senses.d: To embellish with flowers; to adorn with imitated flowers; as, flowered silk.
That flows or for flowing (in various sense of the verb); gliding along smoothly; copious.

A musical wind instrument, consisting of a hollow cylinder or pipe, with holes along its length, stopped by the fingers or by keys which are opened by the fingers. The modern flute is closed at the upper end, and blown with the mouth at a lateral hole.
q: The breathing flute's soft notes are heard around.

senses.d: A channel of curved section; — usually applied to one of a vertical series of such channels used to decorate columns and pilasters in classical architecture. See Illust. under Base, n.
A similar channel or groove made in wood or other material, esp. in plaited cloth, as in a lady's ruffle.
A long French breakfast roll.
A stop in an organ, having a flutelike sound.

Flute.etym: [OE. floute, floite, fr. OF. flaüte, flahute, flahuste, F. fl�te; cf. LL. flauta, D. fluit. See Flute, v. i.]

senses.d: A kind of flyboat; a storeship.

Flute.etym: [Cf. F. flûte a transport, D. fluit.]

senses.d: To play on, or as on, a flute; to make a flutelike sound.

Flute.etym: [OE. flouten, floiten, OF. flaüter, fleüter, flouster, F. flûter, cf. D. fluiten; ascribed to an assumed LL. flautare, flatuare, fr. L. flatus a blowing, fr. flare to blow. Cf. Flout, Flageolet, Flatulent.]

senses.d: To play, whistle, or sing with a clear, soft note, like that of a flute.
q: Knaves are men, That lute and flute fantastic tenderness.
The redwing flutes his o-ka-lee.

senses.d: To form flutes or channels in, as in a column, a ruffle, etc.
To vibrate or move quickly; as, a bird flutters its wings.
To drive in disorder; to throw into confusion.
q: Like an eagle in a dovecote, I Fluttered your Volscians in Corioli.

senses.d: The act of fluttering; quick and irregular motion; vibration; as, the flutter of a fan.
q: The chirp and flutter of some single bird

senses.d: Hurry; tumult; agitation of the mind; confusion; disorder.
The act of flowing; a continuous moving on or passing by, as of a flowing stream; constant succession; change.
q: By the perpetual flux of the liquids, a great part of them is thrown out of the body.
Her image has escaped the flux of things, And that same infant beauty that she wore Is fixed upon her now forevermore.
Languages, like our bodies, are in a continual flux.

senses.d: The setting in of the tide toward the shore, — the ebb being called the reflux.
The state of being liquid through heat; fusion.
Any substance or mixture used to promote the fusion of metals or minerals, as alkalies, borax, lime, fluorite.
A fluid discharge from the bowels or other part; especially, an excessive and morbid discharge; as, the bloody flux or dysentery. See Bloody flux.
The quantity of a fluid that crosses a unit area of a given surface in a unit of time.

Flux.etym: [L. fluxus, fr. fluere, fluxum, to flow: cf.F. flux. See Fluent, and cf. 1st & 2d Floss, Flush, n., 6.]

senses.d: Flowing; unstable; inconstant; variable.
q: The flux nature of all things here.

Flux.etym: [L. fluxus, p. p. of fluere. See Flux, n.]

senses.d: To affect, or bring to a certain state, by flux.
q: He might fashionably and genteelly . . . have been dueled or fluxed into another world.

senses.d: To cause to become fluid; to fuse.
To cause a discharge from; to purge.
To move in or pass through the air with wings, as a bird.
To move through the air or before the wind; esp., to pass or be driven rapidly through the air by any impulse.
To float, wave, or rise in the air, as sparks or a flag.
q: Man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward.

senses.d: To move or pass swiftly; to hasten away; to circulate rapidly; as, a ship flies on the deep; a top flies around; rumor flies.
q: Fly, envious Time, till thou run out thy race.
The dark waves murmured as the ships flew on.

senses.d: To run from danger; to attempt to escape; to flee; as, an enemy or a coward flies. See Note under Flee.
q: Fly, ere evil intercept thy flight.
Whither shall I fly to escape their hands ?

senses.d: To move suddenly, or with violence; to do an act suddenly or swiftly; — usually with a qualifying word; as, a door flies open; a bomb flies apart.

Fly.etym: [OE. fleen, fleen, fleyen, flegen, AS. fleógan; akin to D. vliegen, OHG. fliogan, G. fliegen, Icel. fljūga, Sw. flyga, Dan. flyve, Goth. us-flaugjan to cause to fly away, blow about, and perh. to L. pluma feather, E. plume. √84. Cf. Fledge, Flight, Flock of animals.]

senses.d: To cause to fly or to float in the air, as a bird, a kite, a flag, etc.
q: The brave black flag I fly.

senses.d: To fly or flee from; to shun; to avoid.
q: Sleep flies the wretch.
To fly the favors of so good a king.

senses.d: To hunt with a hawk.
Any winged insect; esp., one with transparent wings; as, the Spanish fly; firefly; gall fly; dragon fly.
A hook dressed in imitation of a fly, — used for fishing.
A familiar spirit; a witch's attendant.
q: A trifling fly, none of your great familiars.

senses.d: A parasite.
A kind of light carriage for rapid transit, plying for hire and usually drawn by one horse.
The length of an extended flag from its staff; sometimes, the length from the “union” to the extreme end.
The part of a vane pointing the direction from which the wind blows.
That part of a compass on which the points are marked; the compass card.
Two or more vanes set on a revolving axis, to act as a fanner, or to equalize or impede the motion of machinery by the resistance of the air, as in the striking part of a clock.
The piece hinged to the needle, which holds the engaged loop in position while the needle is penetrating another loop; a latch.
The pair of arms revolving around the bobbin, in a spinning wheel or spinning frame, to twist the yarn.
A shuttle driven through the shed by a blow or jerk.

Fly.etym: [OE. flie, flege, AS. flȳge, fleóge, fr. fleógan to fly; akin to D. vlieg, OHG. flioga, G. fliege, Icel. & Sw. fluga, Dan. flue. √ 84. See Fly, v. i.]

senses.d: Knowing; wide awake; fully understanding another's meaning.
To manage (an aircraft) in flight; as, to fly an aëroplane.
Waste cotton.
Moving in the air with, or as with, wings; moving lightly or rapidly; intended for rapid movement.
The Chinese name of Buddha.
The young of any animal of the Horse family (Equidæ); a colt; a filly.

Foal.etym: [OE. fole, AS. fola; akin to OHG. folo, G. fohlen, Goth. fula, Icel. foli, Sw. fåle, Gr. πω̑λοσ, L. pullus a young animal. Cf. Filly, Poultry, Pullet.]

senses.d: To bring forth (a colt); — said of a mare or a she ass.
To bring forth young, as an animal of the horse kind.

The white substance, consisting of an aggregation of bubbles, which is formed on the surface of liquids, or in the mouth of an animal, by violent agitation or fermentation; froth; spume; scum; as, the foam of the sea.

Foam.etym: [OE. fam, fom, AS. fām; akin to OHG. & G. feim.]

senses.d: To gather foam; to froth; as, the billows foam.
q: He foameth, and gnasheth with his teeth.

senses.d: To form foam, or become filled with foam; — said of a steam boiler when the water is unduly agitated and frothy, as because of chemical action.
To cause to foam; as, to foam the goblet; also (with out), to throw out with rage or violence, as foam.
A weight by which lead and some other metals were formerly sold, in England, varying from 19½ to 24 cwt.; a fother.
That which is fed out to cattle horses, and sheep, as hay, cornstalks, vegetables, etc.

Fodder.etym: [AS. fōdder, fōddor, fodder (also sheath case), fr. fōda food; akin to D. voeder, OHG. fuotar, G. futter, Icel. fōðr, Sw. & Dan. foder. √75. See Food and cf. Forage, Fur.]

senses.d: To feed, as cattle, with dry food or cut grass, etc.; to furnish with hay, straw, oats, etc.
One who entertains personal enmity, hatred, grudge, or malice, against another; an enemy.
q: A man's foes shall be they of his own household.

senses.d: An enemy in war; a hostile army.
One who opposes on principle; an opponent; an adversary; an ill-wisher; as, a foe to religion.
q: A foe to received doctrines.

Foe.etym: [OE. fo, fa, AS. fāh hostile; prob. akin to E. fiend. √81. See Fiend, and cf. Feud a quarrel.]

senses.d: To treat as an enemy.
To lap or lay in plaits or folds; to lay one part over another part of; to double; as, to fold cloth; to fold a letter.
q: As a vesture shalt thou fold them up.

senses.d: To double or lay together, as the arms or the hands; as, he folds his arms in despair.
To inclose within folds or plaitings; to envelop; to infold; to clasp; to embrace.
q: A face folded in sorrow.
We will descend and fold him in our arms.

senses.d: To cover or wrap up; to conceal.
q: Nor fold my fault in cleanly coined excuses.

Fold.etym: [OE. folden, falden, AS. fealdan; akin to OHG. faltan, faldan, G. falten, Icel. falda, Dan. folde, Sw. fålla, Goth. falþan, cf. Gr. δι-πλάσιοσ twofold, Skr. puṭa a fold. Cf. Fauteuil.]

senses.d: To become folded, plaited, or doubled; to close over another of the same kind; to double together; as, the leaves of the door fold.
A doubling,esp. of any flexible substance; a part laid over on another part; a plait; a plication.
q: Mummies . . . shrouded in a number of folds of linen.
Folds are most common in the rocks of mountainous regions.

senses.d: Times or repetitions; — used with numerals, chiefly in composition, to denote multiplication or increase in a geometrical ratio, the doubling, tripling, etc., of anything; as, fourfold, four times, increased in a quadruple ratio, multiplied by four.
That which is folded together, or which infolds or envelops; embrace.
q: Shall from your neck unloose his amorous fold.

Fold.etym: [From Fold, v. In sense 2 AS. -feald, akin to fealdan to fold.]

senses.d: An inclosure for sheep; a sheep pen.
q: Leaps o'er the fence with ease into the fold.

senses.d: A flock of sheep; figuratively, the Church or a church; as, Christ's fold.
q: There shall be one fold and one shepherd.
The very whitest lamb in all my fold.

senses.d: A boundary; a limit.
To confine in a fold, as sheep.
To confine sheep in a fold.
q: The star that bids the shepherd fold.

senses.d: The act of making a fold or folds; also, a fold; a doubling; a plication.
q: The lower foldings of the vest.

senses.d: The keepig of sheep in inclosures on arable land, etc.
In Anglo-Saxon times, the people of a group of townships or villages; a community; a tribe.
q: The organization of each folk, as such, sprang mainly from war.

senses.d: People in general, or a separate class of people; — generally used in the plural form, and often with a qualifying adjective; as, the old folks; poor folks.
q: In winter's tedious nights, sit by the fire With good old folks, and let them tell thee tales.

senses.d: The persons of one's own family; as, our folks are all well.

Folk.etym: [AS. folc; akin to D. volk, OS. & OHG. folk, G. volk, Icel. fōlk, Sw. & Dan. folk, Lith. pulkas crowd, and perh. to E. follow.]

senses.d: To go or come after; to move behind in the same path or direction; hence, to go with (a leader, guide, etc.); to accompany; to attend.
q: It waves me forth again; I'll follow it.

senses.d: To endeavor to overtake; to go in pursuit of; to chase; to pursue; to prosecute.
q: I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians, and they shall follow them.

senses.d: To accept as authority; to adopt the opinions of; to obey; to yield to; to take as a rule of action; as, to follow good advice.
q: Approve the best, and follow what I approve
Follow peace with all men.
It is most agreeable to some men to follow their reason; and to others to follow their appetites.

senses.d: To copy after; to take as an example.
q: We had rather follow the perfections of them whom we like not, than in defects resemble them whom we love.

senses.d: To succeed in order of time, rank, or office.
To result from, as an effect from a cause, or an inference from a premise.

To watch, as a receding object; to keep the eyes fixed upon while in motion; to keep the mind upon while in progress, as a speech, musical performance, etc.; also, to keep up with; to understand the meaning, connection, or force of, as of a course of thought or argument.
q: He followed with his eyes the flitting shade.

senses.d: To walk in, as a road or course; to attend upon closely, as a profession or calling.
q: O, had I but followed the arts!
O Antony! I have followed thee to this.

Follow.syn: To pursue; chase; go after; attend; accompany; succeed; imitate; copy; embrace; maintain.
Follow.etym: [OE. foluwen, folwen, folgen, AS. folgian, fylgean, fylgan; akin to D. volgen, OHG. folg�n, G. folgen, Icel. fylgja, Sw. följa, Dan. fölge, and perh. to E. folk.]

senses.d: To go or come after; — used in the various senses of the transitive verb: To pursue; to attend; to accompany; to be a result; to imitate.
The art or process of following; specif., in some games, as billiards, a stroke causing a ball to follow another ball after hitting it. Also used adjectively; as, follow shot.
One who follows; a pursuer; an attendant; a disciple; a dependent associate; a retainer.
A sweetheart; a beau.
The removable flange, or cover, of a piston. See Illust. of Piston.
The part of a machine that receives motion from another part. See Driver.
Among law stationers, a sheet of parchment or paper which is added to the first sheet of an indenture or other deed.

Follower.syn: Imitator; copier; disciple; adherent; partisan; dependent; attendant.

senses.d: One's followers, adherents, or dependents, collectively.
Vocation; business; profession.
Next after; succeeding; ensuing; as, the assembly was held on the following day.

(In the field of a telescope) In the direction from which stars are apparently moving (in consequence of the earth's rotation); as, a small star, north following or south following. In the direction toward which stars appear to move is called preceding.
The state of being foolish; want of good sense; levity, weakness, or derangement of mind.
A foolish act; an inconsiderate or thoughtless procedure; weak or light-minded conduct; foolery.
q: What folly 'tis to hazard life for ill.

senses.d: Scandalous crime; sin; specifically, as applied to a woman, wantonness.
q: wrought folly in Israel.
When lovely woman stoops to folly.

senses.d: The result of a foolish action or enterprise.
q: It is called this man's or that man's “folly,” and name of the foolish builder is thus kept alive for long after years.

Folly.etym: [OE. folie, foli, F. folie, fr. fol, fou, foolish, mad. See Fool.]

senses.d: What is fed upon; that which goes to support life by being received within, and assimilated by, the organism of an animal or a plant; nutriment; aliment; especially, what is eaten by animals for nourishment.
Anything that instructs the intellect, excites the feelings, or molds habits of character; that which nourishes.
q: This may prove food to my displeasure.
In this moment there is life and food For future years.

Food.syn: Aliment; sustenance; nutriment; feed; fare; victuals; provisions; meat.
Food.etym: [OE. fode, AS. fōda; akin to Icel. fæða, fæði, Sw. föda, Dan. & LG. föde, OHG. fatunga, Gr. πατει̑σθαι to eat, and perh. to Skr. pā to protect, L. pascere to feed, pasture, pabulum food, E. pasture. √75. Cf. Feed, Fodder food, Foster to cherish.]

senses.d: To supply with food.
A compound of gooseberries scalded and crushed, with cream; — commonly called gooseberry fool.

Fool.etym: [Cf. F. fouler to tread, crush. Cf. 1st Foil.]

senses.d: One destitute of reason, or of the common powers of understanding; an idiot; a natural.
A person deficient in intellect; one who acts absurdly, or pursues a course contrary to the dictates of wisdom; one without judgment; a simpleton; a dolt.
q: Extol not riches, then, the toil of fools.
Experience keeps a dear school, but fools will learn in no other.

senses.d: One who acts contrary to moral and religious wisdom; a wicked person.
q: The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.

senses.d: One who counterfeits folly; a professional jester or buffoon; a retainer formerly kept to make sport, dressed fantastically in motley, with ridiculous accouterments.
q: Can they think me . . . their fool or jester?

Fool.etym: [OE. fol, n. & adj., F. fol, fou, foolish, mad; a fool, prob. fr. L. follis a bellows, wind bag, an inflated ball; perh. akin to E. bellows. Cf. Folly, Follicle.]

senses.d: To play the fool; to trifle; to toy; to spend time in idle sport or mirth.
q: Is this a time for fooling?

senses.d: To infatuate; to make foolish.
q: For, fooled with hope, men favor the deceit.

senses.d: To use as a fool; to deceive in a shameful or mortifying manner; to impose upon; to cheat by inspiring foolish confidence; as, to fool one out of his money.
q: You are fooled, discarded, and shook off By him for whom these shames ye underwent.

senses.d: Marked with, or exhibiting, folly; void of understanding; weak in intellect; without judgment or discretion; silly; unwise.
q: I am a very foolish fond old man.

senses.d: Such as a fool would do; proceeding from weakness of mind or silliness; exhibiting a want of judgment or discretion; as, a foolish act.
Absurd; ridiculous; despicable; contemptible.
q: A foolish figure he must make.

Foolish.syn: Absurd; shallow; shallow-brained; brainless; simple; irrational; unwise; imprudent; indiscreet; incautious; silly; ridiculous; vain; trifling; contemptible. See Absurd.

senses.d: In a foolish manner.
The quality of being foolish.
A foolish practice; an absurdity.
q: The preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness.

senses.d: The terminal part of the leg of man or an animal; esp., the part below the ankle or wrist; that part of an animal upon which it rests when standing, or moves. See Manus, and Pes.
The muscular locomotive organ of a mollusk. It is a median organ arising from the ventral region of body, often in the form of a flat disk, as in snails. See Illust. of Buccinum.
That which corresponds to the foot of a man or animal; as, the foot of a table; the foot of a stocking.

The lowest part or base; the ground part; the bottom, as of a mountain or column; also, the last of a row or series; the end or extremity, esp. if associated with inferiority; as, the foot of a hill; the foot of the procession; the foot of a class; the foot of the bed.
q: And now at foot Of heaven's ascent they lift their feet.

senses.d: Fundamental principle; basis; plan; — used only in the singular.
q: Answer directly upon the foot of dry reason.

senses.d: Recognized condition; rank; footing; — used only in the singular.
q: As to his being on the foot of a servant.

senses.d: A measure of length equivalent to twelve inches; one third of a yard. See Yard.
Soldiers who march and fight on foot; the infantry, usually designated as the foot, in distinction from the cavalry.
A combination of syllables consisting a metrical element of a verse, the syllables being formerly distinguished by their quantity or length, but in modern poetry by the accent.
The lower edge of a sail.

Foot.etym: [OE. fot, foot, pl. fet, feet. AS. fōt, pl. fēt; akin to D. voet, OHG. fuoz, G. fuss, Icel. fōtr, Sw. fot, Dan. fod, Goth. fōtus, L. pes, Gr. πούσ, Skr. pād, Icel. fet step, pace measure of a foot, feta to step, find one's way. √77, 250. Cf. Antipodes, Cap-a-pie, Expedient, Fet to fetch, Fetlock, Fe

senses.d: To tread to measure or music; to dance; to trip; to skip.
To walk; — opposed to ride or fly.
To kick with the foot; to spurn.
To set on foot; to establish; to land.
q: What confederacy have you with the traitors Late footed in the kingdom?

senses.d: To tread; as, to foot the green.
To sum up, as the numbers in a column; — sometimes with up; as, to foot (or foot up) an account.
To seize or strike with the talon.
To renew the foot of, as of a stocking.
q: If you are for a merry jaunt, I'll try, for once, who can foot it farthest.

senses.d: The mark or impression of the foot; a track; hence, visible sign of a course pursued; token; mark; as, the footsteps of divine wisdom.
q: How on the faltering footsteps of decay Youth presses.

senses.d: An inclined plane under a hand printing press.
A low stool to support the feet of one when sitting.
In the most general sense, indicating that in consideration of, in view of, or with reference to, which anything is done or takes place.

Indicating the antecedent cause or occasion of an action; the motive or inducement accompanying and prompting to an act or state; the reason of anything; that on account of which a thing is or is done.
q: With fiery eyes sparkling for very wrath.
How to choose dogs for scent or speed.
Now, for so many glorious actions done, For peace at home, and for the public wealth, I mean to crown a bowl for Cæsar's health.
That which we, for our unworthiness, are afraid to crave, our prayer is, that God, for the worthiness of his Son, would, notwithstanding, vouchsafe to grant.

senses.d: Indicating the remoter and indirect object of an act; the end or final cause with reference to which anything is, acts, serves, or is done.
q: The oak for nothing ill, The osier good for twigs, the poplar for the mill.
It was young counsel for the persons, and violent counsel for the matters.
Shall I think the worls was made for one, And men are born for kings, as beasts for men, Not for protection, but to be devoured?
For he writes not for money, nor for praise.

senses.d: Indicating that in favor of which, or in promoting which, anything is, or is done; hence, in behalf of; in favor of; on the side of; — opposed to against.
q: We can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.
It is for the general good of human society, and consequently of particular persons, to be true and just; and it is for men's health to be temperate.
Aristotle is for poetical justice.

senses.d: Indicating that toward which the action of anything is directed, or the point toward which motion is made; �ntending to go to.
q: We sailed from Peru for China and Japan.

senses.d: Indicating that on place of or instead of which anything acts or serves, or that to which a substitute, an equivalent, a compensation, or the like, is offered or made; instead of, or place of.
q: And if any mischief follow, then thou shalt give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.

senses.d: Indicating that in the character of or as being which anything is regarded or treated; to be, or as being.
q: We take a falling meteor for a star.
If a man can be fully assured of anything for a truth, without having examined, what is there that he may not embrace for tru�?
Most of our ingenious young men take up some cried-up English poet for their model.
But let her go for an ungrateful woman.

senses.d: Indicating that instead of which something else controls in the performing of an action, or that in spite of which anything is done, occurs, or is; hence, equivalent to notwithstanding, in spite of; — generally followed by all, aught, anything, etc.
q: The writer will do what she please for all me.
God's desertion shall, for aught he knows, the next minute supervene.
For anything that legally appears to the contrary, it may be a contrivance to fright us.

senses.d: Indicating the space or time through which an action or state extends; hence, during; in or through the space or time of.
q: For many miles about There 's scarce a bush.
Since, hired for life, thy servile muse sing.
To guide the sun's bright chariot for a day.

senses.d: Indicating that in prevention of which, or through fear of which, anything is done.
q: We 'll have a bib, for spoiling of thy doublet.

For.etym: [AS. for, fore; akin to OS. for, fora, furi, D. voor, OHG. fora, G. vor, OHG. furi, G. für, Icel. fyrir, Sw. för, Dan. for, adv. för, Goth. faúr, faúra, L. pro, Gr. �, Skr. pra-. √ 202. Cf. Fore, First, Foremost, Forth, Pro-.]

senses.d: Because; by reason that; for that; indicating, in Old English, the reason of anything.
q: And for of long that way had walkéd none, The vault was hid with plants and bushes hoar.
And Heaven defend your good souls, that you think I will your serious and great business scant, For she with me.

senses.d: Since; because; introducing a reason of something before advanced, a cause, motive, explanation, justification, or the like, of an action related or a statement made. It is logically nearly equivalent to since, or because, but connects less closely, and is sometimes used as a very general introduction to something suggested by what has gone before.
q: Give thanks unto the Lord; for he is good; for his mercy endureth forever.
Heaven doth with us as we with torches do, Not light them for themselves; for if our virtues Did not go forth of us, 't were all alike As if we had them not.

senses.d: One who takes, or that which is said on, the affrimative side; that which is said in favor of some one or something; — the antithesis of against, and commonly used in connection with it.
In consideration that; seeing that; since; because that; — followed by as. See under For, prep.
An ancestor; a forefather; — usually in the plural.
To refrain from proceeding; to pause; to delay.
q: Shall I go against Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I forbear?

senses.d: To refuse; to decline; to give no heed.
q: Thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear.

senses.d: To control one's self when provoked.
q: The kindest and the happiest pair Will find occasion to forbear.
Both bear and forbear.

Forbear.etym: [OE. forberen, AS. forberan; pref. for- + beran to bear. See Bear to support.]

senses.d: To keep away from; to avoid; to abstain from; to give up; as, to forbear the use of a word of doubtful propriety.
q: But let me that plunder forbear.
The King In open battle or the tilting field Forbore his own advantage.

senses.d: To treat with consideration or indulgence.
q: Forbearing one another in love.

senses.d: To cease from bearing.
q: Whenas my womb her burden would forbear.

senses.d: The act of forbearing or waiting; the exercise of patience.
q: He soon shall find Forbearance no acquittance ere day end.

senses.d: The quality of being forbearing; indulgence toward offenders or enemies; long-suffering.
q: Have a continent forbearance, till the speed of his rage goes slower.

senses.d: Disposed or accustomed to forbear; patient; long-suffering.
To command against, or contrary to; to prohibit; to interdict.
q: More than I have said . . . The leisure and enforcement of the time Forbids to dwell upon.

senses.d: To deny, exclude from, or warn off, by express command; to command not to enter.
q: Have I not forbid her my house?

senses.d: To oppose, hinder, or prevent, as if by an effectual command; as, an impassable river forbids the approach of the army.
q: A blaze of glory that forbids the sight.

senses.d: To accurse; to blast.
q: He shall live a man forbid.

senses.d: To defy; to challenge.

Forbid.syn: To prohibit; interdict; hinder; preclude; withhold; restrain; prevent. See Prohibit.
Forbid.etym: [OE. forbeden, AS. forbeódan; pref. for- + beódan to bid; akin to D. verbieden, G. verbieten, Icel. fyrirbjōða, forboða, Sw. förbjuda, Dan. forbyde. See Bid, v. t.]

senses.d: To utter a prohibition; to prevent; to hinder.
Prohibited; interdicted.
q: I know no spells, use no forbidden arts.

senses.d: Repelling approach; repulsive; raising abhorrence, aversion, or dislike; disagreeable; prohibiting or interdicting; as, a forbidding aspect; a forbidding formality; a forbidding air.

Forbidding.syn: Disagreeable; unpleasant; displeasing; offensive; repulsive; odious; abhorrent.

senses.d: To stuff; to lard; to farce.
q: Wit larded with malice, and malice forced with wit.

senses.d: A waterfall; a cascade.
q: To see the falls for force of the river Kent.

Force.etym: [Of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. fors, foss, Dan. fos.]

senses.d: Strength or energy of body or mind; active power; vigor; might; often, an unusual degree of strength or energy; capacity of exercising an influence or producing an effect; especially, power to persuade, or convince, or impose obligation; pertinency; validity; special signification; as, the force of an appeal, an argument, a contract, or a term.
q: He was, in the full force of the words, a good man.

senses.d: Power exerted against will or consent; compulsory power; violence; coercion.
q: Which now they hold by force, and not by right.

senses.d: Strength or power for war; hence, a body of land or naval combatants, with their appurtenances, ready for action; — an armament; troops; warlike array; — often in the plural; hence, a body of men prepared for action in other ways; as, the laboring force of a plantation.
q: Is Lucius general of the forces?

senses.d: Strength or power exercised without law, or contrary to law, upon persons or things; violence.

Any action between two bodies which changes, or tends to change, their relative condition as to rest or motion; or, more generally, which changes, or tends to change, any physical relation between them, whether mechanical, thermal, chemical, electrical, magnetic, or of any other kind; as, the force of gravity; cohesive force; centrifugal force.
q: Thy tears are of no force to mollify This flinty man.
More huge in strength than wise in works he was.
Adam and first matron Eve Had ended now their orisons, and found Strength added from above, new hope to spring Out of despair.

Force.syn: Strength; vigor; might; energy; stress; vehemence; violence; compulsion; coaction; constraint; coercion.
Force.etym: [F. force, LL. forcia, fortia, fr. L. fortis strong. See Fort, n.]

senses.d: To constrain to do or to forbear, by the exertion of a power not resistible; to compel by physical, moral, or intellectual means; to coerce; as, masters force slaves to labor.
To compel, as by strength of evidence; as, to force conviction on the mind.
To do violence to; to overpower, or to compel by violence to one's will; especially, to ravish; to violate; to commit rape upon.
q: To force their monarch and insult the court.
I should have forced thee soon wish other arms.
To force a spotless virgin's chastity.

senses.d: To obtain or win by strength; to take by violence or struggle; specifically, to capture by assault; to storm, as a fortress.
To impel, drive, wrest, extort, get, etc., by main strength or violence; — with a following adverb, as along, away, from, into, through, out, etc.
q: It stuck so fast, so deeply buried lay That scarce the victor forced the steel away.
To force the tyrant from his seat by war.
Ethelbert ordered that none should be forced into religion.

senses.d: To put in force; to cause to be executed; to make binding; to enforce.
q: What can the church force more?

senses.d: To exert to the utmost; to urge; hence, to strain; to urge to excessive, unnatural, or untimely action; to produce by unnatural effort; as, to force a conceit or metaphor; to force a laugh; to force fruits.
q: High on a mounting wave my head I bore, Forcing my strength, and gathering to the shore.

senses.d: To compel (an adversary or partner) to trump a trick by leading a suit of which he has none.
To provide with forces; to reënforce; to strengthen by soldiers; to man; to garrison.
To allow the force of; to value; to care for.
q: For me, I force not argument a straw.

Force.syn: To compel; constrain; oblige; necessitate; coerce; drive; press; impel.
Force.etym: [OF. forcier, F. forcer, fr. LL. forciare, fortiare. See Force, n.]

senses.d: To use violence; to make violent effort; to strive; to endeavor.
q: Forcing with gifts to win his wanton heart.

senses.d: To make a difficult matter of anything; to labor; to hesitate; hence, to force of, to make much account of; to regard.
q: Your oath once broke, you force not to forswear.
I force not of such fooleries.

senses.d: To be of force, importance, or weight; to matter.
q: It is not sufficient to have attained the name and dignity of a shepherd, not forcing how.

senses.d: Done or produced with force or great labor, or by extraordinary exertion; hurried; strained; produced by unnatural effort or pressure; as, a forced style; a forced laugh.
Possessing force; characterized by force, efficiency, or energy; powerful; efficacious; impressive; influential.
q: How forcible are right words!
Sweet smells are most forcible in dry substances, when broken.
But I have reasons strong and forcible.
That punishment which hath been sometimes forcible to bridle sin.
He is at once elegant and sublime, forcible and ornamented.

senses.d: Violent; impetuous.
q: Like mingled streams, more forcible when joined.

senses.d: Using force against opposition or resistance; obtained by compulsion; effected by force; as, forcible entry or abduction.
q: In embraces of King James . . . forcible and unjust.

Forcible.syn: Violent; powerful; strong; energetic; mighty; potent; weighty; impressive; cogent; influential.
Forcible.etym: [Cf. OF. forcible forcible, forceable that may be forced.]

senses.d: The accomplishing of any purpose violently, precipitately, prematurely, or with unusual expedition.
The art of raising plants, flowers, and fruits at an earlier season than the natural one, as in a hitbed or by the use of artificial heat.
A place in a river, or other water, where it may be passed by man or beast on foot, by wading.
q: He swam the Esk river where ford there was none.

senses.d: A stream; a current.
q: With water of the ford Or of the clouds.
Permit my ghost to pass the Stygian ford.

Ford.etym: [AS. ford; akin to G. furt, Icel. fjörðr bay, and to E. fare. √ 78. See Fare, v. i., and cf. Frith arm of the sea.]

senses.d: To pass or cross, as a river or other water, by wading; to wade through.
q: His last section, which is no deep one, remains only to be forted.

senses.d: Journey; way; method of proceeding.

Fore.etym: [AS. f�r, fr. faran to go. See Fare, v. i.]

senses.d: In the part that precedes or goes first; — opposed to aft, after, back, behind, etc.
Formerly; previously; afore.
q: The eyes, fore duteous, now converted are.

senses.d: In or towards the bows of a ship.

Fore.etym: [AS. fore, adv. & prep., another form of for. See For, and cf. Former, Foremost.]

senses.d: Advanced, as compared with something else; toward the front; being or coming first, in time, place, order, or importance; preceding; anterior; antecedent; earlier; forward; — opposed to back or behind; as, the fore part of a garment; the fore part of the day; the fore and of a wagon.
q: The free will of the subject is preserved, while it is directed by the fore purpose of the state.

senses.d: The front; hence, that which is in front; the future.
Before; — sometimes written 'fore as if a contraction of afore or before.
To plan beforehand; to scheme; to project.
q: He shall forecast his devices against the strongholds.

senses.d: To foresee; to calculate beforehand, so as to provide for.
q: It is wisdom to consider the end of things before we embark, and to forecast consequences.

senses.d: To contrive or plan beforehand.
q: If it happen as I did forecast.

senses.d: Previous contrivance or determination; predetermination.
q: He makes this difference to arise from the forecast and predetermination of the gods themselves.

senses.d: Foresight of consequences, and provision against them; prevision; premeditation.
q: His calm, deliberate forecast better fitted him for the council than the camp.

senses.d: One who precedes another in the line of genealogy in any degree, but usually in a remote degree; an ancestor.
q: Respecting your forefathers, you would have been taught to respect yourselves.

senses.d: Foremost part or place.
q: Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle.
Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, standing in the forefront for all time, the masters of those who know.

senses.d: The front of that part of the head which incloses the brain; that part of the face above the eyes; the brow.
The aspect or countenance; assurance.
q: To look with forehead bold and big enough Upon the power and puissance of the king.

senses.d: The front or fore part of anything.
q: Flames in the forehead of the morning sky.
So rich advantage of a promised glory As smiles upon the forehead of this action.

senses.d: Outside; extraneous; separated; alien; as, a foreign country; a foreign government.
Not native or belonging to a certain country; born in or belonging to another country, nation, sovereignty, or locality; as, a foreign language; foreign fruits.
q: Hail, foreign wonder! Whom certain these rough shades did never breed.

senses.d: Remote; distant; strange; not belonging; not connected; not pertaining or pertient; not appropriate; not harmonious; not agreeable; not congenial; — with to or from; as, foreign to the purpose; foreign to one's nature.
q: This design is not foreign from some people's thoughts.

senses.d: Held at a distance; excluded; exiled.
q: Kept him a foreign man still; which so grieved him, That he ran mad and died.

Foreign.syn: Outlandish; alien; exotic; remote; distant; extraneous; extrinsic.
Foreign.etym: [OE. forein, F. forain, LL. foraneus, fr. L. foras, foris, out of doors, abroad, without; akin to fores doors, and E. door. See Door, and cf. Foreclose, Forfeit, Forest, Forum.]

senses.d: A person belonging to or owning allegiance to a foreign country; one not native in the country or jurisdiction under consideration, or not naturalized there; an alien; a stranger.
q: Joy is such a foreigner, So mere a stranger to my thoughts.
Nor could the majesty of the English crown appear in a greater luster, either to foreigners or subjects.

senses.d: To have previous knowledge of; to know beforehand.
q: Who would the miseries of man foreknow?

senses.d: Knowledge of a thing before it happens, or of whatever is to happen; prescience.
q: If I foreknew, Foreknowledge had no influence on their fault.

senses.d: First in time or place; most advanced; chief in rank or dignity; as, the foremost troops of an army.
q: THat struck the foremost man of all this world.

Foremost.etym: [OE. formest first, AS. formest, fyrmest, superl. of forma first, which is a superl. fr. fore fore; cf. Goth. frumist, fruma, first. See Fore, adv., and cf. First, Former, Frame, v. t., Prime, a.]

senses.d: To ordain or appoint beforehand; to preordain; to predestinate; to predetermine.
The part most advanced, or first in time or in place; the beginning.
To turn before; to precede; to be in advance of (something following).
To come before as an earnest of something to follow; to introduce as a harbinger; to announce.
q: These signs forerun the death or fall of kings.

senses.d: A messenger sent before to give notice of the approach of others; a harbinger; a sign foreshowing something; a prognostic; as, the forerunner of a fever.
q: Whither the forerunner in for us entered, even Jesus.
My elder brothers, my forerunners, came.

senses.d: A predecessor; an ancestor.
A piece of rag terminating the log line.
To see beforehand; to have prescience of; to foreknow.
q: A prudent man foreseeth the evil.

senses.d: To provide.
q: Great shoals of people, which go on to populate, without foreseeing means of life.

Foresee.etym: [AS. foreseón; fore + seón to see. See See, v. t.]

senses.d: To have or exercise foresight.
The fore part of a ship.
The fold of skin which covers the glans of the penis; the prepuce.
An extensive wood; a large tract of land covered with trees; in the United States, a wood of native growth, or a tract of woodland which has never been cultivated.

A large extent or precinct of country, generally waste and woody, belonging to the sovereign, set apart for the keeping of game for his use, not inclosed, but distinguished by certain limits, and protected by certain laws, courts, and officers of its own.

Forest.etym: [OF. forest, F. forêt, LL. forestis, also, forestus, forestum, foresta, prop., open ground reserved for the chase, fr. L. foris, foras, out of doors, abroad. See Foreign.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a forest; sylvan.
To cover with trees or wood.
To predict; to tell before occurence; to prophesy; to foreshow.
q: Deeds then undone my faithful tongue foretold.
Prodigies, foretelling the future eminence and luster of his character.

senses.d: To utter predictions.
To warn beforehand; to give previous warning, admonition, information, or notice to; to caution in advance.
q: We were forewarned of your coming.

senses.d: Injury; wrong; mischief.
q: To seek arms upon people and country that never did us any forfeit.

senses.d: A thing forfeit or forfeited; what is or may be taken from one in requital of a misdeed committed; that which is lost, or the right to which is alienated, by a crime, offense, neglect of duty, or breach of contract; hence, a fine; a mulct; a penalty; as, he who murders pays the forfeit of his life.
q: Thy slanders I forgive; and therewithal Remit thy other forfeits.

senses.d: Something deposited and redeemable by a sportive fine; — whence the game of forfeits.
q: Country dances and forfeits shortened the rest of the day.

Forfeit.etym: [OE. forfet crime, penalty, F. forfait crime (LL. forefactum, forifactum), prop. p. p. of forfaire to forfeit, transgress, fr. LL. forifacere, prop., to act beyond; L. foris out of doors, abroad, beyond + facere to do. See Foreign, and Fact.]

senses.d: Lost or alienated for an offense or crime; liable to penal seizure.
q: Thy wealth being forfeit to the state.
To tread the forfeit paradise.

Forfeit.etym: [F. forfait, p. p. of forfaire. See Forfeit, n.]

senses.d: To lose, or lose the right to, by some error, fault, offense, or crime; to render one's self by misdeed liable to be deprived of; to alienate the right to possess, by some neglect or crime; as, to forfeit an estate by treason; to forfeit reputation by a breach of promise; — with to before the one acquiring what is forfeited.
q: had forfeited their property by their crimes.
Undone and forfeited to cares forever!

senses.d: To be guilty of a misdeed; to be criminal; to transgress.
To fail to keep an obligation.
q: I will have the heart of him if he forfeit.

senses.d: In the condition of being forfeited; subject to alienation.
q: Once more I will renew His lapsèd powers, though forfeite.

senses.d: A place or establishment where iron or other metals are wrought by heating and hammering; especially, a furnace, or a shop with its furnace, etc., where iron is heated and wrought; a smithy.
q: In the quick forge and working house of thought.

senses.d: The works where wrought iron is produced directly from the ore, or where iron is rendered malleable by puddling and shingling; a shingling mill.
The act of beating or working iron or steel; the manufacture of metallic bodies.
q: In the greater bodies the forge was easy.

Forge.etym: [F. forge, fr. L. fabrica the workshop of an artisan who works in hard materials, fr. faber artisan, smith, as adj., skillful, ingenious; cf. Gr. � soft, tender. Cf. Fabric.]

senses.d: To form by heating and hammering; to beat into any particular shape, as a metal.
q: Mars's armor forged for proof eterne.

senses.d: To form or shape out in any way; to produce; to frame; to invent.
q: Those names that the schools forged, and put into the mouth of scholars, could never get admittance into common use.
Do forge a life-long trouble for ourselves.

senses.d: To coin.
To make falsely; to produce, as that which is untrue or not genuine; to fabricate; to counterfeit, as, a signature, or a signed document.
q: That paltry story is untrue, And forged to cheat such gulls as you.
Forged certificates of his . . . moral character.

Forge.etym: [F. forger, OF. forgier, fr. L. fabricare, fabricari, to form, frame, fashion, from fabrica. See Forge, n., and cf. Fabricate.]

senses.d: To commit forgery.
To move heavily and slowly, as a ship after the sails are furled; to work one's way, as one ship in outsailing another; — used especially in the phrase to forge ahead.
q: And off she forged without a shock.

Forge.etym: [See Forge, v. t., and for sense 2, cf. Forge compel.]

senses.d: To impel forward slowly; as, to forge a ship forward.
One who forges, makes, of forms; a fabricator; a falsifier.
Especially: One guilty of forgery; one who makes or issues a counterfeit document.

Forger.etym: [Cf. F. forgeur metal worker, L. fabricator artificer. See Forge, n. & v. t., and cf. Fabricator.]

senses.d: To lose the remembrance of; to let go from the memory; to cease to have in mind; not to think of; also, to lose the power of; to cease from doing.
q: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits.
Let my right hand forget her cunning.
Hath thy knee forget to bow?

senses.d: To treat with inattention or disregard; to slight; to neglect.
q: Can a woman forget her sucking child? . . . Yes, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.

Forget.etym: [OE. forgeten, foryeten, AS. forgietan, forgitan; pref. for- + gietan, gitan (only in comp.), to get; cf. D. vergeten, G. vergessen, Sw. förgäta, Dan. forgiette. See For-, and Get, v. t.]

senses.d: Apt to forget; easily losing remembrance; as, a forgetful man should use helps to strengthen his memory.
Heedless; careless; neglectful; inattentive.
q: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers.

senses.d: Causing to forget; inducing oblivion; oblivious.
The quality of being forgetful; prononess to let slip from the mind.
Loss of remembrance or recollection; a ceasing to remember; oblivion.
q: A sweet forgetfulness of human care.

senses.d: Failure to bear in mind; careless omission; inattention; as, forgetfulness of duty.
To give wholly; to make over without reservation; to resign.
q: To them that list the world's gay shows I leave, And to great ones such folly do forgive.

senses.d: To give up resentment or claim to requital on account of (an offense or wrong); to remit the penalty of; to pardon; — said in reference to the act forgiven.
q: And their sins should be forgiven them.
He forgive injures so readily that he might be said to invite them.

senses.d: To cease to feel resentment against, on account of wrong committed; to give up claim to requital from or retribution upon (an offender); to absolve; to pardon; — said of the person offending.
q: Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.
I as free forgive you, as I would be fforgiven.

Forgive.etym: [OE. forgiven, foryiven, foryeven, AS. forgiefan, forgifan; perh. for- + giefan, gifan to give; cf. D. vergeven, G. vergeben, Icel. fyrirgefa, Sw. f�rgifva, Goth. fragiban to give, grant. See For-, and Give, v. t.]

senses.d: The act of forgiving; the state of being forgiven; as, the forgiveness of sin or of injuries.
q: To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgivenesses.
In whom we have . . . the forgiveness of sin.

senses.d: Disposition to pardon; willingness to forgive.
q: If thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared.

senses.d: Disposed to forgive; inclined to overlook offenses; mild; merciful; compassionate; placable; as, a forgiving temper.

An instrument consisting of a handle with a shank terminating in two or more prongs or tines, which are usually of metal, parallel and slightly curved; — used for piercing, holding, taking up, or pitching anything.
Anything furcate or like a fork in shape, or furcate at the extremity; as, a tuning fork.
One of the parts into which anything is furcated or divided; a prong; a branch of a stream, a road, etc.; a barbed point, as of an arrow.
q: Let it fall . . . though the fork invade The region of my heart.
A thunderbolt with three forks.

senses.d: The place where a division or a union occurs; the angle or opening between two branches or limbs; as, the fork of a river, a tree, or a road.
The gibbet.

Fork.etym: [AS. forc, fr. L. furca. Cf. Fourché, Furcate.]

senses.d: To shoot into blades, as corn.
q: The corn beginneth to fork.

senses.d: To divide into two or more branches; as, a road, a tree, or a stream forks.
To raise, or pitch with a fork, as hay; to dig or turn over with a fork, as the soil.
q: Forking the sheaves on the high-laden cart.

senses.d: The shape and structure of anything, as distinguished from the material of which it is composed; particular disposition or arrangement of matter, giving it individuality or distinctive character; configuration; figure; external appearance.
q: The form of his visage was changed.
And woven close close, both matter, form, and style.

senses.d: Constitution; mode of construction, organization, etc.; system; as, a republican form of government.
Established method of expression or practice; fixed way of proceeding; conventional or stated scheme; formula; as, a form of prayer.
q: Those whom form of laws Condemned to die.

senses.d: Show without substance; empty, outside appearance; vain, trivial, or conventional ceremony; conventionality; formality; as, a matter of mere form.
q: Though well we may not pass upon his life Without the form of justice.

senses.d: Orderly arrangement; shapeliness; also, comeliness; elegance; beauty.
q: The earth was without form and void.
He hath no form nor comeliness.

senses.d: A shape; an image; a phantom.
That by which shape is given or determined; mold; pattern; model.
A long seat; a bench; hence, a rank of students in a school; a class; also, a class or rank in society.
The seat or bed of a hare.
q: As in a form sitteth a weary hare.

senses.d: The type or other matter from which an impression is to be taken, arranged and secured in a chase.
The boundary line of a material object. In painting, more generally, the human body.
The particular shape or structure of a word or part of speech; as, participial forms; verbal forms.

Form.etym: [OE. & F. forme, fr. L. forma; cf. Skr. dhariman. Cf. Firm.]

senses.d: To give form or shape to; to frame; to construct; to make; to fashion.
q: God formed man of the dust of the ground.
The thought that labors in my forming brain.

senses.d: To give a particular shape to; to shape, mold, or fashion into a certain state or condition; to arrange; to adjust; also, to model by instruction and discipline; to mold by influence, etc.; to train.
q: 'T is education forms the common mind.
Thus formed for speed, he challenges the wind.

senses.d: To go to make up; to act as constituent of; to be the essential or constitutive elements of; to answer for; to make the shape of; — said of that out of which anything is formed or constituted, in whole or in part.
q: The diplomatic politicians . . . who formed by far the majority.

senses.d: To provide with a form, as a hare. See Form, n., 9.
q: The melancholy hare is formed in brakes and briers.

senses.d: To derive by grammatical rules, as by adding the proper suffixes and affixes.

Form.etym: [F. former, L. formare, fr. forma. See Form, n.]

senses.d: To take a form, definite shape, or arrangement; as, the infantry should form in column.
To run to a form, as a hare.

To treat (plates) so as to bring them to fit condition for introduction into a storage battery, causing one plate to be composed more or less of spongy lead, and the other of lead peroxide. This was formerly done by repeated slow alternations of the charging current, but now the plates or grids are coated or filled, one with a paste of red lead and the other with litharge, introduced into the cell, and formed by a direct charging current.
First.
Arranged, as stars in a constellation; as, formed stars.
Having structure; capable of growth and development; organized; as, the formed or organized ferments. See Ferment, n.
One who forms; a maker; a creator.
A shape around which an article is to be shaped, molded, woven wrapped, pasted, or otherwise constructed.
Preceding in order of time; antecedent; previous; prior; earlier; hence, ancient; long past.
q: For inquire, I pray thee, of the former age.
The latter and former rain.

senses.d: Near the beginning; preceeding; as, the former part of a discourse or argument.
Earlier, as between two things mentioned together; first mentioned.
q: A bad author deserves better usage than a bad critic; a man may be the former merely through the misfortune of an ill judgment; but he can not be latter without both that and an ill temper.

Former.syn: Prior; previous; anterior; antecedent; preceding; foregoing.
Former.etym: [A compar. due to OE. formest. See Foremost.]

senses.d: Unlawful sexual intercourse on the part of an unmarried person; the act of such illicit sexual intercourse between a man and a woman as does not by law amount to adultery.
Adultery.
An unmarried person, male or female, who has criminal intercourse with the other sex; one guilty of fornication.

Fornicator.etym: [F. fornicateur, OF. fornicator, from L. fornicator.]

senses.d: To quit or leave entirely; to desert; to abandon; to depart or withdraw from; to leave; as, false friends and flatterers forsake us in adversity.
q: If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments.

senses.d: To renounce; to reject; to refuse.
q: If you forsake the offer of their love.

Forsake.syn: To abandon; quit; desert; fail; relinquish; give up; renounce; reject. See Abandon.
Forsake.etym: [AS. forsacan to oppose, refuse; for- + sacan to contend, strive; akin to Goth. sakan. See For-, and Sake.]

senses.d: To reject or renounce upon oath; hence, to renounce earnestly, determinedly, or with protestations.
q: I . . . do forswear her.

senses.d: To deny upon oath.
q: Like innocence, and as serenely bold As truth, how loudly he forswears thy gold!

Forswear.etym: [OE. forsweren, forswerien, AS. forswerian; pref. for- + swerian to swear. See For-, and Swear, v. i.]

senses.d: To swear falsely; to commit perjury.

A strong or fortified place; usually, a small fortified place, occupied only by troops, surrounded with a ditch, rampart, and parapet, or with palisades, stockades, or other means of defense; a fortification.
q: Detached works, depending solely on their own strength, belong to the class of works termed forts.

Fort.etym: [F., from fort strong, L. fortis; perh. akin to Skr. darh to fix, make firm, and to E. firm Cf. Forte, Force, Fortalice, Comfort, Effort.]

senses.d: Forward; onward in time, place, or order; in advance from a given point; on to end; as, from that day forth; one, two, three, and so forth.
q: Lucas was Paul's companion, at the leastway from the sixteenth of the Acts forth.
From this time forth, I never will speak word.
I repeated the Ave Maria; the inquisitor bad me say forth; I said I was taught no more.

senses.d: Out, as from a state of concealment, retirement, confinement, nondevelopment, or the like; out into notice or view; as, the plants in spring put forth leaves.
q: When winter past, and summer scarce begun, Invites them forth to labor in the sun.

senses.d: Beyond a (certain) boundary; away; abroad; out.
q: I have no mind of feasting forth to-night.

senses.d: Throughly; from beginning to end.

Forth.etym: [AS. forð, fr. for akin to D. voort, G. fort √78. See Fore, For, and cf. Afford, Further, adv.]

senses.d: Forth from; out of.
q: Some forth their cabins peep.

senses.d: A way; a passage or ford.
Immediately; without delay; directly.
q: Immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales; and he received sight forthwith.

senses.d: As soon as the thing required may be done by reasonable exertion confined to that object.
Following the thirty-ninth, or preceded by thirty-nine units, things, or parts.
Constituting one of forty equal parts into which anything is divided.
One of forty equal parts into which one whole is divided; the quotient of a unit divided by forty; one next in order after the thirty-ninth.
To add strength to; to strengthen; to confirm; to furnish with power to resist attack.
q: Timidity was fortified by pride.
Pride came to the aid of fancy, and both combined to fortify his resolution.

senses.d: To strengthen and secure by forts or batteries, or by surrounding with a wall or ditch or other military works; to render defensible against an attack by hostile forces.

Fortify.etym: [F. fortifier, L. fortificare; fortis strong + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Fort, and -fy.]

senses.d: To raise defensive works.
A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification, sometimes including a town; a fort; a castle; a stronghold; a place of defense or security.

Fortress.etym: [F. forteresse, OF. forteresce, fortelesce, LL. foralitia, fr. L. fortis strong. See Fort, and cf. Fortalice.]

senses.d: To furnish with a fortress or with fortresses; to guard; to fortify.
Four times ten; thirty-nine and one more.

Forty.etym: [OE. forti, fourti, fowerti, AS. feówertig; feówer four + suff. -tig ten; akin to OS. fiwartig, fiartig, D. veertig, G. vierzig, Icel. fjörutīu, Sw. fyratio, Dan. fyrretyve, Goth. fidwōr tigjus. See Four, and Ten, and cf. Fourteen.]

senses.d: The sum of four tens; forty units or objects.
A symbol expressing forty units; as, 40, or xl.
A market place or public place in Rome, where causes were judicially tried, and orations delivered to the people.
A tribunal; a court; an assembly empowered to hear and decide causes.
q: He was . . . more eminent in the senate than in the forum.

Forum.etym: [L.; akin to foris, foras, out of doors. See Foreign.]

senses.d: An agreement; a covenant; a promise.
q: Tell us a tale anon, as forward is.

Forward.etym: [OE., fr. AS. foreweard; fore before + weard a ward. See Ward, n.]

senses.d: Toward a part or place before or in front; onward; in advance; progressively; — opposed to backward.

Forward.etym: [AS. forweard, foreweard; for, fore + -weardes; akin to G. vorwärts. The s is properly a genitive ending. See For, Fore, and -ward, -wards.]

senses.d: Near, or at the fore part; in advance of something else; as, the forward gun in a ship, or the forward ship in a fleet.
Ready; prompt; strongly inclined; in an ill sense, overready; too hasty.
q: Only they would that we should remember the poor; the same which I also was forward to do.
Nor do we find him forward to be sounded.

senses.d: Ardent; eager; earnest; in an ill sense, less reserved or modest than is proper; bold; confident; as, the boy is too forward for his years.
q: I have known men disagreeably forward from their shyness.

senses.d: Advanced beyond the usual degree; advanced for the season; as, the grass is forward, or forward for the season; we have a forward spring.
q: The most forward bud Is eaten by the canker ere it blow.

senses.d: To help onward; to advance; to promote; to accelerate; to quicken; to hasten; as, to forward the growth of a plant; to forward one in improvement.
To send forward; to send toward the place of destination; to transmit; as, to forward a letter.
The quality of being forward; cheerful readiness; promtness; as, the forwardness of Christians in propagating the gospel.
An advanced stage of progress or of preparation; advancement; as, his measures were in great forwardness.
Eagerness; ardor; as, it is difficult to restrain the forwardness of youth.
Boldness; confidence; assurance; want of due reserve or modesty.
q: In France it is usual to bring children into company, and cherish in them, from their infancy, a kind of forwardness and assurance.

senses.d: A state of advance beyond the usual degree; prematureness; precocity; as, the forwardnessof spring or of corn; the forwardness of a pupil.
q: He had such a dexterous proclivity, as his teachers were fain to restrain his forwardness.

Forwardness.syn: Promptness; promptitude; eagerness; ardor; zeal; assurance; confidence; boldness; impudence; presumption.

senses.d: A bird.

Covered with, or containing, extraneous matter which is injurious, noxious, offensive, or obstructive; filthy; dirty; not clean; polluted; nasty; defiled; as, a foul cloth; foul hands; a foul chimney; foul air; a ship's bottom is foul when overgrown with barnacles; a gun becomes foul from repeated firing; a well is foul with polluted water.
q: My face is foul with weeping.

senses.d: Scurrilous; obscene or profane; abusive; as, foul words; foul language.
Hateful; detestable; shameful; odious; wretched.
q: Who first seduced them to that foul revolt?

senses.d: Loathsome; disgusting; as, a foul disease.
Ugly; homely; poor.
q: Let us, like merchants, show our foulest wares.

senses.d: Not favorable; unpropitious; not fair or advantageous; as, a foul wind; a foul road; cloudy or rainy; stormy; not fair; — said of the weather, sky, etc.
q: So foul a sky clears not without a storm.

senses.d: Not conformed to the established rules and customs of a game, conflict, test, etc.; unfair; dishonest; dishonorable; cheating; as, foul play.
Having freedom of motion interfered with by collision or entanglement; entangled; — opposed to clear; as, a rope or cable may get foul while paying it out.

Foul.etym: [OE. foul, ful, AS. fūl; akin to D. vuil, G. faul rotten, OHG. fūl, Icel. fūl foul, fetid; Dan. fuul, Sw. ful foul, Goth. fūls fetid, Lith. puti to be putrid, L. putere to stink, be putrid, pus pus, Gr. πύον pus, to cause to rot, Skr. pūy to stink. √82. Cf. Defile to foul, File to foul, Filth, Pus,

senses.d: To make filthy; to defile; to daub; to dirty; to soil; as, to foul the face or hands with mire.
To incrust (the bore of a gun) with burnt powder in the process of firing.
To cover (a ship's bottom) with anything that impered its sailing; as, a bottom fouled with barnacles.
To entangle, so as to impede motion; as, to foul a rope or cable in paying it out; to come into collision with; as, one boat fouled the other in a race.
To become clogged with burnt powder in the process of firing, as a gun.
To become entagled, as ropes; to come into collision with something; as, the two boats fouled.
An entanglement; a collision, as in a boat race.
In various games or sports, an act done contrary to the rules; a foul stroke, hit, play, or the like.
Foully.
To form by melting a metal, and pouring it into a mold; to cast.

Found.etym: [F. fondre, L. fundere to found, pour.]

senses.d: A thin, single-cut file for combmakers.
To lay the basis of; to set, or place, as on something solid, for support; to ground; to establish upon a basis, literal or figurative; to fix firmly.
q: I had else been perfect, Whole as the marble, founded as the rock.
A man that all his time Hath founded his good fortunes on your love.
It fell not, for it was founded on a rock.

senses.d: To take the ffirst steps or measures in erecting or building up; to furnish the materials for beginning; to begin to raise; to originate; as, to found a college; to found a family.
q: There they shall found Their government, and their great senate choose.

Found.syn: To base; ground; institute; establish; fix. See Predicate.
Found.etym: [F. fonder, L. fundare, fr. fundus bottom. See 1st Bottom, and cf. Founder, v. i., Fund.]

senses.d: The act of founding, fixing, establishing, or beginning to erect.
That upon which anything is founded; that on which anything stands, and by which it is supported; the lowest and supporting layer of a superstructure; groundwork; basis.
q: Behold, I lay in Zion, for a foundation, a stone . . . a precious corner stone, a sure foundation.
The foundation of a free common wealth.

senses.d: The lowest and supporting part or member of a wall, including the base course (see Base course (a), under Base, n.) and footing courses; in a frame house, the whole substructure of masonry.
A donation or legacy appropriated to support a charitable institution, and constituting a permanent fund; endowment.
q: He was entered on the foundation of Westminster.

senses.d: That which is founded, or established by endowment; an endowed institution or charity.
q: Against the canon laws of our foundation.

Foundation.etym: [F. fondation, L. fundatio. See Found to establish.]

senses.d: One who founds, establishes, and erects; one who lays a foundation; an author; one from whom anything originates; one who endows.

Founder.etym: [Cf. OF. fondeor, F. fondateur, L. fundator.]

senses.d: One who founds; one who casts metals in various forms; a caster; as, a founder of cannon, bells, hardware, or types.
To become filled with water, and sink, as a ship.
To fall; to stumble and go lame, as a horse.
q: For which his horse fearé gan to turn, And leep aside, and foundrede as he leep.

senses.d: To fail; to miscarry.

Founder.etym: [OF. fondrer to fall in, cf. F. s'effondrer, fr. fond bottom, L. fundus. See Found to establish.]

senses.d: To cause internal inflammation and soreness in the feet or limbs of (a horse), so as to disable or lame him.
A lameness in the foot of a horse, occasioned by inflammation; closh.
An inflammatory fever of the body, or acute rheumatism; as, chest founder. See Chest ffounder.
A spring of water issuing from the earth.

An artificially produced jet or stream of water; also, the structure or works in which such a jet or stream rises or flows; a basin built and constantly supplied with pure water for drinking and other useful purposes, or for ornament.
A reservoir or chamber to contain a liquid which can be conducted or drawn off as needed for use; as, the ink fountain in a printing press, etc.
The source from which anything proceeds, or from which anything is supplied continuously; origin; source.
q: Judea, the fountain of the gospel.
Author of all being, Fountain of light, thyself invisible.

Fountain.etym: [F. fontaine, LL. fontana, fr. L. fons, fontis. See 2d Fount.]

senses.d: One more than three; twice two.

Four.etym: [OE. four, fower, feower, AS. feówer; akin to OS. fiwar, D. & G. vier, OHG. fior, Icel. fjōrir, Sw. fyra, Dan. fire, Goth. fidwōr, Russ. chetuire, chetvero, W. pedwar, L. quatuor, Gr. τέτταρεσ, τέσσαρεσ, πίσυρεσ, Skr. catur. √302. Cf. Farthing, Firkin, Forty, Cater four, Quater-cousin, Quatuor, Quir

senses.d: The sum of four units; four units or objects.
A symbol representing four units, as 4 or iv.
Four things of the same kind, esp. four horses; as, a chariot and four.
Four times; quadruple; as, a fourfold division.
q: He shall restore the lamb fourfold.

senses.d: Four times as many or as much.
To make four times as much or as many, as an assessment; to quadruple.
Having four feet; quadruped; as, fourfooted beasts.
Four times twenty; eighty.
The product of four times twenty; eighty units or objects.
Having four sides and four equal angles.
Four and ten more; twice seven.

Fourteen.etym: [OE. fourtene, feowertene, AS. feówertȳne, feówertēne. See Four, and Ten, and cf. Forty.]

senses.d: The sum of ten and four; forteen units or objects.
A symbol representing fourteen, as 14 or xiv.
Next in order after the thirteenth; as, the fourteenth day of the month.
Making or constituting one of fourteen equal parts into which anything may be divided.
One of fourteen equal parts into which one whole may be divided; the quotient of a unit divided by fourteen; one next after the thirteenth.
The octave of the seventh.
Next in order after the third; the ordinal of four.
Forming one of four equal parts into which anything may be divided.

Fourth.etym: [OE. fourthe, ferthe, feorthe, AS. feórða, fr. feówer four.]

senses.d: One of four equal parts into which one whole may be divided; the quotient of a unit divided by four; one coming next in order after the third.
The interval of two tones and a semitone, embracing four diatonic degrees of the scale; the subdominant of any key.
Any bird; esp., any large edible bird.
q: Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air.
Behold the fowls of the air; for they sow not.
Like a flight of fowl Scattered by winds and high tempestuous gusts.

senses.d: Any domesticated bird used as food, as a hen, turkey, duck; in a more restricted sense, the common domestic cock or hen (Gallus domesticus).

Fowl.etym: [OE. foul, fowel, foghel, fuhel, fugel, AS. fugol; akin to OS. fugal D. & G. vogel, OHG. fogal, Icel. & Dan. fugl, Sw. fogel, fågel, Goth. fugls; of unknown origin, possibly by loss of l, from the root of E. fly, or akin to E. fox, as being a tailed animal.]

senses.d: To catch or kill wild fowl, for game or food, as by shooting, or by decoys, nets, etc.
q: Such persons as may lawfully hunt, fish, or fowl.

senses.d: A sportsman who pursues wild fowl, or takes or kills for food.

A carnivorous animal of the genus Vulpes, family Canidæ, of many species. The European fox (V. vulgaris or V. vulpes), the American red fox (V. fulvus), the American gray fox (V. Virginianus), and the arctic, white, or blue, fox (V. lagopus) are well-known species.
q: Subtle as the fox for prey.

senses.d: The European dragonet.
The fox shark or thrasher shark; — called also sea fox. See Thrasher shark, under Shark.
A sly, cunning fellow.
q: We call a crafty and cruel man a fox.

senses.d: Rope yarn twisted together, and rubbed with tar; — used for seizings or mats.
A sword; — so called from the stamp of a fox on the blade, or perhaps of a wolf taken for a fox.
q: Thou diest on point of fox.

senses.d: A tribe of Indians which, with the Sacs, formerly occupied the region about Green Bay, Wisconsin; — called also Outagamies.

Fox.etym: [AS. fox; akin to D. vos, G. fuchs, OHG. fuhs, foha, Goth. faúh�, Icel. f�a fox, fox fraud; of unknown origin, cf. Skr. puccha tail. Cf. Vixen.]

senses.d: To intoxicate; to stupefy with drink.
q: I drank . . . so much wine that I was almost foxed.

senses.d: To make sour, as beer, by causing it to ferment.
To repair the feet of, as of boots, with new front upper leather, or to piece the upper fronts of.

Fox.etym: [See Fox, n., cf. Icel. fox imposture.]

senses.d: To turn sour; — said of beer, etc., when it sours in fermenting.
A part broken off; a small, detached portion; an imperfect part; as, a fragment of an ancient writing.
q: Gather up the fragments that remain.

Fragment.etym: [L. fragmentum, fr. frangere to break: cf. F. fragment. See Break, v. t.]

senses.d: A basket made of rushes, used chiefly for containing figs and raisins.
The quantity of raisins — about thirty-two, fifty-six, or seventy-five pounds, — contained in a frail.
A rush for weaving baskets.

Frail.etym: [OE. fraiel, fraile, OF. fraiel, freel, frael, fr. LL. fraellum.]

senses.d: Easily broken; fragile; not firm or durable; liable to fail and perish; easily destroyed; not tenacious of life; weak; infirm.
q: That I may know how frail I am.
An old bent man, worn and frail.

senses.d: Tender.
q: Deep indignation and compassion frail.

senses.d: Liable to fall from virtue or be led into sin; not strong against temptation; weak in resolution; also, unchaste; — often applied to fallen women.
q: Man is frail, and prone to evil.

Frail.etym: [OE. frele, freile, OF. fraile, frele, F. frêle, fr. L. fragilis. See Fragile.]

senses.d: To construct by fitting and uniting the several parts of the skeleton of any structure; specifically, in woodwork, to put together by cutting parts of one member to fit parts of another. See Dovetail, Halve, v. t., Miter, Tenon, Tooth, Tusk, Scarf, and Splice.
To originate; to plan; to devise; to contrive; to compose; in a bad sense, to invent or fabricate, as something false.
q: How many excellent reasonings are framed in the mind of a man of wisdom and study in a length of years.

senses.d: To fit to something else, or for some specific end; to adjust; to regulate; to shape; to conform.
q: And frame my face to all occasions.
We may in some measure frame our minds for the reception of happiness.
The human mind is framed to be influenced.

senses.d: To cause; to bring about; to produce.
q: Fear frames disorder, and disorder wounds.

senses.d: To support.
q: That on a staff his feeble steps did frame.

senses.d: To provide with a frame, as a picture.

Frame.etym: [OE. framen, fremen, to execute, build, AS. fremman to further, perform, effect, fr. fram strong, valiant; akin to E. foremost, and prob. to AS. fram from, Icel. fremja, frama, to further, framr forward, G. fromm worthy, excellent, pious. See Foremost, From, and cf. Furnish.]

senses.d: To shape; to arrange, as the organs of speech.
To proceed; to go.
q: The bauty of this sinful dame Made many princes thither frame.

senses.d: Anything composed of parts fitted and united together; a fabric; a structure; esp., the constructional system, whether of timber or metal, that gives to a building, vessel, etc., its model and strength; the skeleton of a structure.
q: These are thy glorious works, Parent of good, Almighty! thine this universal frame.

senses.d: The bodily structure; physical constitution; make or build of a person.
q: Some bloody passion shakes your very frame.
No frames could be strong enough to endure it.

senses.d: A kind of open case or structure made for admitting, inclosing, or supporting things, as that which incloses or contains a window, door, picture, etc.; that on which anything is held or stretched
A term applied, especially in England, to certain machines built upon or within framework; as, a stocking frame; lace frame; spinning frame, etc.
Form; shape; proportion; scheme; structure; constitution; system; as, a frameof government.
q: She that hath a heart of that fine frame To pay this debt of love but to a brother.
Put your discourse into some frame.

senses.d: Particular state or disposition, as of the mind; humor; temper; mood; as, to be always in a happy frame.
Contrivance; the act of devising or scheming.
q: John the bastard Whose spirits toil in frame of villainies.

senses.d: In games: (a) In pool, the triangular form used in setting up the balls; also, the balls as set up, or the round of playing required to pocket them all; as, to play six frames in a game of 50 points. (b) In bowling, as in tenpins, one of the several innings forming a game.
A pigsty.
To shut up in a frank or sty; to pen up; hence, to cram; to fatten.
The common heron; — so called from its note.
Unbounded by restrictions, limitations, etc.; free.
Free in uttering one's real sentiments; not reserved; using no disguise; candid; ingenuous; as, a frank nature, conversation, manner, etc.
Liberal; generous; profuse.
q: Frank of civilities that cost them nothing.

senses.d: Unrestrained; loose; licentious; — used in a bad sense.

Frank.syn: Ingenuous; candid; artless; plain; open; unreserved; undisguised; sincere. See Candid, Ingenuous.
Frank.etym: [F. franc free, frank, L. Francus a Frank, fr. OHG. Franko the name of a Germanic people on the Rhine, who afterward founded the French monarchy; cf. AS. franca javelin, Icel. frakka. Cf. Franc, French, a., Franchise, n.]

senses.d: To send by public conveyance free of expense.
To extempt from charge for postage, as a letter, package, or packet, etc.
The privilege of sending letters or other mail matter, free of postage, or without charge; also, the sign, mark, or signature denoting that a letter or other mail matter is to free of postage.
q: I have said so much, that, if I had not a frank, I must burn my letter and begin again.

senses.d: A member of one of the German tribes that in the fifth century overran and conquered Gaul, and established the kingdom of France.
A native or inhabitant of Western Europe; a European; — a term used in the Levant.
A French coin. See Franc.

A fragrant, aromatic resin, or gum resin, burned as an incense in religious rites or for medicinal fumigation. The best kinds now come from East Indian trees, of the genus Boswellia; a commoner sort, from the Norway spruce (Abies excelsa) and other coniferous trees. The frankincense of the ancient Jews is still unidentified.
In a frank manner; freely.
q: Very frankly he confessed his treasons.

Frankly.syn: Openly; ingenuously; plainly; unreservedly; undisguisedly; sincerely; candidly; artlessly; freely; readily; unhesitatingly; liberally; willingly.

senses.d: Deception deliberately practiced with a view to gaining an unlawful or unfair advantage; artifice by which the right or interest of another is injured; injurious stratagem; deceit; trick.
q: If success a lover's toil attends, Few ask, if fraud or force attained his ends.

senses.d: An intentional perversion of truth for the purpose of obtaining some valuable thing or promise from another.
A trap or snare.
q: To draw the proud King Ahab into fraud.

Fraud.syn: Deception; deceit; guile; craft; wile; sham; strife; circumvention; stratagem; trick; imposition; cheat. See Deception.
Fraud.etym: [F. fraude, L. fraus, fraudis; prob. akin to Skr. dhūrv to injure, dhvṛ to cause to fall, and E. dull.]

senses.d: Affray; broil; contest; combat.
q: Who began this bloody fray?

senses.d: To frighten; to terrify; to alarm.
q: What frays ye, that were wont to comfort me affrayed?

senses.d: To bear the expense of; to defray.
q: The charge of my most curious and costly ingredients frayed, I shall acknowledge myself amply satisfied.

Fray.etym: [Cf. OF. fraier. See Defray, v. t.]

senses.d: To rub; to wear off, or wear into shreds, by rubbing; to fret, as cloth; as, a deer is said to fray her head.

Fray.etym: [OF. freier, fraier, froier, to rub. L. fricare; cf. friare to crumble, E. friable; perh. akin to Gr. χρίειν to anoint, χρι̑σμα an anointing, Skr. ghṛsh to rub, scratch. Cf. Friction.]

senses.d: To rub.
q: We can show the marks he made When 'gainst the oak his antlers frayed.

senses.d: To wear out or into shreads, or to suffer injury by rubbing, as when the threads of the warp or of the woof wear off so that the cross threads are loose; to ravel; as, the cloth frays badly.
q: A suit of frayed magnificience.

senses.d: A fret or chafe, as in cloth; a place injured by rubbing.
A small yellowish or brownish spot in the skin, particularly on the face, neck, or hands.
Any small spot or discoloration.

Freckle.etym: [Dim., from the same root as freak, v. t.]

senses.d: To sprinkle or mark with freckles or small discolored spots; to spot.
To become covered or marked with freckles; to be spotted.
Marked with freckles; spotted.
q: The freckled cowslip, burnet, and green clover.

senses.d: Exempt from subjection to the will of others; not under restraint, control, or compulsion; able to follow one's own impulses, desires, or inclinations; determining one's own course of action; not dependent; at liberty.
q: That which has the power, or not the power, to operate, is that alone which is or is not free.

senses.d: Not under an arbitrary or despotic government; subject only to fixed laws regularly and fairly administered, and defended by them from encroachments upon natural or acquired rights; enjoying political liberty.
Liberated, by arriving at a certain age, from the control of parents, guardian, or master.
Not confined or imprisoned; released from arrest; liberated; at liberty to go.
q: Set an unhappy prisoner free.
