senses.d: Not subjected to the laws of physical necessity; capable of voluntary activity; endowed with moral liberty; — said of the will.
q: Not free, what proof could they have given sincere Of true allegiance, constant faith, or love.

senses.d: Clear of offense or crime; guiltless; innocent.
q: My hands are guilty, but my heart is free.

senses.d: Unconstrained by timidity or distrust; unreserved; ingenuous; frank; familiar; communicative.
q: He was free only with a few.

senses.d: Unrestrained; immoderate; lavish; licentious; — used in a bad sense.
q: The critics have been very free in their censures.
A man may live a free life as to wine or women.

senses.d: Not close or parsimonious; liberal; open-handed; lavish; as, free with his money.
Exempt; clear; released; liberated; not encumbered or troubled with; as, free from pain; free from a burden; — followed by from, or, rarely, by of.
q: Princes declaring themselves free from the obligations of their treaties.

senses.d: Characteristic of one acting without restraint; charming; easy.
Ready; eager; acting without spurring or whipping; spirited; as, a free horse.

Free.etym: [OE. fre, freo, AS. freó, frī; akin to D. vrij, OS. & OHG. frī, G. frei, Icel. frī, Sw. & Dan. fri, Goth. freis, and also to Skr. prija beloved, dear, fr. prī to love, Goth. frijōn. Cf. Affray, Belfry, Friday, Friend, Frith inclosure.]

senses.d: Freely; willingly.
q: I as free forgive you As I would be forgiven.

senses.d: Without charge; as, children admitted free.

To make free; to set at liberty; to rid of that which confines, limits, embarrasses, oppresses, etc.; to release; to disengage; to clear; — followed by from, and sometimes by off; as, to free a captive or a slave; to be freed of these inconveniences.
q: Our land is from the rage of tigers freed.
Arise, . . . free thy people from their yoke.

senses.d: To remove, as something that confines or bars; to relieve from the constraint of.
q: This master key Frees every lock, and leads us to his person.

senses.d: To frank.

Free.etym: [OE. freen, freoien, AS. freógan. See Free, a.]

senses.d: The state of being free; exemption from the power and control of another; liberty; independence.
q: Made captive, yet deserving freedom more.

senses.d: Privileges; franchises; immunities.
q: Your charter and your caty's freedom.

senses.d: Exemption from necessity, in choise and action; as, the freedom of the will.
Ease; facility; as, he speaks or acts with freedom.
Frankness; openness; unreservedness.
q: I emboldened spake and freedom used.

senses.d: Improper familiarity; violation of the rules of decorum; license.
Generosity; liberality.
In a free manner; without restraint or compulsion; abundantly; gratuitously.
q: Of every tree of the garden thou mayst freely eat.
Freely ye have received, freely give.
Freely they stood who stood, and fell who fell.
Freely we serve Because we freely love.

Freely.syn: Independently; voluntarily; spontaneously; unconditionally; unobstructedly; willingly; readily; liberally; generously; bounteously; munificently; bountifully; abundantly; largely; copiously; plentifully; plenteously.

senses.d: One who enjoys liberty, or who is not subject to the will of another; one not a slave or vassal.
A member of a corporation, company, or city, possessing certain privileges; a member of a borough, town, or State, who has the right to vote at elections. See Liveryman.
q: Both having been made freemen on the same day.

senses.d: A will free from improper coercion or restraint.
q: To come thus was I not constrained, but did On my free will.

senses.d: The power asserted of moral beings of willing or choosing without the restraints of physical or absolute necessity.
Of or pertaining to free will; voluntary; spontaneous; as, a freewill offering.
Often to be met with; happening at short intervals; often repeated or occurring; as, frequent visits.
Addicted to any course of conduct; inclined to indulge in any practice; habitual; persistent.
q: He has been loud and frequent in declaring himself hearty for the government.

senses.d: Full; crowded; thronged.
q: 'T is Cæsar's will to have a frequent senate.

senses.d: Often or commonly reported.
q: 'T is frequent in the city he hath subdued The Catti and the Daci.

Frequent.etym: [L. frequens, -entis, crowded, frequent, akin to farcire to stuff: cf. F. fréquent. Cf. Farce, n.]

senses.d: To visit often; to resort to often or habitually.
q: He frequented the court of Augustus.

senses.d: To make full; to fill.
q: With their sighs the air Frequenting, sent from hearts contrite.

Frequent.etym: [L. frequentare: cf. F. fréquenter. See Frequent, a.]

senses.d: Possessed of original life and vigor; new and strong; unimpaired; sound.
New; original; additional.
q: A fresh pleasure in every fresh posture of the limbs.

senses.d: Lately produced, gathered, or prepared for market; not stale; not dried or preserved; not wilted, faded, or tainted; in good condition; as, fresh vegetables, flowers, eggs, meat, fruit, etc.; recently made or obtained; occurring again; repeated; as, a fresh supply of goods; fresh tea, raisins, etc.; lately come or made public; as, fresh news; recently taken from a well or spring; as, fresh water.
Youthful; florid; as, these fresh nymphs.
In a raw, green, or untried state; uncultivated; uncultured; unpracticed; as, a fresh hand on a ship.
Renewed in vigor, alacrity, or readiness for action; as, fresh for a combat; hence, tending to renew in vigor; rather strong; cool or brisk; as, a fresh wind.
Not salt; as, fresh water, in distinction from that which is from the sea, or brackish; fresh meat, in distinction from that which is pickled or salted.

Fresh.syn: Sound; unimpaired; recent; unfaded: ruddy; florid; sweet; good: inexperienced; unpracticed: unused; lively; vigorous; strong.
Fresh.etym: [OE. fresch, AS. fersc; akin to D. versch, G. frisch, OHG. frisc, Sw. frisk, Dan. frisk, fersk, Icel. frīskr frisky, brisk, ferskr fresh; cf. It. fresco, OF. fres, freis, fem. freske, fresche, F. frais, fem. fraîche, which are of German origin. Cf. Fraischeur, Fresco, Frisk.]

senses.d: A stream or spring of fresh water.
q: He shall drink naught but brine; for I'll not show him Where the quick freshes are.

senses.d: A flood; a freshet.
The mingling of fresh water with salt in rivers or bays, as by means of a flood of fresh water flowing toward or into the sea.
To refresh; to freshen.
To devour.
q: The sow frete the child right in the cradle.

senses.d: To rub; to wear away by friction; to chafe; to gall; hence, to eat away; to gnaw; as, to fret cloth; to fret a piece of gold or other metal; a worm frets the plants of a ship.
q: With many a curve my banks I fret.

senses.d: To impair; to wear away; to diminish.
q: By starts His fretted fortunes give him hope and fear.

senses.d: To make rough, agitate, or disturb; to cause to ripple; as, to fret the surface of water.
To tease; to irritate; to vex.
q: Fret not thyself because of evil doers.

Fret.etym: [OE. freten to eat, consume; AS. fretan, for foretan; pref. for- + etan to eat; akin to D. vreten, OHG. frezzan, G. fressen, Sw. fräta, Goth. fra-itan. See For, and Eat, v. t.]

senses.d: To be worn away; to chafe; to fray; as, a wristband frets on the edges.
To eat in; to make way by corrosion.
q: Many wheals arose, and fretted one into another with great excoriation.

senses.d: To be agitated; to be in violent commotion; to rankle; as, rancor frets in the malignant breast.
To be vexed; to be chafed or irritated; to be angry; to utter peevish expressions.
q: He frets, he fumes, he stares, he stamps the ground.

senses.d: The agitation of the surface of a fluid by fermentation or other cause; a rippling on the surface of water.
Agitation of mind marked by complaint and impatience; disturbance of temper; irritation; as, he keeps his mind in a continual fret.
q: Yet then did Dennis rave in furious fret.

senses.d: Herpes; tetter.
The worn sides of river banks, where ores, or stones containing them, accumulate by being washed down from the hills, and thus indicate to the miners the locality of the veins.
To ornament with raised work; to variegate; to diversify.
q: Whose skirt with gold was fretted all about.
Yon gray lines, That fret the clouds, are messengers of day.

Fret.etym: [OE. fretten to adorn, AS. frætwan, frætwian; akin to OS. fratahōn, cf. Goth. us-fratwjan to make wise, also AS. frætwe ornaments, OS. fratahī adornment.]

senses.d: Ornamental work in relief, as carving or embossing. See Fretwork.
An ornament consisting of small fillets or slats intersecting each other or bent at right angles, as in classical designs, or at oblique angles, as often in Oriental art.
q: His lady's cabinet is a adorned on the fret, ceiling, and chimney-piece with . . . carving.

senses.d: The reticulated headdress or net, made of gold or silver wire, in which ladies in the Middle Ages confined their hair.
q: A fret of gold she had next her hair.

senses.d: A saltire interlaced with a mascle.
A short piece of wire, or other material fixed across the finger board of a guitar or a similar instrument, to indicate where the finger is to be placed.

Fret.etym: [F. frette a saltire, also a hoop, ferrule, prob. a dim. of L. ferrum iron. For sense 2, cf. also E. fret to rub.]

senses.d: To furnish with frets, as an instrument of music.
The worn side of the bank of a river. See 4th Fret, n., 4.
A vitreous compound, used by potters in glazing, consisting of lime, silica, borax, lead, and soda.
Rubbed or worn away; chafed.
Agitated; vexed; worried.
Ornamented with fretwork; furnished with frets; variegated; made rough on the surface.
Interlaced one with another; — said of charges and ordinaries.
One who entertains for another such sentiments of esteem, respect, and affection that he seeks his society and welfare; a wellwisher; an intimate associate; sometimes, an attendant.
q: Want gives to know the flatterer from the friend.
A friend that sticketh closer than a brother.

senses.d: One not inimical or hostile; one not a foe or enemy; also, one of the same nation, party, kin, etc., whose friendly feelings may be assumed. The word is some times used as a term of friendly address.
q: Friend, how camest thou in hither?

senses.d: One who looks propitiously on a cause, an institution, a project, and the like; a favorer; a promoter; as, a friend to commerce, to poetry, to an institution.

One of a religious sect characterized by disuse of outward rites and an ordained ministry, by simplicity of dress and speech, and esp. by opposition to war and a desire to live at peace with all men. They are popularly called Quakers.
q: America was first visited by Friends in 1656.

senses.d: A paramour of either sex.

Friend.etym: [OE. frend, freond, AS. freónd, prop. p. pr. of freón, freógan, to love; akin to D. vriend friend, OS. friund friend, friohan to love, OHG. friunt friend, G. freund, Icel. frændi kinsman, Sw. frände. Goth. frijōnds friend, frijōn to love. √83. See Free, and cf. Fiend.]

senses.d: To act as the friend of; to favor; to countenance; to befriend.
q: Fortune friends the bold.

senses.d: Having the temper and disposition of a friend; disposed to promote the good of another; kind; favorable.
Appropriate to, or implying, friendship; befitting friends; amicable.
q: In friendly relations with his moderate opponents.

senses.d: Not hostile; as, a friendly power or state.
Promoting the good of any person; favorable; propitious; serviceable; as, a friendly breeze or gale.
q: On the first friendly bank he throws him down.

Friendly.syn: Amicable; kind; conciliatory; propitious; favorable. See Amicable.

senses.d: In the manner of friends; amicably; like friends.
q: In whom all graces that can perfect beauty Are friendly met.

senses.d: A friendly person; — usually applied to natives friendly to foreign settlers or invaders.
q: These were speedily routed by the friendlies, who attacked the small force before them in fine style.

senses.d: The state of being friends; friendly relation, or attachment, to a person, or between persons; affection arising from mutual esteem and good will; friendliness; amity; good will.
q: There is little friendship in the world.
There can be no friendship without confidence, and no confidence without integrity.
Preferred by friendship, and not chosen by sufficiency.

senses.d: Kindly aid; help; assistance,
q: Some friendship will it lend you gainst the tempest.

senses.d: Aptness to unite; conformity; affinity; harmony; correspondence.
q: Those colors . . . have a friendship with each other.

senses.d: An ornamental appendage to the border of a piece of stuff, originally consisting of the ends of the warp, projecting beyond the woven fabric; but more commonly made separate and sewed on, consisting sometimes of projecting ends, twisted or plaited together, and sometimes of loose threads of wool, silk, or linen, or narrow strips of leather, or the like.
Something resembling in any respect a fringe; a line of objects along a border or edge; a border; an edging; a margin; a confine.
q: The confines of grace and the fringes of repentance.

senses.d: One of a number of light or dark bands, produced by the interference of light; a diffraction band; — called also interference fringe.
The peristome or fringelike appendage of the capsules of most mosses. See Peristome.

Fringe.etym: [OF, fringe, F. frange, prob. fr. L. fimbria fiber, thread, fringe, cf. fibra fiber, E. fiber, fimbriate.]

senses.d: To adorn the edge of with a fringe or as with a fringe.
q: Precipices fringed with grass.

senses.d: From; away; back or backward; — now used only in opposition to the word to, in the phrase to and fro, that is, to and from. See To and fro under To.

Fro.etym: [OE. fra, fro, adv. & prep., Icel. frā, akin to Dan. fra from, E. from. See From.]

senses.d: From.
An amphibious animal of the genus Rana and related genera, of many species. Frogs swim rapidly, and take long leaps on land. Many of the species utter loud notes in the springtime.
The triangular prominence of the hoof, in the middle of the sole of the foot of the horse, and other animals; the fourchette.
A supporting plate having raised ribs that form continuations of the rails, to guide the wheels where one track branches from another or crosses it.
An oblong cloak button, covered with netted thread, and fastening into a loop instead of a button hole.
The loop of the scabbard of a bayonet or sword.

Frog.etym: [AS. froggu, frocga a frog (in sensel); akin to D. vorsch, OHG. frosk, G. frosch, Icel. froskr, fraukr, Sw. & Dan. frö.]

senses.d: To ornament or fasten (a coat, etc.) with trogs. See Frog, n., 4.

Out of the neighborhood of; lessening or losing proximity to; leaving behind; by reason of; out of; by aid of; — used whenever departure, setting out, commencement of action, being, state, occurrence, etc., or procedure, emanation, absence, separation, etc., are to be expressed. It is construed with, and indicates, the point of space or time at which the action, state, etc., are regarded as setting out or beginning; also, less frequently, the source, the cause, the occasion, out of which anything proceeds; — the antithesis and correlative of to; as, it, is one hundred miles from Boston to Springfield; he took his sword from his side; light proceeds from the sun; separate the coarse wool from the fine; men have all sprung from Adam, and often go from good to bad, and from bad to worse; the merit of an action depends on the principle from which it proceeds; men judge of facts from personal knowledge, or from testimony.
q: Experience from the time past to the time present.
The song began from Jove.
From high Mæonia's rocky shores I came.
If the wind blow any way from shore.
Sudden partings such as press The life from out young hearts.

From.etym: [AS. fram, from; akin to OS. fram out, OHG. & Icel. fram forward, Sw. fram, Dan. frem, Goth. fram from, prob. akin to E. forth. �202. Cf. Fro, Foremost.]

senses.d: The forehead or brow, the part of the face above the eyes; sometimes, also, the whole face.
q: Bless'd with his father's front, his mother's tongue.
Grim-visaged war hath smoothed his wrinkled front.
His front yet threatens, and his frowns command.

senses.d: The forehead, countenance, or personal presence, as expressive of character or temper, and especially, of boldness of disposition, sometimes of impudence; seeming; as, a bold front; a hardened front.
q: With smiling fronts encountering.
The inhabitants showed a bold front.

senses.d: The part or surface of anything which seems to look out, or to be directed forward; the fore or forward part; the foremost rank; the van; — the opposite to back or rear; as, the front of a house; the front of an army.
q: Had he his hurts before? Ay, on the front.

senses.d: A position directly before the face of a person, or before the foremost part of a thing; as, in front of un person, of the troops, or of a house.
The most conspicuous part.
q: The very head and front of my offending.

senses.d: That which covers the foremost part of the head: a front piece of false hair worn by women.
q: Like any plain Miss Smith's, who wears s front.

senses.d: The beginning.

Front.etym: [F. frant forehead, L. frons, frontis; perh. akin to E. brow.]

senses.d: Of or relating to the front or forward part; having a position in front; foremost; as, a front view.
To oppose face to face; to oppose directly; to meet in a hostile manner.
q: You four shall front them in the narrow lane.

senses.d: To appear before; to meet.
q: daily fronted him In some fresh splendor.

senses.d: To face toward; to have the front toward; to confront; as, the house fronts the street.
q: And then suddenly front the changed reality.

senses.d: To stand opposed or opposite to, or over against as, his house fronts the church.
To adorn in front; to supply a front to; as, to front a house with marble; to front a head with laurel.
q: Yonder walls, that pertly front your town.

senses.d: To have or turn the face or front in any direction; as, the house fronts toward the east.
All the works along one side of the polygon inclosing the site which is fortified.

The middle of the upper part of the tongue, — the part of the tongue which is more or less raised toward the palate in the pronunciation of certain sounds, as the vowel i in machine, e in bed, and consonant y in you. See Guide to Pronunciation, §10.
The call boy whose turn it is to answer the call, which is often the word “front,” used as an exclamation.

That part of a country which fronts or faces another country or an unsettled region; the marches; the border, confine, or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country; the border of the settled and cultivated part of a country; as, the frontier of civilization.
An outwork.
q: Palisadoes, frontiers, parapets.

senses.d: Lying on the exterior part; bordering; conterminous; as, a frontier town.
Of or relating to a frontier.
To constitute or form a frontier; to have a frontier; — with on.
A frontal or brow band; a fillet or band worn on the forehead.
q: They shall be as frontlets between thine eyes.

senses.d: A frown (likened to a frontlet).
q: What makes that frontlet on? Methinks you are too much of late i' the frown.

senses.d: The margin of the head, behind the bill of birds, often bearing rigid bristles.

Frontlet.etym: [OF. frontelet brow band, dim. of frontel, frontal. See Frontal, n.]

senses.d: The act of freezing; — applied chiefly to the congelation of water; congelation of fluids.
The state or temperature of the air which occasions congelation, or the freezing of water; severe cold or freezing weather.
q: The third bay comes a frost, a killing frost.

senses.d: Frozen dew; — called also hoarfrost or white frost.
q: He scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes.

senses.d: Coldness or insensibility; severity or rigidity of character.
q: It was of those moments of intense feeling when the frost of the Scottish people melts like a snow wreath.

Frost.etym: [OE. frost, forst, AS. forst, frost. fr. freósan to freeze; akin to D. varst, G., OHG., Icel., Dan., & Sw. frost. √18. See Freeze, v. i.]

senses.d: To injure by frost; to freeze, as plants.
To cover with hoarfrost; to produce a surface resembling frost upon, as upon cake, metals, or glass.
q: While with a hoary light she frosts the ground.

senses.d: To roughen or sharpen, as the nail heads or calks of horseshoes, so as to fit them for frosty weather.
Not willing to yield or compIy with what is required or is reasonable; perverse; disobedient; peevish; as, a froward child.
q: A froward man soweth strife.
A froward retention of custom is as turbulent a thing as innovation.

Froward.syn: Untoward; wayward; unyielding; ungovernable: refractory; obstinate; petulant; cross; peevish. See Perverse.

senses.d: Congealed with cold; affected by freezing; as, a frozen brook.
q: They warmed their frozen feet.

senses.d: Subject to frost, or to long and severe cold; chilly; as, the frozen north; the frozen zones.
Cold-hearted; unsympathetic; unyielding.
q: Be not ever frozen, coy.

senses.d: Whatever is produced for the nourishment or enjoyment of man or animals by the processes of vegetable growth, as corn, grass, cotton, flax, etc.; — commonly used in the plural.
q: Six years thou shalt sow thy land, and shalt gather in the fruits thereof.

senses.d: The pulpy, edible seed vessels of certain plants, especially those grown on branches above ground, as apples, oranges, grapes, melons, berries, etc. See 3.
The ripened ovary of a flowering plant, with its contents and whatever parts are consolidated with it.
The spore cases or conceptacles of flowerless plants, as of ferns, mosses, algae, etc., with the spores contained in them.
The produce of animals; offspring; young; as, the fruit of the womb, of the loins, of the body.
q: King Edward's fruit, true heir to the English crown.

senses.d: That which is produced; the effect or consequence of any action; advantageous or desirable product or result; disadvantageous or evil consequence or effect; as, the fruits of labor, of self-denial, of intemperance.
q: The fruit of rashness.
What I obtained was the fruit of no bargain.
They shall eat the fruit of their doings.
The fruits of this education became visible.

Fruit.etym: [OE. fruit, frut, F. fruit, from L. fructus enjoyment, product, fruit, from frui, p. p. fructus, to enjoy; akin to E. brook, v. t. See Brook, v. t., and cf. Fructify, Frugal.]

senses.d: To bear fruit.
Full of fruit; producing fruit abundantly; bearing results; prolific; fertile; liberal; bountiful; as, a fruitful tree, or season, or soil; a fruitful wife.
q: Be fruitful and multiply and replenish the earth.
By disburdening grows More fruitful.
The great fruitfulness of the poet's fancy.

Fruitful.syn: Fertile; prolific; productive; fecund; plentiful; rich; abundant; plenteous. See Fertile.

senses.d: Vain; ineffectual; useless; unprofitable; null; voil; nugatory; of no effect.

Frustrate.etym: [L. frustratus, p. p. of frustrare, frustrari, to deceive, frustrate, fr. frustra in vain, witout effect, in erorr, prob. for frudtra and akin to fraus, E. fraud.]

senses.d: To bring to nothing; to prevent from attaining a purpose; to disappoint; to defeat; to baffle; as, to frustrate a plan, design, or attempt; to frustrate the will or purpose.
q: Shall the adversary thus obtain His end and frustrate thine ?

senses.d: To make null; to nullifly; to render invalid or of no effect; as, to frustrate a conveyance or deed.

Frustrate.syn: To balk; thwart; foil; baffle; defeat.

senses.d: To cook in a pan or on a griddle (esp. with the use of fat, butter, or olive oil) by heating over a fire; to cook in boiling lard or fat; as, to fry fish; to fry doughnuts.

Fry.etym: [OE. frien, F. frire, fr. L. frigere to roast, parch, fry, cf. Gr. �, Skr. bhrajj. Cf. Fritter.]

senses.d: To undergo the process of frying; to be subject to the action of heat in a frying pan, or on a griddle, or in a kettle of hot fat.
To simmer; to boil.
q: With crackling flames a caldron fries.
The frothy billows fry.

senses.d: To undergo or cause a disturbing action accompanied with a sensation of heat.
q: To keep the oil from frying in the stomach.

senses.d: To be agitated; to be greatly moved.
q: What kindling motions in their breasts do fry.

senses.d: A dish of anything fried.
A state of excitement; as, to be in a fry.
The young of any fish.
A swarm or crowd, especially of little fishes; young or small things in general.
q: The fry of children young.
To sever . . . the good fish from the other fry.
We have burned two frigates, and a hundred and twenty small fry.

Fry.etym: [OE. fri, fry, seed, descendants, cf. OF. froye spawning, spawn of. fishes, little fishes, fr. L. fricare tosub (see Friction), but cf. also Icel. fræ, frjō, seed, Sw. & Dan. frö, Goth. fraiw seed, descendants.]

senses.d: Any matter used to produce heat by burning; that which feeds fire; combustible matter used for fires, as wood, coal, peat, etc.
Anything that serves to feed or increase passion or excitement.

Fuel.etym: [OF. fouail, fuail, or fouaille, fuaille, LL. focalium, focale, fr. L. focus hearth, fireplace, in LL., fire. See Focus.]

senses.d: To feed with fuel.
q: Never, alas I the dreadful name, That fuels the infernal flame.

senses.d: To store or furnish with fuel or firing.
q: Well watered and well fueled.

senses.d: Fleeing from pursuit, danger, restraint, etc., escaping, from service, duty etc.; as, a fugitive solder; a fugitive slave; a fugitive debtor.
q: The fugitive Parthians follow.
Can a fugitive daughter enjoy herself while her parents are in tear?
A libellous pamphlet of a fugitive physician.

senses.d: Not fixed; not durable; liable to disappear or fall away; volatile; uncertain; evanescent; liable to fade; — applied to material and immaterial things; as, fugitive colors; a fugitive idea.
q: The me more tender and fugitive parts, the leaves . . . of vegatables.

Fugitive.syn: Fleeting; unstable; wandering; uncertain; volatile; fugacious; fleeing; evanescent.
Fugitive.etym: [OE. fugitif, F. fugitif, fr. L. fugitivus, fr. fugere to flee. See Bow to bend, and cf. Feverfew.]

senses.d: One who flees from pursuit, danger, restraint, service, duty, etc.; a deserter; as, a fugitive from justice.
Something hard to be caught or detained.
q: Or Catch that airy fugitive called wit.

senses.d: To fill up; to make full or complete.
q: Suffer thou that the children be fulfilled first, for it is not good to take the bread of children and give to hounds.

senses.d: To accomplish or carry into effect, as an intention, promise, or prophecy, a desire, prayer, or requirement, etc.; to complete by performance; to answer the requisitions of; to bring to pass, as a purpose or design; to effectuate.
q: He will, fulfill the desire of them fear him.
Here Nature seems fulfilled in all her ends.
Servants must their masters' minds fulfill.

Fulfill.etym: [OE. fulfillen, fulfullen, AS. fulfyllan; ful full + fyllan to fill. See Full, a., and Fill, v. t.]

senses.d: Filled up, having within its limits all that it can contain; supplied; not empty or vacant; — said primarily of hollow vessels, and hence of anything else; as, a cup full of water; a house full of people.
q: Had the throne been full, their meeting would not have been regular.

senses.d: Abundantly furnished or provided; sufficient in quantity, quality, or degree; copious; plenteous; ample; adequate; as, a full meal; a full supply; a full voice; a full compensation; a house full of furniture.
Not wanting in any essential quality; complete; entire; perfect; adequate; as, a full narrative; a person of full age; a full stop; a full face; the full moon.
q: It came to pass, at the end of two full years, that Pharaoh dreamed.
The man commands Like a full soldier.
I can not Request a fuller satisfaction Than you have freely granted.

senses.d: Sated; surfeited.
q: I am full of the burnt offerings of rams.

senses.d: Having the mind filled with ideas; stocked with knowledge; stored with information.
q: Reading maketh a full man.

senses.d: Having the attention, thoughts, etc., absorbed in any matter, and the feelings more or less excited by it, as, to be full of some project.
q: Every one is full of the miracles done by cold baths on decayed and weak constitutions.

senses.d: Filled with emotions.
q: The heart is so full that a drop overfills it.

senses.d: Impregnated; made pregnant.
q: Ilia, the fair, . . . full of Mars.

Full.etym: [OE. & AS. ful; akin to OS. ful, D. vol, OHG. fol, G. voll, Icel. fullr, Sw. full, Dan. fuld, Goth. fulls, L. plenus, Gr. πλήρησ, Skr. pūṛna full, prā to fill, also to Gr. πολύσ much, E. poly-, pref., G. viel, AS. fela. √80. Cf. Complete, Fill, Plenary, Plenty.]

senses.d: Complete measure; utmost extent; the highest state or degree.
q: The swan's-down feather, That stands upon the swell at full of tide.

senses.d: Quite; to the same degree; without abatement or diminution; with the whole force or effect; thoroughly; completely; exactly; entirely.
q: The pawn I proffer shall be full as good.
The diapason closing full in man.
Full in the center of the sacred wood.

senses.d: To become full or wholly illuminated; as, the moon fulls at midnight.
To thicken by moistening, heating, and pressing, as cloth; to mill; to make compact; to scour, cleanse, and thicken in a mill.

Full.etym: [OE. fullen, OF. fuler, fouler, F. fouler, LL. fullare, fr. L. fullo fuller, cloth fuller, cf. Gr. � shining, white, AS. fullian to whiten as a fuller, to baptize, fullere a fuller. Cf. Defile to foul, Foil to frustrate, Fuller. n. ]

senses.d: To become fulled or thickened; as, this material fulls well.
One whose occupation is to full cloth.

Fuller.etym: [AS. fullere, fr. L. fullo. See Full, v. t.]

senses.d: A die; a half-round set hammer, used for forming grooves and spreading iron; — called also a creaser.
To form a groove or channel in, by a fuller or set hammer; as, to fuller a bayonet.
In a full manner or degree; completely; entirely; without lack or defect; adequately; satisfactorily; as, to be fully persuaded of the truth of a proposition.

Fully.syn: Completely; entirely; maturely; plentifully; abundantly; plenteously; copiously; largely; amply; sufficiently; clearly; distinctly; perfectly.

senses.d: To rub or scour to brightness; to clean; to burnish; as, to furbish a sword or spear.
q: Furbish new the name of John a Gaunt.

Furbish.etym: [OE. forbischen, OF. forbir, furbir, fourbir, F. fourbir, fr. OHG. furban to clean. See -ish.]

senses.d: Transported with passion or fury; raging; violent; as, a furious animal.
Rushing with impetuosity; moving with violence; as, a furious stream; a furious wind or storm.

Furious.syn: Impetuous; vehement; boisterous; fierce; turbulent; tumultuous; angry; mad; frantic; frenzied.
Furious.etym: [L. furiosus, fr. furia rage, fury: cf. F. furieux. See Fury.]

senses.d: A measure of length; the eighth part of a mile; forty rods; two hundred and twenty yards.

Furlong.etym: [OE. furlong, furlang, AS. furlang, furlung, prop., the length of a furrow; furh furrow + lang long. See Furrow, and Long, a.]

senses.d: An inclosed place in which heat is produced by the combustion of fuel, as for reducing ores or melting metals, for warming a house, for baking pottery, etc.; as, an iron furnace; a hot-air furnace; a glass furnace; a boiler furnace, etc.
A place or time of punishment, affiction, or great trial; severe experience or discipline.

Furnace.etym: [OE. fornais, forneis, OF. fornaise, F. fournaise, from L. fornax; akin to furnus oven, and prob. to E. forceps.]

senses.d: To throw out, or exhale, as from a furnace; also, to put into a furnace.
q: He furnaces The thick sighs from him.

senses.d: To supply with anything necessary, useful, or appropriate; to provide; to equip; to fit out, or fit up; to adorn; as, to furnish a family with provisions; to furnish one with arms for defense; to furnish a Cable; to furnish the mind with ideas; to furnish one with knowledge or principles; to furnish an expedition or enterprise, a room or a house.
q: That the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works.

senses.d: To offer for use; to provide (something); to give (something); to afford; as, to furnish food to the hungry: to furnish arms for defense.
q: Ye are they . . . that furnish the drink offering unto that number.
His writings and his life furnish abundant proofs that he was not a man of strong sense.

Furnish.etym: [OF. furnir, fornir, to furnish, finish, F. fournir; akin to Pr. formir, furmir, fromir, to accomplish, satisfy, fr. OHG. frumjan to further, execute, do, akin to E. frame. See Frame, v. t., and -ish.]

senses.d: That which is furnished as a specimen; a sample; a supply.
That with which anything is furnished or supplied; supplies; outfit; equipment.
q: The form and all the furniture of the earth.
The thoughts which make the furniture of their minds.

senses.d: Articles used for convenience or decoration in a house or apartment, as tables, chairs, bedsteads, sofas, carpets, curtains, pictures, vases, etc.
The necessary appendages to anything, as to a machine, a carriage, a ship, etc.
A mixed or compound stop in an organ; — sometimes called mixture.
A trench in the earth made by, or as by, a plow.
Any trench, channel, or groove, as in wood or metal; a wrinkle on the face; as, the furrows of age.

Furrow.etym: [OE. forow, forgh, furgh, AS. furh; akin to D. voor, OHG. furuh, G. furche, Dan. fure, Sw. f�ra, Icel. for drain, L. porca ridge between two furrows.]

senses.d: To cut a furrow in; to make furrows in; to plow; as, to furrow the ground or sea.
To mark with channels or with wrinkles.
q: Thou canst help time to furrow me with age.
Fair cheeks were furrowed with hot tears.

senses.d: To a greater distance; in addition; moreover. See Farther.
q: Carries us, I know not how much further, into familiar company.
They sdvanced us far as Eleusis and Thria; but no further.

Further.etym: [A comparative of forth; OE. further, forther, AS. fur�or, far�ur; akin to G. fürder. See Forth, adv.]

senses.d: More remote; at a greater distance; more in advance; farther; as, the further end of the field. See Farther.
Beyond; additional; as, a further reason for this opinion; nothing further to suggest.
To help forward; to promote; to advance; to forward; to help or assist.
q: This binds thee, then, to further my design.
I should nothing further the weal public.

Further.etym: [OE. furthren, forthren, AS. fyrðran, fyrðrian. See Further, adv.]

senses.d: The act of furthering or helping forward; promotion; advancement; progress.
q: I know that I shall abide and continue with you all for your furthersnce and joy of faith.
Built of furtherance and pursuing, Not of spent deeds, but of doing.

senses.d: or conj. Moreover; besides; in addition to what has been said.
A thief.
q: Have an eye to your plate, for there be furies.

senses.d: Violent or extreme excitement; overmastering agitation or enthusiasm.
q: Her wit began to be with a divine fury inspired.

senses.d: Violent anger; extreme wrath; rage; — sometimes applied to inanimate things, as the wind or storms; impetuosity; violence.
q: I do oppose my patience to his fury.

senses.d: pl. (Greek Myth.) The avenging deities, Tisiphone, Alecto, and Megæra; the Erinyes or Eumenides.
q: The Furies, they said, are attendants on justice, and if the sun in heaven should transgress his path would punish him.

senses.d: One of the Parcæ, or Fates, esp. Atropos.
q: Comes the blind Fury with the abhorred shears, And slits the thin-spun life.

senses.d: A stormy, turbulent violent woman; a hag; a vixen; a virago; a termagant.

Fury.syn: Anger; indignation; resentment; wrath; ire; rage; vehemence; violence; fierceness; turbulence; madness; frenzy. See Anger.
Fury.etym: [L. furia, fr. furere to rage: cf. F. furie. Cf. Furor.]

senses.d: A word which expresses blame, dislike, disapprobation, abhorrence, or contempt. See Fie.
